parts.latex:
A population, $P$, which is initially 5000, varies according to the formula

$$P=5000b^{\frac{-t}{10}},$$

where $b$ is a positive constant and $t$ is time in years, $t\ge 0$.

The population is 1250 after 20 years.

Find the value of $t$, correct to one decimal place, for which the instantaneous rate of decrease is 30 people per year.

solutions.latex:
$$P = 5000b^{-\frac{t}{10}}$$
When $t = 20$, $P = 1250$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1250 &= 5000\,b^{-2} \\ b^{-2} &= \dfrac{1}{4} \\ b &= 2 \quad (b > 0) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P = 5000(2)^{-\frac{t}{10}}$$
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 5000\times\ln 2\times\dfrac{-1}{10}\times 2^{\frac{-t}{10}}$$
Find $t$ when $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = -30$:
$$\begin{aligned} -30 &= -500\times\ln 2\times 2^{\frac{-t}{10}} \\ 2^{\frac{t}{10}} &= \dfrac{500\ln 2}{30} \\ 2^{\frac{t}{10}} &= 11.55\ldots \\ \dfrac{t}{10}\ln 2 &= \ln 11.55\ldots \\ t &= 35.3 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Equates $-30$ to a correct derivative, with $b = 2$, or equivalent merit
Finds $b$ and provides correct derivative, or equivalent merit
Provides correct derivative, or equivalent merit

130.stem:
Kenzo has a solar powered phone charger. Its power, $P$, can be modelled by the function

$$P(t)=400\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right),\ 0\le t\le 12,$$

where $t$ is the number of hours after sunrise.

parts.latex: Sketch the graph of $P$ for $0\le t\le 12$.

Power is the rate of change of energy. Hence the amount of energy, $E$ units, generated by the solar powered phone charger from $t=a$ to $t=b$, where $0\le a\le b\le 12$ is given by

$$E=\int_a^b P(t)\,dt.$$

Show that $E=\dfrac{4800}{\pi}\left(\cos\dfrac{a\pi}{12}-\cos\dfrac{b\pi}{12}\right)$.

To make a phone call, a phone battery needs at least 300 units of energy. Kenzo woke up 3 hours after sunrise and found that his phone battery had no units of energy. He immediately began to use his solar powered charger to charge his phone battery.

Find the least amount of time he needed to wait before he could make a phone call. Give your answer correct to the nearest minute.

Rates of change using integration.reason: Reuses E formula from part (b) ('Substitutes into E given in part (b)'); no integration here

parts.latex:
The next day, Kenzo woke up 6 hours after sunrise and again found that his phone battery had no units of energy. He immediately began to use his solar powered charger to charge his phone battery.

Would it take more time or less time or the same amount of time, compared to the answer in part (c), to charge his phone battery in order to make a phone call? Explain your answer by referring to the graph drawn in part (a).

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Period} &= \dfrac{2\pi}{\frac{\pi}{12}} \\ &= 24 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{226_q27_1}
criteria: Provides a sine graph with the correct amplitude, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} E &= \int_a^b P(t)\,dt \\ &= \int_a^b 400\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)dt \\ &= -\dfrac{400(12)}{\pi}\left[\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)\right]_a^b \\ &= -\dfrac{4800}{\pi}\left(\cos\dfrac{b\pi}{12} - \cos\dfrac{a\pi}{12}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{4800}{\pi}\left(\cos\dfrac{a\pi}{12} - \cos\dfrac{b\pi}{12}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Provides correct anti-derivative of $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} 300 &= \dfrac{4800}{\pi}\left(\cos\dfrac{3\pi}{12} - \cos\dfrac{b\pi}{12}\right) \\ \dfrac{\pi}{16} &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \cos\dfrac{b\pi}{12} \\ \cos\dfrac{b\pi}{12} &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{\pi}{16} \\ b &= \dfrac{12}{\pi}\cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{\pi}{16}\right) \\ b &= 3.95 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ He needs to wait $0.95\times 60 = 57$ minutes (to the nearest minute).
criteria: Calculates the value of $b$, or equivalent merit
Substitutes into $E$ given in part (b), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
It would take less time to charge his phone battery.

By starting to charge the battery six hours after sunrise, he is charging the phone at the time when the power is greatest.

157.stem:
A scientist is studying the growth of bacteria. The scientist models the number of bacteria, $N$, by the equation

$$N(t)=200e^{0.013t},$$

where $t$ is the number of hours after starting the experiment.

parts.latex: What is the initial number of bacteria in the experiment?
What is the number of bacteria 24 hours after starting the experiment?
What is the rate of increase in the number of bacteria 24 hours after starting the experiment?

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} N(0) &= 200e^{0} \\ &= 200 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} N(24) &= 200e^{0.013 \times 24} \\ &= 273.23\ldots \\ &\approx 273 \text{ bacteria} \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dN}{dt} = 200 \times 0.013 \times e^{0.013t}$$
When $t = 24$,
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dN}{dt} &= 0.013 \times 273 \quad \text{(from part (b))} \\ &= 3.55 \end{aligned}$$
Rate of increase $= 3.55$ bacteria/hour.

254.stem:
Recycled plastic materials can contain bacteria from previous usage. To ensure the plastic is clean and safe for recycling, it is heated to $135^\circ\text{C}$ for a certain period to kill the bacteria present.

The number of bacteria $N$ in the plastic after $t$ minutes at $135^\circ\text{C}$ is given by:
$$N(t)=4800e^{-0.3t}, \quad t\ge 0$$

parts.latex: Find the initial number of bacteria present in the plastic.
Find the time in minutes to kill 50% of the bacteria. Give your answer correct to the nearest second.
Find the rate of decrease of the bacteria after 5 minutes. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

solutions.latex:
$$N(t) = 50\%\times 4800 = 2400$$
$$\begin{aligned} 4800e^{-0.3t} &= 2400 \\ e^{-0.3t} &= 0.5 \\ -0.3t &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \\ t &= -\dfrac{\ln(0.5)}{0.3} \\ &= 2.310\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ t \approx 2$ minutes $19$ seconds.

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dN}{dt} &= 4800(-0.3)e^{-0.3t} \\ &= -1440e^{-0.3t} \end{aligned}$$
When $t = 5$ min:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dN}{dt} &= -1440\times e^{-1.5} \\ &\approx -321 \text{ bacteria/min} \end{aligned}$$
The number decreases at $321$ bacteria/min.

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

257.stem:
A particle moves in a straight line with acceleration $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=1-2t$, for $0\le t\le 2$.

The particle was initially at rest at the origin.

parts.latex: Determine $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ as a function of $t$.
Sketch the graph of $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ for $0\le t\le 2$ below, showing any stationary points, end points and intercepts with the axes.
Find the distance travelled over the first two seconds.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= \int (1 - 2t)\,dt \\ &= t - t^2 + C \end{aligned}$$
When $t = 0$, $\dfrac{dx}{dt} = C = 0$.
$$\therefore\ \dfrac{dx}{dt} = t - t^2$$
\exfigure{408_q25_s1}

meta.top_criterion_original: Stationary point, end points and intercepts all correct

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} x_1 &= \int_0^1 \left(t - t^2\right)dt \\ &= \left[\dfrac{t^2}{2} - \dfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^1 \\ &= \dfrac{1}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x_2 &= \int_1^2 \left(t - t^2\right)dt \\ &= \left[\dfrac{t^2}{2} - \dfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_1^2 \\ &= \left(\dfrac{4}{2} - \dfrac{8}{3}\right) - \left(\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3}\right) \\ &= -\dfrac{5}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \therefore\ \text{Total distance} &= \dfrac{1}{6} + \left|-\dfrac{5}{6}\right| \\ &= 1 \end{aligned}$$

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

parts.latex:
A particle $P$ moves along a straight line such that its acceleration with respect to time is given by $a=-2t+3$, where $a$ is the acceleration of the particle at time $t$ seconds for $t\ge 0$.

The particle is at rest when $t=1$ and $t=2$.

Which of the following graphs best represents the displacement of the particle?

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration:
$$v = \int(-2t+3)\,dt = -t^2 + 3t + C$$
The particle is at rest at $t = 1$ and $t = 2$, so $v = 0$ there:
$$\begin{aligned} -1 + 3 + C &= 0 \\ C &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
Hence
$$v = -t^2 + 3t - 2 = -(t-1)(t-2)$$
Sign of $v$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &< 0 &&\text{for } 0 \le t < 1 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\\ v &> 0 &&\text{for } 1 < t < 2 &&\text{displacement increasing}\\ v &< 0 &&\text{for } t > 2 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\end{aligned}$$
So the displacement has a local minimum at $t = 1$ and a local maximum at $t = 2$.

Graph A is the only graph with a minimum at $t = 1$, a maximum at $t = 2$ and decreasing afterwards. (Graph B has the turning points the wrong way round; C and D do not have stationary points at both $t = 1$ and $t = 2$.)

parts.latex:
The rate of fuel consumption of a particular vehicle may be modelled by the formula

$$R=5+4e^{-0.5t},$$

where $R$ is the rate of fuel consumption, in litres per hour, after $t$ hours of travel.

In the first hour of travel, the vehicle consumed 25 litres of fuel.

Determine the amount of fuel consumed after 4 hours of travel, correct to the nearest litre.

solutions.latex:
The amount of fuel, $F(t)$ litres, consumed at time $t$ hours is given by
$$\begin{aligned} F(t) &= \int R\,dt \\ &= \int 5+4e^{-0.5t}\,dt \\ &= 5t-8e^{-0.5t}+c \end{aligned}$$

At time $t=1$, the vehicle has consumed 25 litres of fuel since the start of the journey.

Finding the constant of integration, $c$:
$$\begin{aligned} 25 &= 5(1)-8e^{-0.5(1)}+c \\ 20 &= -8e^{-0.5}+c \\ c &= 20+8e^{-0.5} \end{aligned}$$

At time $t=4$, the amount of fuel the vehicle consumed is given by
$$\begin{aligned} F &= 5(4)-8e^{-0.5(4)}+20+8e^{-0.5} \\ &= 43.7695\ldots \end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ After 4 hours of travel, the vehicle has consumed 44 litres of fuel.
criteria: Finds the value of the constant of integration, or equivalent merit
Correctly integrates expression representing rate of fuel consumption, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Water is flowing out of a pool at a rate given by $R=4t-t^2$ cubic metres/minute.

If the volume of water in the pool is initially 20 cubic metres, find the amount of the water in the pool after 4 minutes.

solutions.latex:
Let $V$ be the volume of water in m$^3$. Water flows out, so
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-(4t-t^2)$$
Volume that flows out in the first $4$ minutes:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^4(4t-t^2)\,dt&=\left[2t^2-\dfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^4\\ &=32-\dfrac{64}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{32}{3}\text{ m}^3\end{aligned}$$
Volume left after $4$ minutes:
$$\begin{aligned}V(4)&=20-\dfrac{32}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{28}{3}\approx9.33\text{ m}^3\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the volume lost, $\dfrac{32}{3}\text{ m}^3$, or equivalent merit
Forms $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-(4t-t^2)$ and integrates, or equivalent merit

meta.concern: The question looks flawed: the outflow over 4 minutes (32/3 m^3) is more than the initial 10 m^3, so the literal answer is negative. The wording is also cut off ('minut'). The intended answer is probably either 'empty' or 62/3 m^3 (if the water flows in). Needs human review.
meta.top_criterion_original: $V(4) = 10 - \dfrac{32}{3}$ (negative, so the pool is empty by $t = 4$)
meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

314.stem:
The velocity of a particle is given by $v=2\sin\left(t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ metres per second.

Find:

figures.cap: blank v vs t axes for answer

parts.latex: the equation of the displacement $x$ of the particle as a function of time if the particle is initially at the origin.
when the particle comes to rest for first time.
the exact initial velocity.
the maximum speed of the particle.
Using your graph above or otherwise, find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first $\pi$ seconds.

solutions.latex:
$$x = \int 2\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)dt = -2\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + C$$
When $t = 0$, $x = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -2\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + C \\ 0 &= -2\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} + C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = 1 - 2\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
At rest means $v = 0$: $\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 0$, so $t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = 0, \pi, \dots$

$\therefore$ The first time with $t \ge 0$ is $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ seconds.
$$\begin{aligned} v(0) &= 2\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= 2\left(-\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ &= -\sqrt{3} \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

$v=2\sin\left(t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$. Start from the range of sine:
$$\begin{aligned} -1&\le \sin\left(t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\le 1\\ -2&\le v\le 2 &&(\text{multiply by } 2)\end{aligned}$$

$\therefore$ The maximum speed is $|v|_{\max} = 2$ m/s. (It occurs, for example, at $t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$.)

$v = 2\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ is the graph of $y = 2\sin t$ shifted $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ to the right. It has amplitude $2$ and period $2\pi$.

\exfigure{568_q15_s1}
criteria: Shows the intercepts $(0,-\sqrt{3})$, $\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, $\dfrac{4\pi}{3}$, or equivalent merit
Draws the correct shape (shifted sine, amplitude $2$) over $[0,2\pi]$, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$, so split the time interval there. Using $x = 1 - 2\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ from (i):
$$x(0) = 0, \qquad x\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 1 - 2\cos 0 = -1, \qquad x(\pi) = 1 - 2\cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = 1 + 1 = 2$$
Distance for $0 \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{3}$: $|-1 - 0| = 1$ m.

Distance for $\dfrac{\pi}{3} \le t \le \pi$: $|2 - (-1)| = 3$ m.

$\therefore$ Total distance $= 1 + 3 = 4$ m.
criteria: Splits at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ (change of direction) and finds the displacements, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

32.stem:
A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line, velocity $v\text{ ms}^{-1}$ and acceleration $a=2e^{-t}\text{ ms}^{-2}$.

Initially it is 2 metres to the right of $O$ and is moving towards $O$ with speed $1\text{ ms}^{-1}$.

parts.latex: Show that $v=1-2e^{-t}$ and $x=t+2e^{-t}$.
Find in simplest exact form when and where the particle is at rest.
Find in simplest exact form the distance travelled by the particle in the first $\ln 8$ seconds of its motion.

solutions.latex:
$a=2e^{-t}$

$v=-2e^{-t}+c$

When $t=0$, $v=-1$, so $-1=-2+c$.

$\therefore\ c=1$

$\therefore\ v=1-2e^{-t}$

$x=t+2e^{-t}+d$

When $t=0$, $x=2$, so $2=2+d$.

$\therefore\ d=0$

$\therefore\ x=t+2e^{-t}$
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds $v$ in terms of $t$

meta.top_criterion_original: Uses integration to find required expressions for both $v$ and $x$ in terms of $t$

solutions.latex:
When $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^{-t}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ e^t&=2\\ \therefore\ t&=\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}x&=t+2e^{-t}\\ &=\ln 2+2\times\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\ &=1+\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
At rest $(1+\ln 2)$ m to the right of $O$ at time $\ln 2$ seconds.
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds time when particle at rest

meta.top_criterion_original: Finds time and position when particle at rest

solutions.latex:
When $t=\ln 8$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\ln 8+2e^{\ln\frac{1}{8}}\\ &=3\ln 2+\dfrac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$$
Hence in the first $\ln 8$ seconds:

the particle travels left $2-(1+\ln 2)$ metres,

then is instantaneously at rest before moving off to the right (since $a>0$),

travelling a further $\left(3\ln 2+\dfrac{1}{4}\right)-(1+\ln 2)$ metres.

Required distance is $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}+\ln 2\right)$ metres.
criteria: Substantial progress, e.g. finds simplified expression for $x$ when $t=\ln 8$

meta.top_criterion_original: Adds distances travelled left and right in the first $\ln 8$ seconds

where $R$ is the rate of fuel consumption, in litres per hour, after $t$ hours of travel.

551.stem:
Radioactive cobalt-60 decays to become nickel-60. A 1000 g block of radioactive cobalt-60 is placed in a container.

After a period of 10.54 years, $75\%$ of the cobalt-60 has decayed to become nickel-60.

The decay process can be modelled by the exponential relationship

$$A=1000e^{kt}$$

where $A$ is the amount of cobalt-60 remaining (in grams) at time $t$ (in years).

parts.latex: Find the value of $k$, correct to 4 decimal places.
Find the value of $t$ when the rate of change of $A$ is $-9.48$ g/year, correct to the nearest year.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $A=1000e^{kt}$:
$$\dfrac{dA}{dt}=1000ke^{kt}$$
Setting $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=-9.48$ with $k=-0.1315$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000(-0.1315)e^{-0.1315t}&=-9.48\\ e^{-0.1315t}&=\dfrac{9.48}{131.5}\\ -0.1315t&=\ln\left(\dfrac{9.48}{131.5}\right)\\ t&\approx20.0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx20 \text{ years}$$
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{dA}{dt}=1000ke^{kt}$ and equates it to $-9.48$, or equivalent merit

meta.check: Solved with rounded and unrounded k: t = 19.9987 and 19.9961, both 20.

553.stem:
The velocity, $v$ m/s, of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the function

$$v(t)=1-e^{\cos(\pi t)}$$

where $0\le t\le 1.25$ is the time in seconds. The graph of $v(t)$ is shown.

\exfigure{1632_q26_1}

figures.cap: velocity-time graph v(t) for 0<=t<=1.25

parts.latex: At what value(s) of $t$ does the particle change direction in this interval?

Trigonometric equations.evidence: cos(pi t) = 0, pi t = pi/2 (0<=pi t<=1.25pi)
Trigonometric equations.reason: Solving cos of linear argument on restricted domain.

Exponential equations.reason: Unknown in an index solved by equal bases / logs.

parts.latex: Find the acceleration of the particle when $t=0.5$.

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when $v$ changes sign.
$$\begin{aligned} 1-e^{\cos(\pi t)}&=0\\ e^{\cos(\pi t)}&=1\\ \cos(\pi t)&=0\\ \pi t&=\dfrac{\pi}{2} &&(0\le\pi t\le1.25\pi)\\ t&=0.5\end{aligned}$$
The graph crosses the $t$-axis there ($v<0$ before, $v>0$ after).
$$\therefore\ t=0.5$$

meta.check: Graph crosses at 0.5; cos(pi t)=0 has no other solution in [0,1.25pi].

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$. Using the chain rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}e^{f(t)}=f'(t)e^{f(t)}$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\dfrac{dv}{dt}\\ &=-\big(-\pi\sin(\pi t)\big)e^{\cos(\pi t)}\\ &=\pi\sin(\pi t)\,e^{\cos(\pi t)}\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0.5$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\pi\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)e^{\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}\\ &=\pi\times1\times e^0\\ &=\pi \text{ m/s}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=\pi\sin(\pi t)\,e^{\cos(\pi t)}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Distance is the area between the graph and the $t$-axis, so use $|v|$ ($v\le0$ for $0\le t\le0.5$ and $v\ge0$ for $0.5\le t\le1$):
$$\text{distance}=\int_0^1|v|\,dt$$
Four subintervals of $[0,1]$: $h=\dfrac{1-0}{4}=0.25$, with $t=0,\ 0.25,\ 0.5,\ 0.75,\ 1$ as in the table.

Trapezoidal rule:
$$\int_a^b f(t)\,dt\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\big[f(t_0)+2\big(f(t_1)+f(t_2)+f(t_3)\big)+f(t_4)\big]$$
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1|v|\,dt&\approx\dfrac{0.25}{2}\big[1.72+2(1.03+0+0.51)+0.63\big]\\ &=0.125\times5.43\\ &=0.67875\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{distance}\approx0.68 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Applies the trapezoidal rule with $h=0.25$ to the table values (e.g. finds the displacement), or equivalent merit

meta.check: Hand sum 5.43 x 0.125; exact integral of |v| is 0.710, so the estimate is reasonable.
meta.concern: Distance (not displacement) needs |v|; since v=0 at the node t=0.5, applying the rule to |v| equals splitting at t=0.5. Rounding of final answer (0.68 vs 0.679) not specified.

616.stem: The population of two towns Melbtown and Brisbay are given by $P_M=1200e^{0.04t}$ and $P_B=1500e^{0.025t}$ respectively, where $t$ is the number of years elapsed since January 2010.

parts.latex: In which year will the population of Melbtown exceed 1500?
In which year will the rate of growth of the population in Melbtown be double the rate of growth of Brisbay?

solutions.latex:
The population of Melbtown exceeds 1500 when
$$\begin{aligned}1200e^{0.04t}&>1500\\ e^{0.04t}&>\dfrac{5}{4}\\ 0.04t&>\ln\left(\dfrac{5}{4}\right)\\ t&>5.57\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$t$ is measured from January 2010, so $t=5.57\ldots$ is during 2015.

$\therefore$ In 2015 the population will exceed 1500.

meta.concern: transcribed from handwritten solutions on scanned pages (no text layer); marking guideline gives no mark criteria; criteria written to house style

solutions.latex:
Differentiate each population:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dP_M}{dt}&=0.04\times 1200e^{0.04t}\\ &=48e^{0.04t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dP_B}{dt}&=0.025\times 1500e^{0.025t}\\ &=37.5e^{0.025t}\end{aligned}$$
Find $t$ when $\dfrac{dP_M}{dt}=2\dfrac{dP_B}{dt}$:
$$\begin{aligned}48e^{0.04t}&=75e^{0.025t}\\ e^{(0.04-0.025)t}&=\dfrac{75}{48}\\ e^{0.015t}&=1.5625\\ 0.015t&=\ln(1.5625)\\ t&=\dfrac{1}{0.015}\ln(1.5625)\\ &=29.75247\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$t$ is measured from January 2010, so $t=29.75\ldots$ is during 2039.

$\therefore$ During 2039 the rate of growth of Melbtown will be double that of Brisbay.

645.stem: The acceleration of a particle is given by $a=5e^{-2t}$. Initially the particle is at rest.

figures.cap: blank v-t axes
solution sketch: velocity curve from origin approaching asymptote v=2.5

parts.latex: Write an equation for the velocity.
Explain why the particle is always speeding up for $t>0$.

On the number plane below, sketch the graph of the particle's velocity as a function of time.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration to find the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=\int 5e^{-2t}\,dt\\&=-\dfrac{5}{2}e^{-2t}+c\end{aligned}$$
The particle is initially at rest, so $v=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=-\dfrac{5}{2}e^{-2(0)}+c\\c&=\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ v=-\dfrac{5}{2}e^{-2t}+\dfrac{5}{2}$$

$a=5e^{-2t}>0$ for all $t$, since $e^{-2t}>0$.

For $t>0$, $e^{-2t}<1$, so $v=\dfrac{5}{2}\left(1-e^{-2t}\right)>0$.

Velocity and acceleration are both positive for $t>0$, so the particle is always speeding up.

When $t=40$:
$$\begin{aligned} V &= 300\times 40-3.75\times 40^2+350\\ &= 6350 \text{ L}\end{aligned}$$

588.stem: The mass of a decaying radioactive substance, in kg, at time $t$ years is given by $M=2e^{-kt}$, where $k$ is a positive constant.

parts.latex: State the initial mass of the radioactive substance.
Find the half-life of the radioactive substance. Give your answer as an exact value in terms of $k$.
Find $\dfrac{dM}{dt}$.

A biomaterial is also decaying simultaneously, but at every instance in time its rate of decay is twice as fast as the radioactive substance. Find an expression for the mass of the biomaterial, in terms of $k$ and $t$, given that its initial mass is $3$ kg.

solutions.latex: $2\text{ kg}$

Half-life: the mass halves to $1$ kg:
$$\begin{aligned} 1&=2e^{-kt} \\ e^{kt}&=2 \\ kt&=\ln 2 \\ t&=\dfrac{1}{k}\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
$\dfrac{dM}{dt}=-2ke^{-kt}$

The biomaterial decays twice as fast, so $\dfrac{dB}{dt}=2\times\dfrac{dM}{dt}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dB}{dt}&=-4ke^{-kt} \\ B&=\int -4ke^{-kt}\,dt \\ &=4e^{-kt}+C \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $B=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3&=4+C \\ C&=-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ B=4e^{-kt}-1$$

589.stem:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis. Its velocity in metres per second, at time $t$ seconds, is given by

$$v=\dfrac{2}{t+1}-1.$$

parts.latex: Find the time at which the particle is stationary.
Find the acceleration of the particle when it is stationary.
The total distance travelled by the particle in the first two seconds is $\ln b$ metres, for some constant $b>0$. Find the value of $b$.

solutions.latex:
Stationary when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2}{t+1}-1&=0 \\ \dfrac{2}{t+1}&=1 \\ 2&=t+1 \\ t&=1\text{ second} \end{aligned}$$

Acceleration $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$, with $v=2(t+1)^{-1}-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} a&=-2(t+1)^{-2} \\ &=-\dfrac{2}{(t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
At $t=1$ (from part (a)):
$$a(1)=-\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ ms}^{-2}$$

$a<0$ for all $t$ and $v=0$ at $t=1$, so
$$\begin{aligned} v&>0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<1 &&\text{moving right} \\ v&<0 &&\text{for } 1<t\le 2 &&\text{moving left} \end{aligned}$$
Distance in the first second:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^1\left(\dfrac{2}{t+1}-1\right)dt&=\Big[2\ln|t+1|-t\Big]_0^1 \\ &=2\ln 2-1 \end{aligned}$$
Distance in the next second (velocity negative):
$$\begin{aligned} \Big[t-2\ln|t+1|\Big]_1^2&=2-2\ln 3-(1-2\ln 2) \\ &=1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
Total distance:
$$\begin{aligned} 2\ln 2-1+1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2&=4\ln 2-2\ln 3 \\ &=\ln 2^4-\ln 3^2 \\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{16}{9}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ b=\dfrac{16}{9}$$
criteria: Finds both distances, $2\ln 2-1$ for $0\le t\le 1$ and $1-2\ln 3+2\ln 2$ for $1\le t\le 2$, or equivalent merit
Finds the distance $2\ln 2-1$ for $0\le t\le 1$, or equivalent merit

673.stem:
A particle moves along the $x$ axis with a displacement at time $t$ seconds given by

$$x=\dfrac{32}{(t+1)^2}+t-12$$

parts.latex: Where is the particle initially?

Find the total distance the particle travels in the first 5 seconds.

When $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\dfrac{32}{(0+1)^2}+0-12\\ &=20 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ initially the particle is 20 m to the right of the origin.

$$\begin{aligned} v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}&=(-2)(32)(1)(t+1)^{-3}+1\\ &=-\dfrac{64}{(t+1)^3}+1 \end{aligned}$$
At rest, $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=-\dfrac{64}{(t+1)^3}+1\\ (t+1)^3&=64\\ t+1&=4\\ t&=3 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle comes to rest when $t=3$.

797.stem: The velocity of a particle is given by $\dot{x}(t)=8t^3e^{t^4}$, where $\dot{x}(t)$ is velocity in metres per second and $t$ is time in seconds. Initially, the particle is at the origin.

parts.latex: Determine the times(s) the particle is at rest.
Show that the displacement function is $x(t)=2e^{t^4}-2$.
At what time does the particle reach a displacement of 100 metres? (Give your answer to 2 d.p.)

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$8t^3e^{t^4}=0$$
$e^{t^4}>0$ for all $t$, so $t^3=0$.
$$\therefore\ t=0$$

Displacement is the integral of velocity. The derivative of $t^4$ is $4t^3$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int 8t^3e^{t^4}\,dt\\ &= 2\int 4t^3e^{t^4}\,dt\\ &= 2e^{t^4}+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially the particle is at the origin: when $t=0$, $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2e^0+C &= 0\\ C &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x(t)=2e^{t^4}-2$$

solutions.latex:
Let $x(t)=100$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2e^{t^4}-2 &= 100\\ e^{t^4} &= 51\\ t^4 &= \ln 51\\ t &\approx 1.41 \text{ s} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A population of insects varies according to the formula $P = 3000n^{\frac{t}{10}}$, where $n$ is a positive constant and $t$ is the time in days.

The initial population was 3000. After 20 days the population had grown to 12 000.

Find the value of $t$, correct to one decimal place, for which the instantaneous rate of increase is 6000 insects per day.

solutions.latex:
Initially $P=3000$; after 20 days $P=12\,000$. Find $n$:
$$\begin{aligned} 12000 &= 3000n^{\frac{20}{10}} \\ n^2 &= 4 \\ n &= \pm 2 \end{aligned}$$
$n > 0$, so $n = 2$ and $P=3000\times 2^{\frac{t}{10}}$.

Using
$$\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{kt}\right)=k\ln a\cdot a^{kt}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 3000 \times \ln 2 \times \dfrac{1}{10} \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \\ &= 300\ln 2 \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \end{aligned}$$
Set $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 6000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6000 &= 300\ln 2 \times 2^{\frac{t}{10}} \\ 2^{\frac{t}{10}} &= \dfrac{20}{\ln 2} \\ \dfrac{t}{10} &= \log_2\left(\dfrac{20}{\ln 2}\right) \\ &= \log_2 20 - \log_2(\ln 2) \\ t &= 10\left(\dfrac{\ln 20}{\ln 2} - \dfrac{\ln(\ln 2)}{\ln 2}\right) \\ &\approx 48.5 \text{ days} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Three of: finds $n$, finds $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$, substitutes 6000 into $\dfrac{dP}{dt}$, calculates $t$ (or 1 error), or equivalent merit
Two of the above (or 2 errors), or equivalent merit
One of the above, or equivalent merit

861.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v(t)=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ metres per second. The particle starts at $O$.

parts.latex: Show that $x(t)=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$.
Find when and where the particle is at rest in relation to the fixed point $O$.
Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 24 seconds.

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} v(t)&=3\sqrt{t+1}-9\\ &=3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9\\ x(t)&=\int\left(3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9\right)dt\\ &=\dfrac{3(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+C\\ &=2\sqrt{(t+1)^3}-9t+C\\ &=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t+C \end{aligned}$$
The particle starts at $O$, so $x=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=2(1)\sqrt{1}-9(0)+C\\ \therefore\ C&=-2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x(t)=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2 \text{ as required}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates $v(t)$ but does not evaluate the constant of integration or makes an error, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides correct solution with appropriate and logical steps shown

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{t+1}-9&=0\\ \sqrt{t+1}&=3\\ t+1&=9\\ \therefore\ t&=8 \end{aligned}$$
Using part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} x(8)&=2(8+1)\sqrt{8+1}-9(8)-2\\ &=-20 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The particle is at rest after 8 seconds, 20 m from $O$ in the initial direction of motion.
criteria: Finds when the particle is at rest, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides correct solution, accept 20 m away from the origin
meta.marker_note: Accept 20 m away from the origin.

solutions.latex:
Using part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} x(24)&=2(25)\sqrt{25}-9(24)-2\\ &=32 \end{aligned}$$
The particle travels from $x=0$ to $x=-20$ (at rest at $t=8$), then to $x=32$ in the first 24 seconds.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance}&=20+20+32\\ &=72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

899.stem:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis such that at a time $t$ seconds its displacement from the origin is $x$ metres. The acceleration of the particle is given by $a=\dfrac{8}{e^{2t}}+\dfrac{3}{e^t}$.

Initially its velocity is $-6$ m/s and its displacement is 5 m.

parts.latex: Find the equation for the displacement ($x$) of the particle in terms of $t$.
At what time and where does the particle come to rest?

Displacement, velocity and acceleration.reason: v and x were found in part (a); this part solves v=0 and evaluates x, covered by agreed skills.

e and natural logarithms.reason: ln step is part of the agreed Exponential equations; x evaluated to decimals, e^{ln} property not needed.

solutions.latex:
$$a=8e^{-2t}+3e^{-t}$$
Integrating to find the velocity:
$$v=\dfrac{8e^{-2t}}{-2}+\dfrac{3e^{-t}}{-1}+c$$
When $t=0$, $v=-6$:
$$\begin{aligned} -6&=-4e^0-3e^0+c\\ -6&=-7+c\\ c&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$v=-4e^{-2t}-3e^{-t}+1$$
Integrating again:
$$x=\dfrac{-4e^{-2t}}{-2}-\dfrac{3e^{-t}}{-1}+t+k$$
When $t=0$, $x=5$:
$$\begin{aligned} 5&=2e^0+3e^0+0+k\\ 5&=5+k\\ k&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x&=2e^{-2t}+3e^{-t}+t\\ &=\dfrac{2}{e^{2t}}+\dfrac{3}{e^t}+t \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct velocity, or equivalent merit

meta.rubric_note: Rewritten top-down from a one-mark-per-step rubric (owner rule, 11 Nov).

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=-4e^{-2t}-3e^{-t}+1\\ 0&=4e^{-2t}+3e^{-t}-1\\ &=4(e^{-t})^2+3e^{-t}-1 \end{aligned}$$
Let $m=e^{-t}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=4m^2+3m-1\\ &=(4m-1)(m+1)\\ m&=\dfrac{1}{4} \text{ or } m=-1 \end{aligned}$$
$e^{-t}=-1$ has no solution, since $e^{-t}>0$.
$$\begin{aligned} e^{-t}&=\dfrac{1}{4}\\ \ln e^{-t}&=\ln\dfrac{1}{4}\\ -t&=\ln 4^{-1}=-\ln 4\\ t&=\ln 4=1.386294361 \end{aligned}$$
When $t=\ln 4$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=2e^{-2\ln 4}+3e^{-\ln 4}+\ln 4\\ &=2e^{\ln 4^{-2}}+3e^{\ln 4^{-1}}+\ln 4\\ &=2\times 4^{-2}+3\times 4^{-1}+\ln 4\\ &=\dfrac{2}{16}+\dfrac{3}{4}+\ln 4\\ &=\dfrac{7}{8}+\ln 4\\ &=2.261294361 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The particle is at rest when $t=\ln 4\approx 1.386$ seconds, at $x\approx 2.26$ m.
criteria: Forms the quadratic in $e^{-t}$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Marks not itemised on the copy (3 marks): quadratic in $e^{-t}$; $t=\ln 4$; $x=\dfrac{7}{8}+\ln 4\approx 2.26$ m
meta.rubric_note: Source gives 3 marks without itemising them (quadratic in e^(-t); t = ln 4; x = 7/8 + ln 4); written top-down in that order.

914.stem:
The population of stray cats can be modelled by the equation $P=P_0e^{kt}$, where $P_0$ and $k$ are constants.

Initially, a town had 30 stray cats. In 12 days, the population of cats increased to 120.

parts.latex: Show that $P_0=30$.
Determine the exact value of $k$.
Determine the population of cats in 30 days.

solutions.latex:
Initially ($t=0$), $P=30$:
$$\begin{aligned} 30&=P_0e^{k\times0}\\ 30&=P_0\times1\\ P_0&=30 \end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Substitutes $t=0$ and $P=30$ into the equation and solves to obtain $P_0=30$
meta.marker_note: Very well done.

solutions.latex:
When $t=12$, $P=120$:
$$\begin{aligned} 120&=30e^{12k}\\ 4&=e^{12k}\\ \ln 4&=\ln e^{12k}\\ 12k&=\ln 4\\ k&=\dfrac{\ln 4}{12} \end{aligned}$$
Optionally,
$$k=\dfrac{\ln 4}{12}=\dfrac{2\ln 2}{12}=\dfrac{\ln 2}{6}$$
criteria: Correctly substitutes values for $t$ and $P$ into the equation, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Correctly obtains the exact value of $k$ by substituting values then solving for $k$
meta.marker_note: Very well done; bizarrely, many students when dividing 120 by 30 wrote 40 rather than 4.

solutions.latex:
Substituting $t=30$ and $k=\dfrac{\ln 4}{12}$:
$$\begin{aligned} P&=30e^{\frac{\ln 4}{12}\times30}\\ &=960 \end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Obtains 960 by substituting in correct values for $t$ and $k$
meta.marker_note: Very well done.

parts.latex:
Arnold, a Year 12 student, runs his own business selling eco-friendly toothpaste. He supplies his product to a national supermarket chain.

The \textbf{price–demand function} $(p(x))$ models the relationship between the price per tube and the number of tubes demanded per week $(x)$. In general, price decreases as demand increases.

The \textbf{marginal price–demand function} $(p'(x))$, represents the rate of change of price with respect to quantity demanded, measured in tubes per week.

These functions are used in business to analyse the \textbf{price–elasticity of demand} and assist in determining profitable pricing strategies.

Arnold knows that when the demand is 50 tubes per week, the price is \$2.35 per tube.

He is also given the following marginal price–demand function $p'(x)=-0.015e^{-0.01x}$.

Find the \textbf{price–demand equation}, given the marginal price–demand function and the information above.

solutions.latex:
Integrating the marginal price–demand function:
$$\begin{aligned}p(x)&=\int-0.015e^{-0.01x}\,dx\\ &=-0.015\int e^{-0.01x}\,dx\\ &=\dfrac{-0.015}{-0.01}e^{-0.01x}+c\\ &=1.5e^{-0.01x}+c\end{aligned}$$
The price is $\$2.35$ per tube for $50$ tubes per week, so $p(50)=2.35$:
$$\begin{aligned}2.35&=1.5e^{-0.01(50)}+c\\ c&=2.35-0.91\\ &=1.44\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore p(x)=1.5e^{-0.01x}+1.44$$
criteria: Finds the correct integral with $+c$ and substitutes $x=50$ and $p=2.35$ correctly, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct integral with $+c$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: Correct integral + c; substitution of 50 and \$2.35 was correct; correct value of c
meta.marker_note: A lot of students incorrectly divided $2.35$ by $\dfrac{3}{2}$ or $1.5$ after substitution. Some incorrectly substituted the values for $x$ and $p(x)$.

963.stem:
The velocity of a particle moving in a straight line at the end of $t$ seconds is given by

$$v(t)=3t^2-15t+18,\quad\text{where } 0\le t\le 4$$

parts.latex: Show that the particle is stationary at $t=2$ and $t=3$.
Hence, or otherwise find the total distance travelled by the particle between $t=1$ to $t=3$.

solutions.latex:
The particle is stationary when $v(t)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}3t^2-15t+18&=0\\ t^2-5t+6&=0\\ (t-2)(t-3)&=0\\ t&=2\text{ or } t=3\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Lets $v(t)=0$ and attempts to find the values of $t$, or attempts to substitute the given values of $t$ to show $v=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the working sets $v(t)=0$ and divides by $3$ (source wrote $v(t)=3t^2-15t+18=t^2-5t+6$).

solutions.latex:
From part (a), the particle changes direction at $t=2$, so split the distance there:
$$\begin{aligned}d&=\int_1^2\left(3t^2-15t+18\right)dt+\left|\int_2^3\left(3t^2-15t+18\right)dt\right|\\ &=\dfrac{5}{2}+\left|-\dfrac{1}{2}\right|\\ &=3\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds two definite integrals using the correct bounds, but makes minor arithmetic errors, or equivalent merit

Initially there are 250 litres of water in a tank. Water starts to flow into the tank.

The rate of increase of the volume of water in litres is given by

$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=250-7.5t$$

where $t$ is the time in hours.

Find the volume of water in the tank (correct to the nearest litre) when $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$.

solutions.latex:
Integrating the rate:
$$V(t)=250t-3.75t^2+C$$
Initially $V(0)=250$, so $C=250$:
$$V(t)=250t-3.75t^2+250$$
$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$ when
$$\begin{aligned}250-7.5t&=0\\ t&=\dfrac{100}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}V\left(\dfrac{100}{3}\right)&=250\left(\dfrac{100}{3}\right)-3.75\left(\dfrac{100}{3}\right)^2+250\\ &=4416.66\ldots\\ &\approx 4417\text{ litres}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the value of $t$, or equivalent merit

988.stem:
The number of concert tickets sold, $N$, is given by

$$N=1000\times 1.6^{kt}$$

Where $t$ is the number of weeks after being available for sale, and $k$ is a constant. Initially, 1000 tickets were sold, and after 2 weeks, the total number of tickets sold was doubled.

parts.latex: Calculate the value of $k$, leaving your answer in exact form.
At what rate was the number of tickets sold increasing after 4 weeks? Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

solutions.latex:
Initially $N=1000$, and after $2$ weeks $N=2000$, so when $t=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}1000\times 1.6^{2k}&=2000\\ 1.6^{2k}&=2\\ 2k&=\dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.6}\\ k&=\dfrac{\ln 2}{2\ln 1.6}\end{aligned}$$

Using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{kt}\right)=ka^{kt}\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dN}{dt}&=1000\times k\times 1.6^{kt}\times\ln 1.6\\ &=1000k\ln(1.6)\times 1.6^{kt}\end{aligned}$$
When $t=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dN}{dt}&=1000\times\dfrac{\ln 2}{2\ln 1.6}\times\ln 1.6\times 1.6^{\frac{\ln 2}{2\ln 1.6}\times 4}\\ &=1386.29\ldots\\ &\approx 1386\text{ tickets/week}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct derivative, or equivalent merit

997.stem: The acceleration of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is given by $\ddot{x}=4\sin 2t$, where $x$ is the displacement of the particle from the origin in metres, and $t$ is the time in seconds. Initially, the particle is at the origin moving to the left at 1 metre per second.

parts.latex: Show that the velocity of the particle is given by $\dot{x}=1-2\cos 2t$.
Find the time when the particle first comes to rest.

solutions.latex:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}&=\int 4\sin 2t\,dt\\ &=-2\cos 2t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially the particle moves left at $1$ m/s, so $\dot{x}=-1$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-1&=-2\cos 0+C\\ C&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\dot{x}=1-2\cos 2t$$
criteria: Integrates the acceleration, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}1-2\cos 2t&=0\\ \cos 2t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\\ 2t&=\dfrac{\pi}{3}\quad(\text{smallest positive solution})\\ t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\text{ seconds}\end{aligned}$$

criteria: Correct expression for the distance, or equivalent merit

1461.stem:
The velocity of two racing cars, $P$ and $Q$, are shown on the graph below.

\exfigure{641_q30_1}

The velocity of car $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by the function

$$v_P=3t^2-6t+4,$$

where $v_P$ is the velocity in metres per second.

The velocity of car $Q$ is accelerating at a constant rate. Both cars start at the same point and have the same velocity at times $t=0$ and $t=4$

figures.cap: velocity-time graph: straight line Q and parabola P starting at the same point on the v-axis and crossing again; NOT TO SCALE

parts.latex: Show that the equation for the velocity, $v_Q$, of car $Q$ is given by $v_Q=6t+4$.

Both cars start the race from the same point.

Find the earliest time when car $P$ will pass car $Q$ after the race starts.

solutions.latex:
Car $Q$ has constant acceleration, so its velocity is linear in $t$: $v_Q=mt+c$.

At $t=0$: $v_Q=v_P=4$

At $t=4$:
$$v_Q=v_P=3(4)^2-6(4)+4=28$$
$$\begin{aligned} m&=\dfrac{28-4}{4-0}=6\\ c&=4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore v_Q=6t+4$$
criteria: Finds an equation in the form $y=mx+c$ with correct gradient and incorrect $y$-intercept, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The signed area between curves $P$ and $Q$ represents the relative displacement between the cars.

The cars are at the same displacement from the start when the displacement between them is zero, so solve for $a$:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^a\big(3t^2-6t+4-(6t+4)\big)\,dt&=0\\ \int_0^a\left(3t^2-12t\right)dt&=0\\ \Big[t^3-6t^2\Big]_0^a&=0\\ a^3-6a^2&=0\\ a^2(a-6)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
$a>0$, so $a=6$: the cars are the same distance from the start at $t=6$.

The integrand $3t^2-12t$ is the velocity of $P$ relative to $Q$, and $v_P>v_Q$ for $t>4$.

Hence car $P$ passes car $Q$ 6 seconds after the start of the race.
criteria: Finds an integral that represents the area between $P$ and $Q$ and attempts to find a time $t$ $(t>0)$ when relative displacement is zero, or equivalent merit
Understands that relative displacement between both cars is represented by the signed area between $P$ and $Q$, or equivalent merit

1032.stem:
A particle moves along a straight line such that its velocity in metres per second, $v$, is given by the equation below, where $t$ is measured in seconds from $t=0$.

$$v=2+\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}$$

parts.latex: What is the particle's initial speed?
Explain why the particle can never be at rest.
can_use: Discriminant and the nature of roots

parts.latex:
What is the particle's change in displacement in the first 4 seconds?

Leave your answer in exact form.
Determine the particle's exact acceleration at $t=5$.

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=2+0\\&=2\text{ ms}^{-1}\end{aligned}$$

$t>0$ and $t^2+1>0$, since square values must be positive.

$\therefore\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}\ge0$, since the quotient of two positives is positive.

$\therefore 2+\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}\ge2$

$\therefore v$ is always positive and never equals zero, so the particle is never at rest.

Or, using the discriminant: if the particle is at rest, $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2+\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}&=0\\2t^2+2+t&=0\\2t^2+t+2&=0\\\Delta&=1^2-4(2)(2)\\&=-15<0\end{aligned}$$
$\Delta<0$, so there is no solution: the particle is never at rest.
criteria: Shows $\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}\ge0$ with a partial justification, or reaches $2t^2+t+2=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 0.5 for any mention of $t^2\ge0$ or $t^2+1>0$. If $\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}>0$ is stated: 1 mark if $t^2>0$ stated previously; 1.5 marks if $t^2>0$ AND $t>0$ stated; 0 marks if only $t>0$ stated. 0.5 for observing large values of $t$ (e.g. stating $\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}>0$ hence $\ne-2$; $\lim_{t\to\infty}\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}=0$). Discriminant method: 1 for reaching $2t^2+t+2=0$; 0.5 for the discriminant or quadratic formula; 0.5 for interpretation of the discriminant. Marker: observing $t\to\infty$ alone does not consider earlier values (e.g. $\lim_{t\to\infty}\dfrac{\sin t}{t}+\dfrac{1}{5}=\dfrac{1}{5}$ but $\dfrac{\sin t}{t}+\dfrac{1}{5}=0$ at $t\approx4.10462$ and $4.9063$); practise supporting arguments in explain questions.
meta.marker_note: $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for any mention of $t^2\ge0$ or $t^2+1>0$. If $\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}>0$ is stated: 1 mark if $t^2>0$ was stated previously; $1\dfrac{1}{2}$ marks if $t^2>0$ and $t>0$ were stated; 0 marks if only $t>0$ was stated. $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for observing large values of $t$ (e.g. stating $\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}>0$, hence $\ne-2$; $\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}=0$). Discriminant method: 1 for reaching $2t^2+t+2=0$, $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for the discriminant or quadratic formula, $\dfrac{1}{2}$ for interpreting the discriminant. Observing $t\to\infty$ alone does not consider earlier values (e.g. $\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\infty}\left(\dfrac{\sin t}{t}+\dfrac{1}{5}\right)=\dfrac{1}{5}$, but $\dfrac{\sin t}{t}+\dfrac{1}{5}=0$ at $t\approx4.10462$ and $4.9063$); practise supporting arguments in explain questions.

solutions.latex:
The change in displacement is the integral of the velocity over the first 4 seconds. Using $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(t)}{f(t)}\,dt=\ln|f(t)|+C$ for the second term:

Method 1:
$$\begin{aligned}&\int_0^4\left(2+\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}\right)dt\\&=\left[2t+\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|t^2+1|\right]_0^4\\&=8+\dfrac{1}{2}\ln17\end{aligned}$$
Method 2:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int\left(2+\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}\right)dt\\&=2t+\dfrac{1}{2}\ln|t^2+1|+C\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $x=C$.

At $t=4$, $x=8+\dfrac{1}{2}\ln17+C$.

$\therefore$ the change in displacement is $8+\dfrac{1}{2}\ln17$ metres.

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity. Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, on $\dfrac{t}{t^2+1}$, with

At $t=5$:

1107.stem:
A particle moves along a line with velocity

$$v(t)=6\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right),$$

where time $t$ is measured in seconds.

Given that the displacement at $t=0$ is 2 metres. Find:

parts.latex: the displacement function $s(t)$.
the acceleration function $a(t)$.
the time at which the particle changes direction within the interval $0<t<1$.

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}s(t)&=\int 6\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)dt\\&=3\sin\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $s(0)=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}2&=3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+C\\C&=2-3\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\&=2-\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore s(t)=3\sin\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)+2-\dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{2}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides the correct answer using the initial condition
meta.marker_note: Answered well.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the integral was written with $dx$; the variable is $t$, so $dt$.

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}a(t)&=\dfrac{dv}{dt}\\&=-12\sin\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: Provides correct answer. Comment: answered well.
meta.marker_note: Answered well.

solutions.latex:
The particle can change direction only where $v(t)=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}6\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)&=0\\2t+\dfrac{\pi}{3}&=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\\2t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6}\\t&=\dfrac{\pi}{12}\text{ seconds}\end{aligned}$$
Testing the nature: the acceleration there is non-zero, so $v$ changes sign.
$$\begin{aligned}a\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}\right)&=-12\sin\left(2\times\dfrac{\pi}{12}+\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\\&=-12\\&<0\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle changes direction at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{12}$ seconds.

parts.latex:
A particle moves along the $x$-axis with the acceleration at time $t$ equal to $a=12(t+3)^2$.

If the particle is initially at rest at the origin find the position of the particle after one second of motion.

solutions.latex:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$v=\int 12(t+3)^2\,dt=4(t+3)^3+C$$
Initially at rest, so $v=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=4(3)^3+C\\C&=-108\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore v=4(t+3)^3-108$$
Integrating the velocity:
$$x=\int\left(4(t+3)^3-108\right)dt=(t+3)^4-108t+C_2$$
Starting at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=81-0+C_2\\C_2&=-81\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=(t+3)^4-108t-81$$
When $t=1$:
$$x=67$$
criteria: Finds the displacement $x=(t+3)^4-108t-81$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A particle travels on a straight line such that its displacement is given by the function

$$x(t)=\begin{cases}5t & 0\le t\le1\\[4pt]6\sqrt{t}-\dfrac{1}{t} & t>1\end{cases}$$

where $x$ is the particle's displacement from the origin in metres, and $t$ is the time, in seconds.
Show that the particle begins its journey at the origin.
Show that the particle is never at rest.

Displacement, velocity and acceleration.reason: not_when: powers-of-t displacement with no acceleration/integration belongs to Velocity as a rate of change.

parts.latex: Find the distance travelled in the first 4 seconds of the particle's journey.

solutions.latex:
For $0\le t\le1$, $x=5t$:
$$\begin{aligned}x(0)&=5(0)\\&=0\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ at $t=0$, $x=0$: the particle starts at the origin.

For $0\le t\le1$, $x=5t$, so the displacement increases linearly (at $5$ m/s).

At $t=1$, the second piece gives
$$\begin{aligned}x(1)&=6\sqrt{1}-\dfrac{1}{1}\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
which matches $5t$, so the displacement is continuous at $t=1$.

For $t>1$:
$$x'(t)=3t^{-\frac{1}{2}}+\dfrac{1}{t^2}$$
Both terms are positive, so $x'(t)>0$ and $x(t)$ is increasing for $t>1$.

$\therefore$ the displacement is increasing for $t>0$.

$\therefore$ the particle never comes to rest.

Alternatively, as $t\to\infty$, $x'(t)\to0^+$ (an asymptote), so $x'(t)$ is never $0$.
criteria: Velocity $5$ m/s for $0\le t\le1$ and $x(1)=5$ (continuity), or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (b), the graph is continuous at $t=1$ and increasing for $t>0$, so the particle does not turn and the distance is $x(4)-x(0)=x(4)$:
$$\begin{aligned}x(4)&=6\sqrt4-\dfrac{1}{4}\\&=12-\dfrac{1}{4}\\&=11\dfrac{3}{4}\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
A particle is moving on a straight line with acceleration given by

$$\ddot{x}=12e^{-2t}+e^{-t}$$

where $x$ is displacement in metres and $t$ is time in seconds.

Initially the particle's velocity is $-6$ m/s and its displacement is 8 m.

Show that the displacement of the particle is given by

$$x=3e^{-2t}+e^{-t}+t+4.$$
Show that the particle comes to rest after $t=\ln3$ seconds.

Find the displacement when the particle comes to rest.

Give a simplified, exact answer.

solutions.latex:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$\begin{aligned}\dot{x}&=\int\ddot{x}\,dt\\&=\dfrac{12e^{-2t}}{-2}+\dfrac{e^{-t}}{-1}+C\\&=-6e^{-2t}-e^{-t}+C\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $\dot{x}=-6$:
$$\begin{aligned}-6&=-6-1+C\\C&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dot{x}=-6e^{-2t}-e^{-t}+1$$
Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int\dot{x}\,dt\\&=\dfrac{-6e^{-2t}}{-2}-\dfrac{e^{-t}}{-1}+t+C_2\\&=3e^{-2t}+e^{-t}+t+C_2\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $x=8$:
$$\begin{aligned}8&=3+1+0+C_2\\C_2&=4\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=3e^{-2t}+e^{-t}+t+4$$

The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$-6e^{-2t}-e^{-t}+1=0$$
Multiplying by $e^{2t}$ gives a quadratic in $e^t$:
$$\begin{aligned}-6-e^t+e^{2t}&=0\\(e^t)^2-e^t-6&=0\\(e^t+2)(e^t-3)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $e^t=-2$ or $e^t=3$.

$e^t>0$, so $e^t=-2$ has no solution.
$$\begin{aligned}e^t&=3\\t&=\ln3\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle is at rest after $t=\ln3$ seconds.

meta.marker_note: Full marks need $t=\ln3$ with $e^t=-2$ rejected.

parts.latex: Ava is managing the growth of a population of bacteria in a laboratory. The population can be modelled by the exponential equation $P(t)=500e^{kt}$ where the initial population is 500 bacteria, $k$ is the growth constant, and $t$ is time in minutes.
Find the value of $k$ correct to 1 significant figure, given that there are 1660 bacteria present after 2 hours.
Determine the rate of change of the population with respect to time after 2 hours. Give your answer to the nearest whole number.

Ava is concerned about the growth of the bacteria and wants to determine if she needs to introduce a control mechanism.

Interpret the nature of the population growth with reference to the derivatives $P'(t)$ and $P''(t)$, and hence determine if a control would be needed.

solutions.latex:
Substituting $P(120)=1660$ ($t=120$ minutes):
$$\begin{aligned}1660&=500e^{120k}\\ \dfrac{83}{25}&=e^{120k}\\ 120k&=\ln\dfrac{83}{25}\\ k&=\dfrac{\ln\frac{83}{25}}{120}\\ &\approx 0.01\ (1\text{ sig. fig.})\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Either the exact or the rounded value of $k$ is accepted.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $P(t)=500e^{kt}$, where $k=\dfrac{\ln\frac{83}{25}}{120}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P'(t)&=500ke^{kt}\\ P'(120)&=500ke^{k\times 120}\\ &=16.6\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the population is increasing at approximately 17 bacteria/min at $t=120$.

meta.marker_note: Also accept 16 or 16.6 bacteria/min.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $P(t)=500e^{kt}$, where $k=\dfrac{\ln\frac{83}{25}}{120}$:
$$\begin{aligned}P'(t)&=500ke^{kt}\\ P''(t)&=500k^2e^{kt}\end{aligned}$$
$e^{kt}>0$ for all $t$, so
$$\begin{aligned}P'(t)&>0 &&\text{for all } t &&P(t)\text{ is increasing}\\ P''(t)&>0 &&\text{for all } t &&P'(t)\text{ is increasing}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore\ P(t)$ is increasing at an increasing rate, so a control mechanism should be introduced.
criteria: Shows $P'(t)$ and $P''(t)$ are both positive for all $t$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: increasing at an increasing rate, so a control is needed

A certain radioactive isotope element decays exponentially according to the model $A=A_0e^{kt}$ where $A$ is the number of grams of the isotope at the end of $t$ days and $A_0$ is the number of grams present initially.

$\therefore$ Velocity is negative and acceleration is positive.

574_q3_1.notes: Rule sweep 12 Nov: 9: displacement curve at 0.8pt

figures.cap: velocity-time graph for 0 to 4 seconds, zeros at t = 0, 1, 3, 4

solutions.latex:
Displacement increases while $v>0$ and decreases while $v<0$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&<0 &&\text{for } 0<t<1 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\\v&>0 &&\text{for } 1<t<3 &&\text{displacement increasing}\\v&<0 &&\text{for } 3<t<4 &&\text{displacement decreasing}\end{aligned}$$
The area above the axis from $t=1$ to $t=3$ is larger than the area below from $t=0$ to $t=1$, so the displacement at $t=3$ is greater than at $t=0$.

$\therefore$ The displacement is greatest at $t=3$.

1267.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line with velocity $v=2e^t+4e^{-t}$, $t$ is in seconds and $v$ m/s. Initially, the particle is at the origin $O$.

parts.latex: What is its initial velocity?
Is the particle ever at rest? Give reasons.
Find the displacement function, $x$, of the particle, at time $t$ seconds.
Find the time when the particle is at $x=4$.(Give your answer in exact form)

solutions.latex:
Initially $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}v(0)&=2e^0+4e^0\\&=6\end{aligned}$$

Since $2e^t>0$ and $4e^{-t}>0$ for all values of $t$,
$$2e^t+4e^{-t}>0$$
for all values of $t$.

$\therefore$ The particle will never be at rest.

meta.top_criterion_original: must state both ($2e^t>0$ and $4e^{-t}>0$ for all $t$); if proving $v=0$ then must show $e^{2t}=-2$
meta.marker_note: Must state both ($2e^t>0$ and $4e^{-t}>0$ for all $t$); if proving $v=0$ has no solution, must show $e^{2t}=-2$.

solutions.latex:
Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int(2e^t+4e^{-t})\,dt\\&=2e^t-4e^{-t}+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially at the origin, so $x=0$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=2e^0-4e^0+C\\C&=-2+4\\\therefore C&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=2e^t-4e^{-t}+2$$

When $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}2e^t-4e^{-t}+2&=4\\2(e^t-2e^{-t}-1)&=0\\e^t-\dfrac{2}{e^t}-1&=0\\e^{2t}-e^t-2&=0 &&(\times e^t)\\(e^t-2)(e^t+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $e^t+1>0$, $e^t-2=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}e^t&=2\\t&=\ln2\end{aligned}$$

1272.stem: An object that was initially at the origin moves with velocity ($v$ m/s) given by $v=24+10t-t^2$.

parts.latex: Find the maximum speed of the object.
Find the acceleration when the object is at rest.
Find the total distance travelled by the object during the first 15 seconds.

solutions.latex:
$v=-t^2+10t+24$

The maximum speed is at the turning point of this concave down parabola, $t=-\dfrac{b}{2a}$:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=-\dfrac{10}{2\times(-1)}\\&=5\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}v_{\max}&=24+10\times5-5^2\\&=49\text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$

meta.concern: marking guideline answers maximum velocity (49 m/s at t = 5); speed |v| is unbounded for t > 12, so 'maximum speed' is only 49 m/s if the domain is limited (e.g. 0 <= t <= 12); guideline line '24 x 10 x 5 - 5^2' transcribed as printed (should be 24 + 10 x 5 - 5^2)
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: $v_{\max}=24\times10\times5-5^2$ written as $24+10\times5-5^2$ (the value $49$ is unchanged).

solutions.latex:
The object is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}-t^2+10t+24&=0\\t^2-10t-24&=0\\(t-12)(t+2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
Since $t\ge0$, $t=12$.

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\dfrac{dv}{dt}\\&=-2t+10\\&=-2\times12+10\\&=-14\text{ m/s}^2\end{aligned}$$

Integrating the velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int v\,dt\\&=\int(-t^2+10t+24)\,dt\\&=-\dfrac{t^3}{3}+5t^2+24t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially at the origin: $t=0$, $x=0$ gives $0=0+0+0+C$, so $C=0$.
$$x=-\dfrac{t^3}{3}+5t^2+24t$$
The object is at rest at $t=12$ (from (b)) and changes direction there, so find the displacement at $t=0$, $12$ and $15$:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=0: & x&=0\\t&=12: & x&=-\dfrac{12^3}{3}+5\times12^2+24\times12=432\\t&=15: & x&=-\dfrac{15^3}{3}+5\times15^2+24\times15=360\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Distance travelled}&=432+(432-360)\\&=504\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct displacement at $t=12$ and at $t=15$, or equivalent merit
Correct displacement at $t=15$ or $t=12$, or equivalent merit

1274.stem: The acceleration ($a$ m/s$^2$) of an object at time $t$ seconds is given by $a=\dfrac{-1}{(5t+1)^2}$. The object is initially 3 metres to the left of the origin travelling with velocity 1 m/s.

parts.latex: Find an expression for the object's velocity ($v$) at time $t$.
Find the limiting speed of the object.
Find the position of the object at the end of the 10$^{\text{th}}$ second. (Answer to the nearest metre)

solutions.latex:
Integrating the acceleration:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=\int a\,dt\\&=\int-(5t+1)^{-2}\,dt\\&=\dfrac{-(5t+1)^{-2+1}}{(-2+1)\times5}+C\\&=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $v=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}1&=\dfrac{1}{5(5\times0+1)}+C\\C&=0.8\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore v=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8$$

$v=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8$

As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}\to0$, so
$$v\to0.8$$
$\therefore$ The limiting speed of the object is $0.8$ m/s.

Integrating $v=\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int v\,dt\\&=\int\left(\dfrac{1}{5(5t+1)}+0.8\right)dt\\&=\dfrac{1}{5}\times\dfrac{\ln(5t+1)}{5}+0.8t+C\\&=\dfrac{\ln(5t+1)}{25}+0.8t+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $x=-3$:
$$\begin{aligned}-3&=\dfrac{\ln(5\times0+1)}{25}+0.8\times0+C\\\therefore C&=-3\end{aligned}$$
$$x=\dfrac{1}{25}\ln(5t+1)+0.8t-3$$
When $t=10$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\dfrac{1}{25}\ln(5\times10+1)+0.8\times10-3\\&=5.157\ldots\\&\approx5\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The object is about $5$ m to the right of the origin.

1300.stem:
A particle $P$ is moving on the $x$ axis and its velocity $v\text{ ms}^{-1}$, $t$ seconds after a given instant, is given by $v=t^2(3-t)$, $t\ge 0$.

When $t=2$, $P$ is observed to be $4\text{ m}$ from the origin $O$, in the positive direction of the $x-$axis.

parts.latex: Find the acceleration of $P$ when $t=2$.
The particle is initially at rest and is also at rest when $t=T$. Determine the distance of $P$ from $O$ when $t=T$.

solutions.latex:
Expanding, $v=3t^2-t^3$. Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$:
$$a=6t-3t^2$$
When $t=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=6(2)-3(2)^2\\&=12-12\\&=0\end{aligned}$$

The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}t^2(3-t)&=0\\t&=0\text{ or }3\end{aligned}$$
So $T=3$.

Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int 3t^2-t^3\,dt\\&=t^3-\dfrac{1}{4}t^4+C\end{aligned}$$
When $t=2$, $x=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}4&=2^3-\dfrac{1}{4}\times 2^4+C\\C&=0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=t^3-\dfrac{1}{4}t^4$$
When $t=T=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=3^3-\dfrac{1}{4}\times 3^4\\&=6.75\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly integrates and finds the constant to find the displacement equation, or equivalent merit

1328.stem:
A farm has a watering system which repeatedly fills a storage tank then empties its’ contents to water different sections of the farm. The volume of water $V$ (in cubic metres) in the tank at a time $t$ is given by the equation

$$V=2-2\sqrt{3}\cos t-2\sin t$$

where $t$ is measured in minutes.

parts.latex: Find $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$.
Determine whether the tank is initially filling or emptying, showing all calculations.
At what time does the tank first become completely full and what is its capacity when it is full?

Related and complementary angles.reason: Evaluating trig ratios of 7π/6 via related angle, beyond solving the equation.

Solving optimisation problems.evidence: The tank is full or empty when dV/dt=0
Solving optimisation problems.reason: Differentiates a contextual function to find its maximum value.

Derivatives of trigonometric functions.reason: dV/dt requires differentiating sin and cos.

Stationary points and their nature.reason: not_when: worded optimisation tags Solving optimisation problems instead (prerequisite applied automatically).

solutions.latex: $$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=2\sqrt{3}\sin t-2\cos t$$

The tank is emptying when $\dfrac{dV}{dt}<0$.

When $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dV}{dt}&=2\sqrt{3}\sin(0)-2\cos(0)\\ &=2\sqrt{3}(0)-2(1)\\ &=-2\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ tank is emptying at this time

The tank is full or empty when $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{3}\sin t-2\cos t&=0\\ 2\sqrt{3}\sin t&=2\cos t\\ \dfrac{\sin t}{\cos t}&=\dfrac{2}{2\sqrt{3}}\\ \tan t&=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\ t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{6},\ \ldots\end{aligned}$$
As the tank is initially emptying, the first value is when it is empty and the second is when it is full.

Tank first full when $t=\dfrac{7\pi}{6}$ minutes.
$$\begin{aligned}V&=2-2\sqrt{3}\cos\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)-2\sin\left(\dfrac{7\pi}{6}\right)\\ &=6\text{ m}^3\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up the equation to find $\tan t=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$, or equivalent merit

1336.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line, starting from the origin. At time $t$ seconds, the particle has displacement $x$ metres from the origin and velocity $v\ m/s$. The displacement is given by $x=5\log_e(2t+1)-3t$.

parts.latex: Find an expression for the velocity $v$.
When does the particle come to rest?

Derivatives of logarithmic functions.reason: v was found in part (a); this part only solves v = 0.

Displacement, velocity and acceleration.reason: v from part (a); finding when v = 0 belongs to Particles at rest (agreed).

parts.latex: Find the initial acceleration.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds. Answer correct to four decimal places.

Derivatives of logarithmic functions.evidence: The particle starts at the origin, is at rest at t=7/6
Derivatives of logarithmic functions.reason: Finding rest time needs v=10/(2t+1)−3; kept when unsure (may come from earlier part).

Displacement, velocity and acceleration.evidence: is at rest at t=7/6 and then turns back
Displacement, velocity and acceleration.reason: Velocity of a log displacement belongs here per Velocity-as-rate not_when.

Particles at rest and changing direction.evidence: is at rest at t=7/6 and then turns back

solutions.latex:
Velocity is $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=5\left(\dfrac{2}{2t+1}\right)-3\\ &=\dfrac{10}{2t+1}-3\end{aligned}$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the displacement was restated as x = 3t - 5 log_e(2t+1); the question gives x = 5 log_e(2t+1) - 3t, which the working uses.

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$; by the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=10(2t+1)^{-1}-3\\ a&=-10\times2(2t+1)^{-2}\\ &=-\dfrac{20}{(2t+1)^2}\end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\dfrac{-20}{(2(0)+1)^2}\\ &=-20\text{ m/s}^2\end{aligned}$$

meta.corrected: Corrected from source: a = -20/(2t+1)^2 (the source dropped the minus sign; its final answer -20 m/s^2 was correct).

solutions.latex:
The particle starts at the origin, is at rest at $t=\dfrac{7}{6}$ and then turns back.

At $t=\dfrac{7}{6}$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=5\ln\left(2\left(\dfrac{7}{6}\right)+1\right)-3\left(\dfrac{7}{6}\right)\\ &=5\ln\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)-\dfrac{7}{2}\end{aligned}$$
At $t=3$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=5\ln(2(3)+1)-3(3)\\ &=5\ln7-9\end{aligned}$$
So the distance is out to $x\left(\dfrac{7}{6}\right)$ and back to $x(3)$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Total distance travelled}&=2\left(5\ln\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)-\dfrac{7}{2}\right)-(5\ln7-9)\\ &=4.310177\ldots\\ &=4.3102\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the displacement at $t=\dfrac{7}{6}$ or $t=3$, or equivalent merit

1357.stem:
The velocity of two racing cars, $P$ and $Q$, are shown on the graph below.

\exfigure{323_q18_1}

The velocity of car $P$ at time $t$ seconds is given by the function $v_P = 3t^2 - 6t + 4$, where $v_P$ is the velocity in metres per second.

The velocity of car $Q$ is accelerating at a constant rate. Both cars start at the same point and have the same velocity at times where $t = 0$ and $t = 4$.

figures.cap: velocity-time graph: a straight line and a parabola both starting at v = 4 when t = 0 and meeting again later

parts.latex: Show that the equation for the velocity of car $Q$, $v_Q$, is given by $v_Q = 6t + 4$.

Both cars start the race from the same point.

Find the earliest time when car $P$ will pass car $Q$ after the race starts.

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$, $v_Q=v_P=4$

At $t=4$, $v_Q=v_P=3(4)^2-6(4)+4=28$

$Q$ accelerates at a constant rate, so $v_Q$ is linear through $(0,4)$ and $(4,28)$:
$$m=\dfrac{28-4}{4-0}=6$$
$$\therefore v_Q=6t+4$$

Both cars start at the same point, so $P$ passes $Q$ at the time $a>0$ when their displacements are equal:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^a \big(3t^2-6t+4-(6t+4)\big)\,dt&=0\\ \int_0^a (3t^2-12t)\,dt&=0\\ \Big[t^3-6t^2\Big]_0^a&=0\\ a^3-6a^2&=0\\ a^2(a-6)&=0\\ a&=0,\ 6 \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ car $P$ will pass $Q$ after 6 seconds from the start of the race.
criteria: Correct primitive of the difference in velocities, or equivalent merit
Sets the difference in displacements equal to zero, or equivalent merit

1528.stem:
A moving particle has an acceleration of $a\ \text{m/s}^2$ at time $t$ seconds $(t\ge 0)$.

The acceleration is given by the equation

$$a=15-6t.$$

Initially the particle is at the origin and has a velocity of $v=-12$ m/s.

figures.cap: solution sketch: number-line path: from 0 to -5.5 at t = 1, then to 8 at t = 4

parts.latex: Find the velocity, $v$, and displacement, $x$, in terms of $t$.
Find the time(s) when the particle is at rest.
Find the distance travelled during the first 4 seconds.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration, using $x=0$ and $v=-12$ when $t=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} v &= \int(15-6t)\,dt \\ &= 15t-3t^2+c \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} -12 &= 0-0+c \\ c &= -12 \end{aligned}$$

$$v=15t-3t^2-12$$

Integrate again:

$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int\left(15t-3t^2-12\right)dt \\ &= \dfrac{15t^2}{2}-t^3-12t+d \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 0-0-0+d \\ d &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$x=\dfrac{15t^2}{2}-t^3-12t$$
criteria: Finds the correct velocity $v=15t-3t^2-12$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 2 marks (no marking criteria shown in source)

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} -3t^2+15t-12 &= 0 \\ t^2-5t+4 &= 0 \\ (t-1)(t-4) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{at rest when } t=1 \text{ and } t=4 \text{ seconds}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 mark (no marking criteria shown in source)

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$, at $t=1$ and $t=4$.

Find the position at $t=0,\ 1,\ 4$ using $x=\dfrac{15t^2}{2}-t^3-12t$:

$$\begin{aligned} t=0: &\quad x=0 \\ t=1: &\quad x=-5.5 \\ t=4: &\quad x=8 \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{339_q30_s1}

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 5.5+5.5+8 \\ &= 19 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$

1565.stem:
The number of daylight hours on the $t^{th}$ day of the year in Sydney can be modelled by the following equation.

$$L(t)=12+k\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]$$

parts.latex: Given that there were 14 hours of daylight 10 days before the start of the year, show that $k=2$.
How many days into the year will the number of daylight hours be increasing the fastest? (Answer to the nearest day)
Hence, find the number of daylight hours from that day until the end of the year.

solutions.latex:
When $t=-10$, $L=14$:

$$\begin{aligned} 14 &= 12+k\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(-10+10)\right] \\ &= 12+k \\ k &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: substitutes in both values, then shows that $k=2$

solutions.latex:
The daylight hours increase fastest where $L'(t)$ is a maximum, so solve $L''(t)=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} L'(t) &= -\dfrac{4\pi}{365}\sin\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right] \\ L''(t) &= -\dfrac{8\pi^2}{365^2}\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right] \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right] &= 0 \\ \dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10) &= \dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \\ t+10 &= 91.25,\ 273.75 \\ t &= 81.25,\ 263.75 \end{aligned}$$

Test which gives the maximum rate:

$$\begin{aligned} L'(81.25) &\approx -0.03 \\ L'(263.75) &\approx 0.03 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{daylight hours increase fastest } 264 \text{ days into the year}$$
criteria: Correctly finds the first or second derivative, or equivalent merit
Uses a correct method to find the steepest gradient, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correct method used to find steepest gradient
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the handwritten $L''(t)$ had denominator $365$; it should be $365^2$ (answer unchanged).

solutions.latex:
Daylight hours from day $264$ to the end of the year ($t=365$):

$$\begin{aligned} \int_{264}^{365}\left(12+2\cos\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]\right)dt &= \left[12t+\dfrac{365}{\pi}\sin\left[\dfrac{2\pi}{365}(t+10)\right]\right]_{264}^{365} \\ &= 4399.90137-3051.81796 \\ &= 1348\text{ hours (nearest hour)} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct bounds of integral chosen, or equivalent merit

1627.stem: The velocity of a particle travelling on the $x$ axis is given by $v(t)=\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}$ for $t\ge 0$.

parts.latex: Show that the particle is stationary when $t=1$.
Explain why the particle is moving to the left for all times $t>1$.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds, correct to one decimal place.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned}v(1)&=\dfrac{1}{1+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=0\end{aligned}$$
So the particle is stationary at $t=1$.

meta.top_criterion_original: must show substitution AND concluding statement
meta.marker_note: Must show the substitution and a concluding statement.

solutions.latex:
$$a(t)=v'(t)=-\dfrac{1}{(t+1)^2}$$
$a(t)<0$ for all $t\ge0$, so $v$ is decreasing.

Since $v(1)=0$ and $v$ is decreasing, $v<0$ for all $t>1$, so the particle always moves to the left for $t>1$.
criteria: Mathematical reasoning, e.g. finding $a(t)$ or use of inequalities, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$v(0)=\dfrac{1}{2}>0$, $v(1)=0$ and $v$ is decreasing, so the direction changes at $t=1$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&>0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<1 &&\text{moving right}\\v&<0 &&\text{for } t>1 &&\text{moving left}\end{aligned}$$
So the distance is
$$d=\int_0^1\left(\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)dt+\left|\int_1^3\left(\dfrac{1}{t+1}-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)dt\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned}d&=\left[\ln|t+1|-\dfrac{t}{2}\right]_0^1+\left|\left[\ln|t+1|-\dfrac{t}{2}\right]_1^3\right|\\&=\ln2-\dfrac{1}{2}-(0-0)+\left|\ln4-\dfrac{3}{2}-\ln2+\dfrac{1}{2}\right|\\&=\ln2-\dfrac{1}{2}+\ln2-\ln4+1\\&=\ln\dfrac{2\times2}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ The distance travelled is $0.5$ m.

meta.top_criterion_original: correct substitution and answer. No marks awarded if the integrated expression has no logs.
meta.marker_note: No marks are awarded if the integrated expression has no logs.

1636.stem: A toxic substance in a lake is degrading naturally according to the formula $A(t)=3000m^{-0.2t}$, where $A$ is the number of grams of the substance remaining at $t$ years and $m>0$ is a constant.

parts.latex: If $A=2400$ after 6 years, find the value of $m$ correct to 1 decimal place.
Fish can be reintroduced to the lake once the rate of change of the toxic substance is greater than $-20$. After how many years can fish be reintroduced? Answer to one decimal place.
People can swim in the lake once the amount of the toxic substance is less than 50. In how many years can this happen, to the nearest year?

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=6$ and $A=2400$:
$$\begin{aligned}2400&=3000m^{-0.2(6)}\\\dfrac{4}{5}&=m^{-\frac{6}{5}}\\m&=\left(\dfrac{4}{5}\right)^{-\frac{5}{6}}\\&=1.2\text{ (1 d.p.)}\end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Some students gave $0.8$.

solutions.latex:
With $m=1.2$, $A(t)=3000(1.2)^{-0.2t}$. Fish can be reintroduced when $A'(t)>-20$:
$$\begin{aligned}3000\ln(1.2)\times(-0.2)(1.2)^{-0.2t}&>-20\\-600\ln(1.2)(1.2)^{-0.2t}&>-20\\(1.2)^{-0.2t}&<\dfrac{1}{30\ln1.2}\end{aligned}$$
Take natural logarithms of both sides:
$$\begin{aligned}-0.2t\ln1.2&<-\ln(30\ln1.2)\\t&>\dfrac{\ln(30\ln1.2)}{0.2\ln1.2}\\&=46.5993724\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ Fish can be reintroduced after $46.6$ years (1 d.p.).
criteria: Correct change of base or similar operation, or equivalent merit
Writes $A'(t)>-20$ with the correct derivative, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The amount is less than 50 when
$$\begin{aligned}3000(1.2)^{-0.2t}&<50\\-0.2t\ln1.2&<\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{60}\right)\\t&>\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{60}\right)}{-0.2\ln1.2}\\&=112.283611\ldots\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ It is safe to swim after 113 years.

meta.marker_note: The answer must be rounded up.

1656.stem: A population of bacteria is modelled by the function $P(t)=P_0\times e^{kt}$, where $P(t)$ is the population at time $t$ (in hours), $P_0$ is the initial population, and $k$ is the constant growth rate.

parts.latex: Given that the initial population $P_0$ is 100 bacteria and the population triples every 4 hours, show that value of $k=\dfrac{\ln 3}{4}$.
Determine the population of bacteria after 12 hours.
Find the time it takes for the population to reach 100,000 bacteria. Leave your answer to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
The population triples every $4$ hours, so $P(4)=3\times100=300$:
$$\begin{aligned} 300&=100e^{4k} \\ 3&=e^{4k} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore k=\dfrac{\ln 3}{4}$$
$$\begin{aligned} P(12)&=100e^{12\times\frac{\ln 3}{4}} \\ &=100\times e^{\ln 3^3} \\ &=2700 \text{ bacteria} \end{aligned}$$

Setting $P(t)=100\,000$ and using the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 100\,000&=100e^{\frac{t\ln 3}{4}} \\ 1000&=e^{\ln 3^{\frac{t}{4}}} \\ 1000&=3^{\frac{t}{4}} \\ \dfrac{t}{4}&=\log_3 1000 \\ t&=\dfrac{4\ln 1000}{\ln 3} \\ &\approx25.15 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
Converting the decimal part to minutes:
$$\begin{aligned} t&\approx25+0.15\times60 \\ &=25 \text{ hours } 9 \text{ minutes} \end{aligned}$$

1663.stem:
The velocity-time graph shows how a particle travels during a period of 7 seconds. Initially, the particle is at the origin and travelling at $5\ m/s$ to the right. The graph has two horizontal intercepts at $t=1$ and $t=5$. It also has a turning point at $t=3$.

\exfigure{361_q26_1}

figures.cap: velocity-time graph: parabola from v=5 at t=0, crossing at t=1 and t=5, minimum about -4 at t=3
the same velocity-time graph repeated
blank displacement-time axes, displacement -5 to 10 m, time 0 to 7 s
solution sketch: displacement-time sketch starting at origin, maximum at t=1, zero at t=2.2, minimum at t=5, zero at t=6.8

parts.latex: Explain the meaning of the horizontal intercept at $t=1$.
When the acceleration is not zero, what is the direction of the acceleration?

Particles at rest and changing direction.evidence: stationary where v=0: at t=1 (v changes from positive to negative)

solutions.latex: The particle is at rest.

Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity-time graph:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{gradient}&<0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<3 &&\text{acceleration to the left} \\ \text{gradient}&>0 &&\text{for } 3<t\le7 &&\text{acceleration to the right} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly describes the acceleration for one interval, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: correctly describe acceleration for both intervals

solutions.latex:
\exfigure{361_q26_s1}

The gradient of the displacement graph is the velocity, so the displacement is stationary where $v=0$: at $t=1$ ($v$ changes from positive to negative) and at $t=5$ ($v$ changes from negative to positive).
criteria: Smoothness of the curve, or equivalent merit
