1707.stem:
A particle is moving such that its displacement in metres after $t$ seconds is given by the equation

$$x=-1.5+3\sin 2t$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of x = -1.5 + 3 sin 2t for 0 <= t <= 2 pi, range -4.5 to 1.5, crossing zero four times

parts.latex: State the maximum displacement of the particle.
can_use: Maxima and minima from the range

parts.latex: Find the first four times when the particle is at the origin.

solutions.latex:
The maximum value of $\sin(2t)$ is $1$:
$$\begin{aligned} x_{\max}&=-1.5+3\times1 \\ &=1.5 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

\exfigure{373_q21_s1}

The particle is at the origin when $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -1.5+3\sin(2t)&=0 \\ 3\sin(2t)&=1.5 \\ \sin(2t)&=\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The related angle is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$; sine is positive in the first and second quadrants, and the pattern repeats every $2\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2t&=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 2\pi+\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ 3\pi-\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the first four times the particle is at the origin are
$$t=\dfrac{\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{13\pi}{12},\ \dfrac{17\pi}{12} \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Four correct values of $2t$, or equivalent merit

1708.stem:
A particle travels in a straight line. Its velocity $\dot{x}$ at time $t$ is given by

$$\dot{x}=\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)\ \text{metres per second}$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: velocity-time graph: parabola through (0, 9), (1, 0), (3, 0) with minimum (2, -3)

parts.latex: Find the expression for the particle's displacement $x$ in terms of $t$, if the particle was initially at $x=2$.
Find an expression for the particle's acceleration in terms of $t$.
At what times is the particle at rest?
Draw a velocity-time graph that represents the motion of this particle, showing all important features.
Find the total distance travelled between $t=0$ to $t=3$.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\int\dot{x}\,dt \\ &=\int\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)dt \\ &=t^3-6t^2+9t+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially ($t=0$) $x=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=0^3-6(0)^2+9(0)+C \\ C&=2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore x=t^3-6t^2+9t+2 \text{ metres}$$
criteria: Correct primitive with constant, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x}&=\dfrac{d}{dt}(\dot{x}) \\ &=6t-12 \text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$

The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3t^2-12t+9&=0 \\ t^2-4t+3&=0 \\ (t-3)(t-1)&=0 \\ t&=1 \text{ or } 3 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

meta.checked_source_ok: source's x is a slip for t; t=1,3 verified, notation only

criteria: Shows the intercepts correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The distance is the area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis, so split where the velocity changes sign ($t=1$, part (c)):
$$\begin{aligned} \dot{x}&>0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<1 &&\text{moving in the positive direction} \\ \dot{x}&<0 &&\text{for } 1<t\le3 &&\text{moving in the negative direction} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance}&=\int_0^1\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)dt+\left|\int_1^3\left(3t^2-12t+9\right)dt\right| \\ &=\Big[t^3-6t^2+9t\Big]_0^1+\left|\Big[t^3-6t^2+9t\Big]_1^3\right| \\ &=(1-6+9)-(0)+\Big|(27-54+27)-(1-6+9)\Big| \\ &=4+|-4| \\ &=8 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct evaluation of both integrals, or equivalent merit
Correct integral expression split at $t=1$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The level of a local dam is being monitored. After $t$ days, the rate at which the volume of water in the dam is changing is given by

$$R=\dfrac{1\,000}{1+t}-500$$

where $R$ is the rate of change of the volume of water in the dam, measured in megalitres per day.

The volume of water in the dam at the end of the fifth day of monitoring was half the volume at the end of the fourth day.

Find an expression for the volume of water $V$ in the dam, $t$ days after the monitoring began.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\int R\,dt \\ &=\int\left(\dfrac{1000}{1+t}-500\right)dt \\ &=1000\ln|1+t|-500t+C \end{aligned}$$
The volume at the end of day $5$ is half that at the end of day $4$, so $V(4)=2V(5)$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000\ln5-2000+C&=2\left(1000\ln6-2500+C\right) \\ 1000\ln5-2000+C&=2000\ln6-5000+2C \\ C&=1000\ln5-2000-2000\ln6+5000 \\ &=1000\left(\ln5-2\ln6\right)+3000 \\ &=1000\ln\dfrac{5}{36}+3000 \\ &=1000\left(\ln\dfrac{5}{36}+3\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore V=1000\ln|1+t|-500t+1000\left(\ln\dfrac{5}{36}+3\right)$$

parts.latex: A particle, initially at the origin, moves in a straight line with velocity $v=8-4t$ metres per second. What is the total distance the particle travels in the first 4 seconds?

solutions.latex:
The velocity is zero when $8-4t=0$, so the particle turns at $t=2$.

Integrating with $x(0)=0$ gives $x=8t-2t^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} x(2) &= 16-8=8 \\ x(4) &= 32-32=0 \end{aligned}$$
The particle goes out $8$ m and back $8$ m, so the total distance is
$$8+8=16 \text{ m}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: correct answer (key circled in the bundled solutions)

parts.latex:
The number $N$ of flies at the Longueville rubbish dump after $t$ weeks is given by the formula $N=N_0e^{0.04\,t}$, where $N_0$ is the initial number of flies.

Which expression represents the number of weeks it takes until the rubbish dump has doubled its population of flies?

solutions.latex:
The population has doubled when $N=2N_0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2N_0 &= N_0e^{0.04t} \\ e^{0.04t} &= 2 \\ 0.04t &= \ln 2 \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln 2}{0.04}=25\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
This is option D.

meta.top_criterion_original: correct answer (key circled in the bundled solutions)

1738.stem:
A tank contains 200 litres of petrol. More petrol is pumped into the tank for 20 minutes, until it is full.

The volume flow rate $R$ of petrol, in litres per minute, is given by

$$R=4\,(20-t)$$

parts.latex: Find a formula for the volume $V$ of petrol in the tank after $t$ minutes, where $t\le 20$.
How many litres of petrol were in the tank when it was full?
How long did it take to half fill the tank? (answer in minutes)

solutions.latex:
The flow rate is the rate of change of volume.
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=R=4(20-t)=80-4t$$
$$\begin{aligned} V &= \int(80-4t)\,dt \\ &= 80t-2t^2+C \end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $V=200$, so $C=200$.
$$\therefore\ V=80t-2t^2+200$$
criteria: Finds the correct primitive, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The tank is full when the flow stops, so $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4(20-t) &= 0 \\ t &= 20 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} V(20) &= 80(20)-2(20)^2+200 \\ &= 1000 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$

Half of the full volume of $1000$ L is $500$ L.
$$\begin{aligned} 80t-2t^2+200 &= 500 \\ 2t^2-80t+300 &= 0 \\ t^2-40t+150 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{40\pm\sqrt{1600-600}}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{40\pm\sqrt{1000}}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$t=35.811$ or $t=4.1886$.

The tank is full at $t=20$, so $t=35.811$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ t=4.1886 \text{ minutes (4 min 11 s)}$$
criteria: Forms the correct quadratic and solves it, or equivalent merit

1770.stem: The motion of a particle is given by $x=10t+4e^{-3.5t}-4$, where $x$ is the displacement from the starting position in metres and $t$ is time after the initial position in seconds.

figures.cap: solution sketch: dx/dt against t: y-intercept -4, asymptote dx/dt = 10, t-intercept -(2/7) ln(5/7)

parts.latex: Find the initial velocity.
Sketch the velocity-time graph.

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement, using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(e^{-3.5t}\right)=-3.5e^{-3.5t}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= 10+4\times(-3.5)e^{-3.5t} \\ &= 10-14e^{-3.5t} \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= 10-14e^0 \\ &= -4\text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

From part (a), the velocity is $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=10-14e^{-3.5t}$.

As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-3.5t}\to 0$, so $v\to 10$: the graph has the horizontal asymptote $v=10$.

The $t$-intercept is where $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10-14e^{-3.5t} &= 0 \\ e^{-3.5t} &= \dfrac{5}{7} \\ -3.5t &= \ln\dfrac{5}{7} \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln\frac{5}{7}}{-3.5} \\ &= -\dfrac{2\ln\frac{5}{7}}{7} \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{382_q23_s1}

meta.corrected: Source line ‘dx/dt = 10 + 4x - 3.5e^{-3.5t}’ is a slip for 10 + 4(-3.5)e^{-3.5t}; written as the correct derivative.
meta.marker_note: Half a mark each for: shape, asymptote, $y$-intercept, $x$-intercept.

Curve dx/dt = 10 - 14e^{-3.5t} plotted from the equation (rule 10) for t >= 0 at the crop's scale (it was close to true scale), 0.9pt with end arrow; asymptote 10 dashed (aux); intercepts -4 and -(2/7)ln(5/7) marked at computed positions (rule 16). t-axis extended past the curve end (rule 13). Low overlay scores are the paper's ruled dotted lines and handwriting, not misplacement.

1822.stem:
Light intensity is measured in lux. The light intensity, $I$ lux, a distance $d$ metres below the surface of the lake is given by:

$$I=6000e^{-kd}$$

where $k$ is a constant.

parts.latex:
The light intensity 6 metres below the surface of the lake is 1000 lux.

Find the value of $k$, correct to four decimal places.
At what rate, in lux per metre, is the light density decreasing 6 metres below the surface of the lake, correct to the nearest lux?

solutions.latex:
Substitute $d=6$ and $I=1000$ into $I=6000e^{-kd}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1000 &= 6000e^{-6k} \\ \dfrac{1}{6} &= e^{-6k} \\ \dfrac{\ln\frac{1}{6}}{-6} &= k \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=0.29862\ldots=0.2986\text{ (4 d.p.)}$$

The rate of change of the intensity is $\dfrac{dI}{dd}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dd} &= -0.2986\times 6000e^{-0.2986d} \\ &= -0.2986I \end{aligned}$$
When $d=6$, $I=1000$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dI}{dd} &= -0.2986\times 1000 \\ &= -298.6 \end{aligned}$$
Check: $-0.2986\times 6000\times e^{-0.2986\times 6}=-298.6$.

So the intensity is decreasing at about $299$ lux per metre.

parts.latex:
The motion of a particle moving in a horizontal line is given by $x=5t\,e^{-3t}$, where $x$ is the displacement of the particle in cm and $t$ is the time in minutes.

Determine the time when the particle is at rest.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when the velocity is zero. Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=5t & v&=e^{-3t}\\ u'&=5 & v'&=-3e^{-3t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 5e^{-3t}+5t\left(-3e^{-3t}\right) \\ &= 5e^{-3t}-15te^{-3t} \\ &= 5e^{-3t}(1-3t) \end{aligned}$$
$v=0$ needs $5e^{-3t}(1-3t)=0$. Since $5e^{-3t}\ne 0$ for all $t$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1-3t &= 0 \\ t &= \dfrac{1}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle is at rest after $\dfrac{1}{3}$ minute (or $20$ seconds).

1857.stem:
A particle moves in a straight line and its velocity $v$ m/s at time $t$ seconds is given by:

$$v=2-\dfrac{4}{t+1}$$

parts.latex: Determine the initial velocity.
Show that the particle is at rest when $t=1$.
Find an expression for the acceleration of the particle at time $t$.
Explain why the force is always to the right for all $t\ge 0$.
Describe the motion of the particle as $t\to\infty$.

solutions.latex:
The initial velocity is at $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}v(0)&=2-\dfrac{4}{0+1} \\ &=-2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{initial velocity }2\text{ m/s to the left}$$

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}0&=2-\dfrac{4}{t+1} \\ \dfrac{4}{t+1}&=2 \\ t+1&=2 \\ t&=1\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore$ the particle is at rest when $t=1$.

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is $a=\dfrac{dv}{dt}$. Write $v=2-4(t+1)^{-1}$:
$$\begin{aligned}a&=\dfrac{dv}{dt} \\ &=4(t+1)^{-2} \\ &=\dfrac{4}{(t+1)^2}\end{aligned}$$

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks

solutions.latex:
The force acts in the direction of the acceleration ($F=ma$ with $m>0$), so look at the sign of $a=\dfrac{4}{(t+1)^2}$.

The numerator $4>0$, and for $t\ge 0$ the denominator $(t+1)^2\ge 1>0$ (a perfect square with minimum value $1$).

$\therefore a>0$ for all $t\ge 0$, so the force is always to the right.

meta.criteria_generated: source rubric empty: rows written from the part marks

solutions.latex:
As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{4}{t+1}\to 0$, so $v\to 2$.

The particle is initially moving to the left, stops after $1$ second and then continues to the right, increasing in speed and approaching $2$ m/s.
criteria: States that $v\to 2$ as $t\to\infty$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source rubric empty; rows written from the 2 marks.

1912.stem:
An object moves along the number line so that its displacement ($x$ metres) from the origin is given by:

$$x(t)=12-2t+12\log_e(t+3)$$

where time $t$ is measured in seconds.

parts.latex: Where is the particle initially?
Show that the particle is at rest when $t=3$.
In which direction is the particle moving when $t>3$ ? Justify your statement with mathematical working or in words.
can_use: Particles at rest and changing direction

solutions.latex:
Initially means $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x(0) &= 12-0+12\ln 3 \\ &= 12+12\ln 3 \\ &\approx 25.2 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is } 12+12\ln 3\approx 25.2\text{ m to the right of the origin}$$

The particle is at rest when the velocity $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$.
$$v=-2+\dfrac{12}{t+3}$$
When $t=3$:
$$v=-2+\dfrac{12}{6}=0$$
$\therefore$ the particle is at rest when $t=3$.

For $t>3$ we have $t+3>6$, so
$$\dfrac{12}{t+3}<\dfrac{12}{6}=2 \quad\text{and hence}\quad v=-2+\dfrac{12}{t+3}<0$$
$\therefore$ the velocity is negative, so the particle moves in the negative direction (to the left).
criteria: Shows $v=-2+\dfrac{12}{t+3}$ and attempts to find its sign, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A substance decomposes at a rate that is proportional to the mass of the substance remaining. The remaining mass (M) can be modelled using the formula $M=M_0e^{-kt}$, where $t$ is the time in hours, $M_0$ is the initial mass and $k$ is a constant.

Initially there is 30 kg of the substance. After 24 hours half of the substance has decomposed.

Determine how long it will take for 90% of the substance to decompose.

solutions.latex:
Half decomposes after $24$ hours, so $M=15$ when $t=24$.
$$\begin{aligned} 15 &= 30e^{-24k} \\ e^{-24k} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ k &= \dfrac{\ln2}{24} \end{aligned}$$
$90\%$ decomposed leaves $10\%$, so $M=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= 30e^{-kt} \\ e^{-kt} &= \dfrac{1}{10} \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln10}{k} \\ &= \dfrac{24\ln10}{\ln2} \\ &\approx79.7 \text{ hours} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Writes $e^{-kt}=\dfrac{1}{10}$ with the correct $k$, or equivalent merit
Substitutes $M=15$ and $t=24$ into the formula, or equivalent merit

1960.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. It’s displacement, $x$ metres, from the origin, $O$ at time $t$ seconds, where $t\ge0$, is given by $x=4+3te^{-2t}$

parts.latex: Show the velocity of the particle is given by $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=3e^{-2t}\left(1-2t\right)$.
Show that the particle is at rest when $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
Find the greatest possible total distance the particle could travel.

solutions.latex:
The derivative of the constant $4$ is $0$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(3te^{-2t}\right)$.

Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=3t & v&=e^{-2t}\\ u'&=3 & v'&=-2e^{-2t}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dx}{dt}&=3e^{-2t}+3t\cdot\left(-2e^{-2t}\right)\\ &=3e^{-2t}-6te^{-2t}\\ &=3e^{-2t}(1-2t)\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Attempts to differentiate using the product rule

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$. At $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&=3e^{-2\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}\left(1-2\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\right)\\ &=3e^{-1}(1-1)\\ &=0\end{aligned}$$
Hence the particle is at rest when $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

The particle starts at $x=4$. Since $3e^{-2t}\ne0$, $v=0$ only when $1-2t=0$, that is at $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$. The sign of $v$:
$$\begin{aligned}v&>0 &&\text{for }0\le t<\dfrac{1}{2} &&\text{moving right}\\ v&<0 &&\text{for }t>\dfrac{1}{2} &&\text{moving left}\end{aligned}$$
At the turning point:
$$x=4+3\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)e^{-1}=4+\dfrac{3}{2e}$$
As $t\to\infty$, $x=4+\dfrac{3t}{e^{2t}}\to4+0=4$, approached from above but never reached.

Distance travelled moving right: $\left(4+\dfrac{3}{2e}\right)-4=\dfrac{3}{2e}$.

Distance travelled moving left, back towards $x=4$: $\left(4+\dfrac{3}{2e}\right)-4=\dfrac{3}{2e}$.
$$\therefore\ \text{greatest total distance}=\dfrac{3}{2e}+\dfrac{3}{2e}=\dfrac{3}{e}\text{ metres}$$
criteria: Calculates distance travelled in first half of journey, namely $\dfrac{3}{2e}$ metres

1986.stem:
A particle with velocity, $v\,ms^{-1}$ moves along a straight line from a fixed point $O$

$$v=-4\cos t$$

where the time $t$ is measured in seconds from $t=0$.

It is initially 1 metre to the right of the origin.

parts.latex: When, and where, does the particle first come to rest?

Show that the total distance travelled by the particle between $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ is

$(8-2\sqrt{3})$ metres.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$; the first time after $t=0$ is the smallest positive solution:
$$\begin{aligned}-4\cos t&=0\\ \cos t&=0\\ t&=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ s}\end{aligned}$$
For the position, integrate the velocity and use $x=1$ when $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}x&=\int-4\cos t\,dt\\ &=-4\sin t+C\\ 1&=0+C\\ x&=-4\sin t+1\end{aligned}$$
At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, $x=-4+1=-3$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle first comes to rest at }t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\text{ s, at }x=-3\text{ (3 m to the left of the origin)}$$
criteria: Finds $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ and an expression for $x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$v=-4\cos t$ changes sign at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, so find the distance in each part separately:
$$\begin{aligned}v&<0 &&\text{for }0\le t<\dfrac{\pi}{2} &&\text{moving left}\\ v&>0 &&\text{for }\dfrac{\pi}{2}<t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3} &&\text{moving right}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}-4\cos t\,dt&=\Big[-4\sin t\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\\ &=-4\end{aligned}$$
The particle moves left, so the distance travelled in this part is $4$ m.
$$\begin{aligned}\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}-4\cos t\,dt&=\Big[-4\sin t\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}\\ &=-4\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-1\right)\\ &=4-2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{total distance}=4+\left(4-2\sqrt{3}\right)=\left(8-2\sqrt{3}\right)\text{ metres}$$
criteria: Finds the distance travelled in one of the two intervals, or equivalent merit
Identifies that the direction changes at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$, or equivalent merit

1992.stem:
A prototype rocket which is initially at rest, takes off from a launchpad on the ground. It has a time of flight of $T$ seconds, and $t$ is the time in seconds, where $0\le t\le T$.

The velocity of the rocket, $v\,ms^{-1}$, is given by:

$$v(t)=0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)$$

parts.latex:
Shortly after the rocket takes off, the engine stops and it begins to descend towards the ground.

Find the time at which the rocket begins to descend.
Before the rocket starts to descend it reaches its maximum velocity. Find the time it takes for the rocket to achieve its maximum velocity. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The rocket rises while $v>0$ and begins to descend when $v$ returns to $0$ after take-off:
$$0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$$
Since $0.5e^t\ne0$, $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$, so
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{10}=0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi,\ \ldots$$
$t=0$ is the take-off, and for $0<t<10$, $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)>0$ so $v>0$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the rocket begins to descend at }t=10\text{ s}$$
criteria: Sets $v=0$ and finds $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For maximum velocity, $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=0$. Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=0.5e^t & v&=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\\ u'&=0.5e^t & v'&=\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dv}{dt}&=0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+0.5e^t\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\\ &=0.5e^t\left(\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\right)\end{aligned}$$
Since $0.5e^t\ne0$:
$$\begin{aligned}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)&=0\\ \tan\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)&=-\dfrac{\pi}{10}\end{aligned}$$
The rocket is rising for $0<t<10$, so $0<\dfrac{\pi t}{10}<\pi$. Tangent is negative in the second quadrant, so
$$\dfrac{\pi t}{10}=\pi-\tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}\right)\approx2.837$$
$$t\approx2.837\cdot\dfrac{10}{\pi}\approx9.03\text{ s}$$
$v=0$ at $t=0$ and at $t=10$ and $v>0$ between them, so this stationary point is the maximum.
$$\therefore\ \text{the rocket reaches its maximum velocity after }9.03\text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Differentiates and forms $\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=-\dfrac{\pi}{10}$, or equivalent merit
Differentiates using the product rule, or equivalent merit

2289.stem:
The population of parrots, $P$, is modelled by the function $P=P_0e^{-kt}$, where $t$ is time in years since May 2004.

In May 2004, there were 2500 parrots and by May 2014 the population had decreased to 1750.

parts.latex: Show that $P_0=2500$.
Find the value of $k$. (Answer correct to four decimal places).
If the population continues to decrease in this manner, what will be the expected population in May 2024? Answer to the nearest whole number.

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$ the population is $P=2500$.
$$\begin{aligned}2500&=P_0e^{-k\cdot 0}\\&=P_0\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P_0=2500$$

In May 2014, $t=10$ and $P=1750$, with $P_0=2500$.
$$\begin{aligned}1750&=2500e^{-10k}\\\dfrac{7}{10}&=e^{-10k}\\\ln\dfrac{7}{10}&=-10k\\k&=-\dfrac{1}{10}\ln\dfrac{7}{10}\\&=0.0357\ \text{(to 4 decimal places)}\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for $1750=2500e^{-10k}$; 1 for $k=0.0357$ (only the first mark is circled in the scan)
meta.format_note: Source scan circled only the first mark; rubric rewritten top-down. Checked: -ln(0.7)/10 = 0.035667.

solutions.latex:
May 2024 is $t=20$. Since $e^{-10k}=\dfrac{7}{10}$, we have $e^{-20k}=\left(\dfrac{7}{10}\right)^2$.
$$\begin{aligned}P&=2500e^{-20k}\\&=2500\times 0.49\\&=1225\ \text{parrots}\end{aligned}$$

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for the substitution with $t=20$; 1 for 1225 (follow through from the previous answer)
meta.marker_note: Follow through from the answer to part (b) is accepted.
meta.format_note: Source skipped the value of k; working completed using e^{-10k}=7/10. Checked: 2500e^{-0.714} = 1224.9, rounds to 1225.

2292.stem:
As a particle moves, its velocity, in metres per second, is described by the equation

$$v(t)=-2t^2+2t+4$$

where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 4 metres right of the origin.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of v against t: downward parabola from v=4 at t=0, crossing the t-axis at t=2, with the area from 0 to 3 shaded

parts.latex: Find the time taken for the particle to reach its maximum velocity.
Find the position of the particle when it first comes to rest.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds.

solutions.latex:
The velocity $v(t)=-2t^2+2t+4$ is a concave-down parabola, so its maximum is at the turning point, where $v'(t)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}v'(t)&=-4t+2\\0&=-4t+2\\t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{1}{2}\text{ s}$$
criteria: Recognises the maximum occurs at the turning point, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for recognising the maximum occurs at the turning point; 1 for $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v(t)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}-2t^2+2t+4&=0\\-2\left(t^2-t-2\right)&=0\\-2(t-2)(t+1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $t=2$ or $t=-1$; since $t\ge 0$, $t=2$.

Integrate the velocity to find the position.
$$x(t)=\int v\,dt=-\dfrac{2t^3}{3}+t^2+4t+C$$
Initially $x(0)=4$, so $C=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}x(2)&=-\dfrac{2\times 2^3}{3}+2^2+4\times 2+4\\&=\dfrac{32}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is }\dfrac{32}{3}\text{ m to the right of the origin}$$
criteria: Integrates to find $x(t)$, or equivalent merit
Factorises and solves $v=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for factorising and solving $v=0$; 1 for integrating to get $x(t)$; 1 for $x(2)=\dfrac{32}{3}$ m
meta.format_note: Rubric was one mark per step; rewritten top-down. Checked: -16/3+4+8+4 = 32/3.

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$, at $t=2$ (part (b)), so the distance is the total area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis, counting the part below the axis as positive.

\exfigure{162_q15_s1}

$$\int_0^2 v\,dt+\left|\int_2^3 v\,dt\right|$$
Using the antiderivative $F(t)=-\dfrac{2}{3}t^3+t^2+4t$:
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Distance}&=F(2)-F(0)+\big|F(3)-F(2)\big|\\&=\dfrac{20}{3}-0+\left|3-\dfrac{20}{3}\right|\\&=\dfrac{20}{3}+\dfrac{11}{3}\\&=\dfrac{31}{3}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the distance travelled is }\dfrac{31}{3}\text{ m}$$
criteria: Writes the two integrals, the second in absolute value, or equivalent merit

meta.top_criterion_original: 1 for the two integrals (second in absolute value); 1 for the evaluation
meta.format_note: Checked: F(2)=20/3, F(3)=3, v(3)=-8 so the particle is moving left on (2,3).

The ruled paper lines and scribbles are left out (rule 17); t ticks evenly spaced on a true scale. parts.latex:
A particle is moving on the $x$ axis. Its velocity, $v$ metres per second, at time $t$ seconds is given by $v=3-6\cos t$.

Initially the particle is at 4 metres on the right of the origin.

Which expression is the displacement function in terms of $t$ ?

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$\begin{aligned}x(t)&=\int(3-6\cos t)\,dt\\&=3t-6\sin t+C\end{aligned}$$
Initially $x(0)=4$:
$$\begin{aligned}4&=0-0+C\\C&=4\end{aligned}$$
$\therefore x(t)=3t-6\sin t+4$, which is option A.

parts.latex: The acceleration of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $a=4t+4$ . Initially the particle has a velocity of $-30$ m/s. When is the particle at rest?

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the integral of acceleration.
$$\begin{aligned}v&=\int(4t+4)\,dt\\&=2t^2+4t+c\end{aligned}$$
Initially $v=-30$, so when $t=0$, $c=-30$.
$$\begin{aligned}v&=2t^2+4t-30\\&=2(t^2+2t-15)\\&=2(t+5)(t-3)\end{aligned}$$
The particle is at rest when $v=0$, so $t=-5$ or $t=3$. Since $t\ge 0$, $t=3$, option C.

2409.stem: The population of ants is growing exponentially according to the equation $P=50e^{kt}$ , where $t$ is the time in days after the insect is first counted. After four days, it is observed that the population has doubled from the initial amount.

parts.latex: Find the initial number of ants and show that $k=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2$
At what rate (to the nearest whole number) is the population increasing at day 15?
How many days will it take for the number of ants to first reach 1500?

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$, $P_0=50e^0=50$, so the initial number of ants is $50$.

After four days the population has doubled, so $P=100$ when $t=4$.
$$\begin{aligned}100&=50e^{4k}\\e^{4k}&=2\\4k&=\ln 2\\k&=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the initial number of ants, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave marks only (no rubric wording); rubric rows written by us.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $P=50e^{kt}$ with $k=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2$.
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=50k\,e^{kt}$$
At $t=15$:
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{dP}{dt}&=50\times\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2\times e^{\frac{1}{4}\ln 2\times 15}\\&\approx 117\text{ ants per day}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave marks only (no rubric wording); rubric rows written by us. Checked: 116.57.

solutions.latex:
Put $P=1500$ with $k=\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2$ and take natural logs.
$$\begin{aligned}1500&=50e^{\left(\frac{1}{4}\ln 2\right)t}\\30&=e^{\left(\frac{1}{4}\ln 2\right)t}\\\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\ln 2\right)t&=\ln 30\\t&=\dfrac{\ln 30}{\frac{1}{4}\ln 2}\\&\approx 19.6\\&\approx 20\text{ days}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Forms and simplifies $30=e^{kt}$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave marks only (no rubric wording); rubric rows written by us. Checked: t = 19.63; the source answer 20 days (nearest whole day) kept.

parts.latex:
A particle is moving in a straight line such that its displacement $x$ metres at time $t$ seconds from the origin is given by the equation $x=k\cos(at+b)$, where $a$, $b$ and $k$ are constants.

The particle is stationary when $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\dfrac{11\pi}{12},\dfrac{17\pi}{12},\ldots$.

The initial acceleration of the particle is $6\sqrt{3}\ \text{ms}^{-2}$.

What could be the values of $a$, $b$ and $k$?

solutions.latex:
The particle is stationary at $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\dfrac{11\pi}{12},\dfrac{17\pi}{12}$. Every second stationary time is one period apart, so
$$\text{period}=\dfrac{17\pi}{12}-\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=\pi \quad\text{so}\quad a=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi}=2$$
Test option D, $x=-3\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 6\sin\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \\ \text{acceleration} &= 12\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$v=0$ when $2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=\pi,\ 2\pi,\ 3\pi,\ldots$ (the first value of $2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ for $t\ge0$ is $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$), giving $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\dfrac{11\pi}{12},\dfrac{17\pi}{12},\ldots$ as required.

At $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{acceleration} &= 12\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6} \\ &= 12\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= 6\sqrt{3}\ \text{ms}^{-2} \end{aligned}$$
Options B and C also have $a=2$ and the same stationary times, but their initial acceleration is $-6\sqrt{3}$, so only D fits.

meta.format_note: Source wrote the stationary condition as 0, pi, 2pi... 'taking the positive values'; written here as pi, 2pi, 3pi (t>0). Rejection of A, B, C added by us and checked: B has initial acceleration 12cos(-5pi/6)=-6sqrt3, C has -12cos(pi/6)=-6sqrt3, A has a=4.

2440.stem:
Ben is cooking a pizza. The temperature of the pizza oven is modelled by the equation

$$T=175-150\times(0.9)^{0.2t},$$

where $T$ is the temperature of the oven ($^\circ$C) at time $t$ minutes since the oven was switched on.

parts.latex: What was the initial temperature of the oven?
Calculate the average rate at which the temperature changes per minute from $t=25$ to $t=75$, correct to two decimal places.

Ben can place the pizza in the oven when the instantaneous rate of change of temperature is less than or equal to $1^\circ$C per minute.

Given that Ben turned the oven on at 10:30 am, find the earliest time that Ben can place the pizza in the oven, correct to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
At the start, $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} T &= 175-150\times(0.9)^{0} \\ &= 175-150 \\ &= 25^\circ\text{C} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; the single 1-mark row was written by us.

solutions.latex:
The average rate of change is $\dfrac{T(75)-T(25)}{75-25}$.
$$\begin{aligned} T(25) &= 175-150\times0.9^{0.2\times25} \\ &\approx 86.4265 \\ T(75) &= 175-150\times0.9^{0.2\times75} \\ &\approx 144.11633 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Average rate} &= \dfrac{144.11633-86.4265}{75-25} \\ &\approx 1.15^\circ\text{C/minute} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $T(25)$ and $T(75)$ and sets up the average rate, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. Checked: 57.6898/50=1.1538.

solutions.latex:
The instantaneous rate of change is $\dfrac{dT}{dt}$. Differentiating with $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^{kt}\right)=ka^{kt}\ln a$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dT}{dt} &= -150\times0.2\times(0.9)^{0.2t}\times\ln0.9 \\ &= -30\ln0.9\times(0.9)^{0.2t} \end{aligned}$$
The cut-off is where $\dfrac{dT}{dt}=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} -30\ln0.9\times(0.9)^{0.2t} &= 1 \\ (0.9)^{0.2t} &\approx 0.316374 \\ 0.2t &\approx \log_{0.9}0.316374 \\ t &\approx \dfrac{5\ln0.316374}{\ln0.9} \\ &\approx 54.6\ \text{minutes} \end{aligned}$$
The rate $-30\ln0.9\times(0.9)^{0.2t}$ decreases as $t$ increases, so it is $\le1$ for $t\ge54.6$. To the nearest minute this is $55$ minutes after $10{:}30$ am.
$$\text{Time}=10{:}30\ \text{am}+55\ \text{min}=11{:}25\ \text{am}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. The 'rate decreases so rate <= 1 for t >= 54.6' step was missing in the handwriting and added by us. Checked: 5 ln(0.316374)/ln(0.9)=54.61.

2449.stem:
A particle is moving along the $x$-axis so that its position, in metres, at time $t$ seconds is given by

$$x=2\ln(t^2+3)-t$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: hand diagram of the motion on a line: at rest at t=1 and t=3, particle path between

parts.latex: Determine the times when the particle is at rest.

Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first second.

Leave your answer in the form $\ln\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)-c$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers.
Find the maximum velocity of the particle.

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of position, using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\ln\left(t^2+3\right)=\dfrac{2t}{t^2+3}$.
$$v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=2\times\dfrac{2t}{t^2+3}-1=\dfrac{4t}{t^2+3}-1$$
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{4t}{t^2+3} &= 1 \\ 4t &= t^2+3 \\ t^2-4t+3 &= 0 \\ (t-1)(t-3) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=1 \text{ or } t=3\ \text{seconds}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style.

solutions.latex:
Factorise the velocity to see whether the particle changes direction in the first second.
$$v=\dfrac{4t-t^2-3}{t^2+3}=-\dfrac{(t-1)(t-3)}{t^2+3}$$
For $0\le t<1$ both $(t-1)$ and $(t-3)$ are negative, so $v<0$. The particle moves in one direction only (it is at rest at $t=1$), so the distance is $x(0)-x(1)$.
$$\begin{aligned} x(0) &= 2\ln3 \\ x(1) &= 2\ln4-1=4\ln2-1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 2\ln3-(4\ln2-1) \\ &= \ln3^2-\ln2^4+1 \\ &= \ln9-\ln16+1 \\ &= \ln\dfrac{9}{16}+1 \\ &\approx 0.42\ \text{m} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. The 'v < 0 on [0,1], no change of direction' step was missing in the handwriting and added by us (checked: v = -(t-1)(t-3)/(t^2+3)). The answer ln(9/16) + 1 fits the requested form ln(a/b) - c with a = 9, b = 16, c = -1. Checked: 0.4246.

solutions.latex:
The acceleration is the derivative of velocity, using the quotient rule on $v=\dfrac{4t}{t^2+3}-1$.
$$a=\dfrac{4(t^2+3)-4t\times2t}{(t^2+3)^2}=\dfrac{12-4t^2}{(t^2+3)^2}$$
Maximum velocity occurs where $a=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 12-4t^2 &= 0 \\ t^2 &= 3 \\ t &= \sqrt{3} \quad(t\ge0) \end{aligned}$$
Test: $a>0$ for $0\le t<\sqrt{3}$ and $a<0$ for $t>\sqrt{3}$, so $v$ increases then decreases and has a maximum at $t=\sqrt{3}$ (between the rest times $t=1$ and $t=3$).
$$\begin{aligned} v_{\max} &= \dfrac{4\sqrt{3}}{3+3}-1 \\ &= \dfrac{2\sqrt{3}}{3}-1 \\ &\approx 0.1547\ \text{m/s} \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{515_q28_s1}
criteria: Finds $t=\sqrt{3}$ and justifies a maximum, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. The sign test for a was added by us (the handwriting only argued the maximum lies between t = 1 and t = 3). \exfigure{515_q28_s1} kept. Checked: v(sqrt3) = 0.1547, and v -> -1 as t -> infinity, v(0) = -1.

Short vertical joins show the turning points (the sketch just stacks the rows). Teacher's note 'Draw a diagram of the motion' not drawn. Overlay not meaningful. Rules 4,17,18,11.

parts.latex:
A heater converts electrical power, measured in watts, into heat in such a way that the heat produced is given by the function $h(x)=\left(f(x)\right)^2$.

The heater is plugged into a faulty socket which outputs $x=g(t)$ watts at time $t$ seconds.

The power output at time $t=1$ is 3 watts and is increasing at a rate of 4 watts per second.

By considering $h'(x)$ and using the fact that $\dfrac{d}{dt}f\left(g(t)\right)=f'\left(g(t)\right)\times g'(t)$, find the rate of change of the heat produced at time $t=1$, given that $f(3)=5$ and $f'(3)=2$.

solutions.latex:
Given $h(x)=\left[f(x)\right]^2$, differentiate with the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{dh}{dx}=2f(x)f'(x)$$
The power output is $x=g(t)$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=g'(t)$.

Given: $g(1)=3$ (so $x=3$ when $t=1$), $g'(1)=4$, $f(3)=5$ and $f'(3)=2$.

By the chain rule, $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{dh}{dx}\cdot\dfrac{dx}{dt}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dh}{dt} &= 2f(x)f'(x)\,g'(t) \end{aligned}$$
At $t=1$, $x=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dh}{dt} &= 2f(3)f'(3)g'(1) \\ &= 2\times5\times2\times4 \\ &= 80 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source gave no marks breakdown; criteria rows written by us in NESA style. The answer is left as the bare number 80 because the question gives no units for h. The question's hint 'f'(x) = f'(g(t)) x g'(t)' is the derivative of f(g(t)), not f'(x); left as printed (question not changed).
meta.edited_from_original: Owner 17 Nov: "if the paper has a mistake, we should fix it." Printed the chain rule as f'(x) = f'(g(t)) × g'(t); now d/dt f(g(t)) = f'(g(t)) × g'(t).

2487.stem:
A radioactive substance decays at a rate proportional to the mass present.

The rate of change is given by $\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$, where $k$ is a positive constant and $M$ grams is the mass present at any time, $t$ years.

parts.latex: Show that $M = 75e^{-kt}$ is a solution to this equation.
If $68$g remains after a period of $2$ years, find $k$ correct to two significant figures.

Find the mass of the substance that remains after $6$ years.

Give your answer to one decimal place.
At what rate is the substance decaying after $6$ years ?

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $M = 75e^{-kt}$ with respect to $t$.
$$\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -k\cdot 75e^{-kt}$$
But $75e^{-kt} = M$, so
$$\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$$
Hence $M = 75e^{-kt}$ is a solution.

Substitute $M=68$ and $t=2$ into $M = 75e^{-kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 68 &= 75e^{-2k} \\ \dfrac{68}{75} &= e^{-2k} \\ -2k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{68}{75}\right) \\ k &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\left(\dfrac{68}{75}\right) \\ &\approx 0.049 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k \approx 0.049$$

Substitute $t=6$ and $k \approx 0.049$ into $M = 75e^{-kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= 75e^{-6k} \\ &\approx 55.9 \text{ g} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ M \approx 55.9 \text{ g}$$

meta.format_note: 55.9 g follows from using the rounded $k=0.049$ from part (b).

solutions.latex:
The rate of decay is given by $\dfrac{dM}{dt} = -kM$, with $k \approx 0.049$ and $M \approx 55.9$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dM}{dt} &= -kM \\ &\approx -2.7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the substance is decaying at approximately } 2.7 \text{ g/year}$$

2489.stem: The velocity, $\dot{x}$, of a particle moving in a straight line is given by $\dot{x} = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$, where $x$ is in metres and $t$ is in seconds. The particle is initially at the origin.

parts.latex: Find the initial velocity.
Find an expression for the displacement of the particle, $x$, in terms of $t$.
Find when the particle first comes to rest.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first $7$ seconds.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=0$ into the velocity.
$$\begin{aligned} \dot{x} &= \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\cdot 0\right) \\ &= \cos 0 \\ &= 1 \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$x = \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) + C$$
When $t = 0$, $x = 0$, so $C = 0$.
$$\therefore\ x = \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right)$$

The particle is at rest when $\dot{x} = 0$.
$$\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}t\right) = 0$$
The first positive solution of $\cos\theta=0$ is $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\pi}{6}t &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 3 \text{ seconds}$$

The particle is at rest at $t=3$ and then reverses, so find the distance in two stages.
$$\begin{aligned} x(3) &= \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ &= \dfrac{6}{\pi} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance travelled} &= \dfrac{6}{\pi} + \left(\dfrac{6}{\pi} + \dfrac{3}{\pi}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{15}{\pi} \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
The displacement of a particle moving along the $x$ axis at time $t$ is given by:

$$x=t^3+\ln\left(2t^3+1\right)\ \text{ for } t\ge 0$$

How many times is the particle stationary?

solutions.latex:
Differentiating:
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=3t^2+\dfrac{6t^2}{2t^3+1}$$
The particle is stationary when $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3t^2(2t^3+1)+6t^2&=0 \\ 3t^2(2t^3+3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Then $t=0$ or $t=-\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{3}{2}}$, and only $t=0$ is valid for $t\ge0$.

Hence there is one solution.

2519.stem:
A quantity $Q$ of the radioactive isotope Carbon-14 decays according the equation of natural decay $Q=Q_0e^{-kt}$ where $Q_0$ is the initial mass of Carbon-14, $k$ is a constant and $t$ is the time in years.

The half-life of a radioactive substance is the time it takes to reduce to half its original mass. Carbon-14 has a half-life of 5730 years.

parts.latex: Find the exact value of $k$.

A fossilised leaf contains $9\%$ of its original amount of Carbon-14.

How old is the fossilised leaf? Give your answer correct to the nearest year.

solutions.latex:
After one half-life, $Q=\dfrac{Q_0}{2}$ when $t=5730$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{Q_0}{2} &= Q_0e^{-5730k} \\ 0.5 &= e^{-5730k} \\ \ln0.5 &= -5730k \\ k &= -\dfrac{\ln0.5}{5730} \\ &= \dfrac{\ln2}{5730} \end{aligned}$$
No penalty for writing $k=0.0001$ to 4 d.p.

The leaf has $9\%$ of its original amount, so $Q=0.09Q_0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.09Q_0 &= Q_0e^{-kt} \\ 0.09 &= e^{-kt} \end{aligned}$$
Using $k=-\dfrac{\ln0.5}{5730}$, this is
$$0.09=e^{\frac{\ln0.5}{5730}t}$$
Taking logarithms:
$$\begin{aligned} \ln0.09 &= \dfrac{\ln0.5}{5730}\,t \\ t &= \dfrac{5730\ln0.09}{\ln0.5} \\ &\approx 19\,906 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the leaf is about } 19\,906 \text{ years old}$$
No penalty for incorrect rounding.
criteria: Correct equation $0.09=e^{-kt}$ or similar, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
In 2025, $t = 45$.
$$\begin{aligned} M &= 0.045e^{45 \times \frac{1}{40}\ln 6\,800\,000} \\ &\approx 2\,186\,679.032 \text{ million} \\ &\approx 2\,186\,679 \text{ million (to the nearest million)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\dfrac{dM}{dt} = kM_0e^{kt}$$

2558.stem:
As a particle moves, its velocity, in metres per second, is described by the equation

$$v(t) = -2t^2 + 2t + 4$$

where $t \geq 0$ is the time in seconds. The particle is initially 4 metres right of the origin.

parts.latex: Find the time taken for the particle to reach its maximum velocity.
Find the position of the particle when it first comes to rest.
Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 3 seconds.

solutions.latex:
Method 1: maximum velocity occurs when $a(t) = 0$.

Differentiating $v(t) = -2t^2 + 2t + 4$,
$$a(t) = -4t + 2$$
$$\begin{aligned} -4t + 2 &= 0 \\ t &= 0.5 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
Method 2: since velocity is a quadratic function, the maximum is at the vertex.
$$t = -\dfrac{b}{2a} = -\dfrac{2}{2(-2)} = 0.5 \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Attempts to solve $a(t) = 0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v(t) = 0$.
$$v(t) = 0 \text{ gives } t = -1 \text{ or } t = 2$$
Since $t \ge 0$, it first comes to rest at $t = 2$.

Since $x(0) = 4$, the position at $t = 2$ is
$$\begin{aligned} x(2) &= 4 + \displaystyle\int_0^2 v(t)\,dt \\ &= 4 + \left[-\dfrac{2}{3}t^3 + t^2 + 4t\right]_0^2 \\ &= 10\dfrac{2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
The particle is $10\dfrac{2}{3}$ metres to the right of the origin.
criteria: Finds the distance travelled in the first two seconds, or equivalent merit
Finds the time the particle comes to rest, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction at $t = 2$, so the distance is the sum of the magnitudes of the displacements on $[0,2]$ and $[2,3]$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Distance travelled} &= \int_0^2 v(t)\,dt + \left|\int_2^3 v(t)\,dt\right| \\ &= 6\dfrac{2}{3} - \int_2^3 v(t)\,dt \\ &= 6\dfrac{2}{3} - \left[-\dfrac{2}{3}t^3 + t^2 + 4t\right]_2^3 \\ &= 6\dfrac{2}{3} - \left[\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}(3)^3 + (3)^2 + 4(3)\right) - \left(-\dfrac{2}{3}(2)^3 + (2)^2 + 4(2)\right)\right] \\ &= 10\dfrac{1}{3} \text{ metres}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the distance travelled by the particle in the third second, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A population, $P$, which is initially 40 500, varies according to the formula $P = 40500\,b^{\frac{-t}{5}}$ where $b$ is a positive constant and $t$ is time in years, $t \ge 0$

The population is 1500 after 15 years.

Find the value of $t$, correct to one decimal place, for which the instantaneous rate of decrease is 25 people per year.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $P = 1500$, $t = 15$ to find $b$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1500 &= 40500\,b^{-\frac{15}{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{27} &= b^{-3} \\ 27 &= b^3 \\ b &= 3 \end{aligned}$$
We want $t$ when $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = -25$.

Using $y = a^x$, $y' = \ln a \cdot a^x$ on $P = 40500 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 40500 \times \dfrac{-1}{5}\ln 3 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} \\ &= -8100\ln 3 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} \end{aligned}$$
Set this equal to $-25$.
$$\begin{aligned} -8100\ln 3 \times 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} &= -25 \\ 3^{-\frac{t}{5}} &= \dfrac{1}{324\ln 3} \\ -\dfrac{t}{5} &= \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{324\ln 3}\right)}{\ln 3} \\ t &= \dfrac{-5\ln\left(\frac{1}{324\ln 3}\right)}{\ln 3} \\ &= 26.737\ldots \\ &\approx 26.7 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t \approx 26.7 \text{ years}$$
criteria: Finds $b$, sets $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=-25$ and finds a correct derivative, or equivalent merit

2606.stem: The water level, measured in meters, at a dam has been changing at a rate of $R = t^3 - 11t^2 + 35t - 29$ for $0 \le t \le 6$ years.

parts.latex: When is the water level decreasing most rapidly?
What is the change in water level of the dam for the 6 years?

solutions.latex:
The water level decreases most rapidly where $R$ is least, so find the stationary points of $R$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dR}{dt} &= 3t^2-22t+35 \\ &= (3t-7)(t-5) \end{aligned}$$
Setting $\dfrac{dR}{dt}=0$ gives $t=\dfrac{7}{3}$ or $t=5$.

Nature, using the second derivative $\dfrac{d^2R}{dt^2}=6t-22$:
$$\begin{aligned} t=\dfrac{7}{3}:\ & \dfrac{d^2R}{dt^2}=-8<0 &&\text{maximum}\\ t=5:\ & \dfrac{d^2R}{dt^2}=8>0 &&\text{minimum, } R=-4\end{aligned}$$
Check the endpoints of the domain:
$$\begin{aligned} t=0:\ & R=-29\\ t=6:\ & R=1\end{aligned}$$
The least value of $R$ is $-29$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the water level decreases most rapidly at } t=0$$
criteria: Finds the stationary points and their nature, or equivalent merit
Finds the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The change in level is the integral of the rate:
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^6\left(t^3-11t^2+35t-29\right)dt &= \left[\dfrac{t^4}{4}-\dfrac{11t^3}{3}+\dfrac{35t^2}{2}-29t\right]_0^6 \\ &= -12 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the water level decreased by } 12 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Writes the correct integral, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The displacement of a particle at time $(t)$ seconds is given by:

$$x=3e^{-2t}+4e^{-t}+2t.$$

Find the exact time at which the particle comes to rest.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when the velocity $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$.
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=-6e^{-2t}-4e^{-t}+2$$
Setting this to zero:
$$-6e^{-2t}-4e^{-t}+2=0$$
Let $u=e^{-t}$, so $e^{-2t}=u^2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6u^2+4u-2&=0 \\ 3u^2+2u-1&=0 \\ (u+1)(3u-1)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Since $e^{-t}>0$, $e^{-t}=-1$ has no solution. So $e^{-t}=\dfrac{1}{3}$.
$$\begin{aligned} -t&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right) \\ t&=-(\ln 1-\ln 3) \\ &=\ln 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\ln 3 \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Correct differentiation and progress towards solving $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=0$

2626.stem: At 7 pm on a Wednesday evening after a storm, Jack's water tank was full. The capacity of the tank was 3 000 litres. The tap on the tank, however, was leaking such that the change in volume at any time ($t$) hours was proportional to the volume ($V$) of the tank and can be modelled by the equation $V=V_0e^{-kt}$.

parts.latex: Find $V_0$, the initial volume of the tank.
Given that the volume of the tank after 3 hours is 1 900 litres, find the value of $k$ correct to 4 decimal places.
By the time Jack discovered that the tank was leaking, there were only 250 litres of water remaining. At what time and on which day did Jack discover the leak (correct to the nearest minute)?

solutions.latex:
The model is $V=V_0e^{-kt}$.

When $t=0$, $V=3\,000$:

$$3\,000=V_0e^0$$

$$\therefore\ V_0=3\,000 \text{ litres}$$

The model is $V=3\,000e^{-kt}$. When $t=3$, $V=1\,900$:

$$\begin{aligned} 1\,900&=3\,000e^{-3k} \\ \dfrac{19}{30}&=e^{-3k} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{19}{30}\right)&=-3k \\ k&=-\dfrac{1}{3}\ln\left(\dfrac{19}{30}\right) \\ &\approx 0.1522528008 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k\approx 0.1523 \text{ (4 decimal places)}$$
criteria: Correct progress towards finding $k$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
When $V=250$:

$$\begin{aligned} 250&=3\,000e^{-kt} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{25}{300}\right)&=-kt \\ t&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{25}{300}\right)}{-0.1522528008} \end{aligned}$$

So $t=16$ hours $19$ minutes.

Adding this to 7 pm Wednesday gives 11:19 am Thursday.

$$\therefore\ \text{The leak was discovered at 11:19 am on Thursday.}$$

2635.stem:
The velocity, in cm/s of a particle moving in a straight line is given by the equation:

$$v=4t^3-24t^2+20t$$

parts.latex: Find an expression for $x$, the position of the particle as a function of time.

solutions.latex:
Integrating the velocity:

$$\begin{aligned} x&=\int(4t^3-24t^2+20t)\,dt \\ &=t^4-8t^3+10t^2+C \end{aligned}$$

When $t=0$, $x=3$, so $C=3$.

$$\therefore\ x=t^4-8t^3+10t^2+3$$
criteria: Integrates to find $x$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
When $t=1$:

$$v=4(1)^3-24(1)^2+20(1)=0$$

So there is a stationary point at $t=1$.

The nature is decided by the sign of the second derivative:

$$\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=12t^2-48t+20$$

When $t=1$:

$$\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=12-48+20=-16<0$$

$$\therefore\ \text{The graph has a maximum turning point at } t=1.$$
criteria: Shows $v=0$ and recognises a stationary point, or equivalent merit

2669.stem:
A water cooler, which is initially full, is drained so that at time $t$ seconds the volume of water $V$, in litres, is given by

$$V=32\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)^{2}\ \text{ for } 0\le t\le 90.$$

parts.latex: How much water was initially in the cooler?
After how many seconds was the cooler one-quarter full?
At what rate was the water draining out when the cooler was one-quarter full?

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} V&=32(1-0)^{2} \\ &=32 \text{ litres} \end{aligned}$$

One-quarter full means $V=\dfrac{32}{4}=8$.
$$\begin{aligned} 8&=32\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)^{2} \\ \dfrac{1}{4}&=\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)^{2} \\ \dfrac{1}{2}&=1-\dfrac{t}{90} \\ \dfrac{t}{90}&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ t&=45 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

Using the chain rule:
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=32\times2\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{90}\right)=-\dfrac{64}{90}\left(1-\dfrac{t}{90}\right)$$
When $t=45$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt}&=-\dfrac{64}{90}\left(1-\dfrac{45}{90}\right) \\ &=-\dfrac{64}{90}\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &=-\dfrac{32}{90} \\ &=-\dfrac{16}{45} \end{aligned}$$
The water is draining at $\dfrac{16}{45}$ litres/sec when the cooler is one-quarter full.

parts.latex: The population, $N$, of a colony of mice grows exponentially and is modelled by the formula $N = 550e^{0.232t}$, where $t$ is the time in days. During which day will the population $N$ reach 13750 mice?

solutions.latex:
Set $N = 13750$ in the model.
$$13750 = 550e^{0.232t}$$
Divide both sides by 550.
$$e^{0.232t} = 25$$
Take natural logarithms of both sides.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.232t &= \ln 25 \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln 25}{0.232} \\ &\approx 13.87 \end{aligned}$$
The population reaches 13750 after 13.87 days, which is during the $14^{\text{th}}$ day.

So the correct option is C.

parts.latex: Given that displacement of the particle, $x$, is increasing at decreasing rate with respect to time $t$. Which of the following pairs of inequalities best describe the given statement?

solutions.latex:
The displacement $x$ is increasing, so the velocity is positive.
$$\dfrac{dx}{dt} > 0$$
The rate of increase is decreasing, so the velocity $\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ is decreasing, which means its gradient is negative.
$$\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} < 0$$
Hence the pair is $\dfrac{dx}{dt} > 0$, $\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2} < 0$, which is option B. Option A would be increasing at an increasing rate, and C and D have $\dfrac{dx}{dt} < 0$, so $x$ would be decreasing.

How many grams of the compound are formed in the first 4 minutes? Express you answer in exact form.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t = 4$ into the formula.
$$\begin{aligned} R &= 20 + \dfrac{5}{4+1} \\ &= 21 \text{ g/min} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the rate is } 21 \text{ g/min}$$

As $t \to \infty$, the term $\dfrac{5}{t+1} \to 0$.
$$R \to 20 + 0 = 20$$
$$\therefore\ R \text{ approaches } 20 \text{ g/min}$$

criteria: Correct shape with correct $R$-intercept, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: graph of $R = 20 + \dfrac{5}{t+1}$ on the question's axes ($t$ horizontal, $R$ vertical), for $t \ge 0$ only. Decreasing curve starting at the $R$-intercept $(0, 25)$, passing through $(4, 21)$, approaching the dashed horizontal asymptote $R = 20$ labelled on the $R$-axis.

solutions.latex:
The amount formed is the integral of the rate over the first 4 minutes.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total grams} &= \int_0^4 \left(20 + \dfrac{5}{t+1}\right) dt \\ &= \Big[20t + 5\ln|t+1|\Big]_0^4 \\ &= 80 + 5\ln 5 - (0 + 5\ln 1) \\ &= 80 + 5\ln 5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ (80 + 5\ln 5) \text{ grams}$$

2778.stem: The velocity of the particle is given by $\dot{x} = 3\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ metres per second for $0 \le t \le 2\pi$.

parts.latex: Find the equation of the acceleration $\ddot{x}$ of the particle as a function of time.
Calculate the maximum speed of the particle and the times at which it occurs in the given domain.
Find the equation of the displacement of the particle, $x$, as a function of time if the particle was initially 3 metres to the left of the origin.

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
$$\ddot{x} = 3\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$

The maximum speed is the amplitude of $\dot{x}$, so it is $3$ m/s.

Speed is $|\dot{x}|$, so it is greatest when $\dot{x} = \pm 3$, which is when the acceleration is zero.
$$\ddot{x} = 3\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 0$$
$$\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 0$$

For $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, we have $-\dfrac{\pi}{3} \le t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} \le \dfrac{5\pi}{3}$, so
$$t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{2} \text{ or } \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$$
$$t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \text{ or } \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$

The maximum speed is $3$ m/s, at $t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$ and $t = \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$ seconds.
criteria: Correct speed and one correct time, or equivalent merit
Correct speed or one correct time, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Added the line giving the range of $t-\frac{\pi}{3}$ to justify the two solutions; mathematics unchanged.

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int \dot{x}\,dt \\ &= \int 3\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) dt \\ &= -3\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + C \end{aligned}$$

Initially $x = -3$ (to the left of the origin), so at $t = 0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -3 &= -3\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) + C \\ C &= -1.5 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = -3\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) - 1.5$$

meta.marker_note: Source also awards 1 mark for finding the constant correctly from an incorrect integration.

2779.stem: The population of the suburb of Baulkham Hills has been growing over the last few years. At the beginning of January 2019, the population was 32500 and at the beginning of January 2022 it is estimated at 37700.

parts.latex: Assume that the population $P$ obeys the law of natural growth $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = kP$, for some positive constant $k$, where $t$ is number of years since the beginning of January 2019. Show that $P = 32500e^{kt}$ satisfies the equation $\dfrac{dP}{dt} = kP$.
Find the value of the positive constant $k$. Leave your answer in exact form.
Calculate the size of the population at the beginning of January 2027.
During which year will the population first exceed 55000?

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $P = 32500e^{kt}$ with respect to $t$.
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = k \times 32500e^{kt}$$

Since $P = 32500e^{kt}$, this gives
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = kP$$

Hence $P = 32500e^{kt}$ satisfies the equation.

meta.format_note: Source began 'Assume P satisfies the equation'; reworded as direct differentiation, same mathematics.

solutions.latex:
At the beginning of January 2019, $t = 0$ and $P = 32500$.

At the beginning of January 2022, $t = 3$ and $P = 37700$.

Substitute into $P = 32500e^{kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 37700 &= 32500e^{3k} \\ \dfrac{37700}{32500} &= e^{3k} \\ 3k &= \ln\dfrac{37700}{32500} \\ k &= \dfrac{1}{3}\ln\dfrac{377}{325} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{3}\ln 1.16 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Significant progress towards finding the equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
January 2027 is $8$ years after January 2019, so $t = 8$.
$$\begin{aligned} P &= 32500e^{\frac{1}{3}\ln 1.16 \times 8} \\ &= 48280.45\ldots \\ &\approx 48280 \end{aligned}$$

meta.marker_note: Ignore rounding.

solutions.latex:
We need $P > 55000$.
$$32500e^{\frac{1}{3}\ln 1.16\, t} > 55000$$
$$\dfrac{55000}{32500} < e^{\frac{1}{3}\ln 1.16\, t}$$
$$t > 10.63$$

Check by trial: at $t = 10$, $P = 53301$; at $t = 11$, $P = 56005$.

The population first exceeds $55000$ during the year $2019 + 10 = 2029$.
$$\therefore\ \text{During } 2029$$

2813.stem: A particle moves in a straight line so that its distance $x$ metres from the origin is given by $x = 4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ for $0 \le t \le \pi$.

figures.cap: blank axes (t horizontal, x vertical) for sketch
solution sketch: sketch of x=4cos(t-pi/3)

parts.latex: Where is the particle initially?
When does the particle first come to rest?
When does the particle first pass through the origin?
Find when the rate of change of velocity is zero.

Hence or otherwise, draw a neat sketch of $x = 4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ for $0 \le t \le \pi$, showing its main features.

\exfigure{1321_q32_1}
Calculate the total distance travelled between $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $t = \dfrac{6\pi}{7}$.

solutions.latex:
Initially $t = 0$:

$$\begin{aligned} x &= 4\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is initially } 2 \text{ m from the origin}$$

The particle is at rest when $v = 0$.

$$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = -4\sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$

$$\begin{aligned} \sin\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) &= 0 \\ t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} &= 0 \\ t &= \dfrac{\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle first comes to rest when } t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$$
criteria: Differentiates correctly to find $v$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle is at the origin when $x = 0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) &= 0 \\ t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle first passes through the origin when } t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$

The rate of change of velocity is the acceleration $a = \dfrac{dv}{dt}$.

$$a = -4\cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$$

Set $a = 0$:

$$\begin{aligned} \cos\left(t - \dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) &= 0 \\ t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} &= \dfrac{\pi}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{5\pi}{6} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ a = 0 \text{ when } t = \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$$
criteria: Differentiates correctly to find $a$ and substitutes $a = 0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1321_q32_s1}
criteria: Correct graph but missing some features, or equivalent merit
Incorrect graph showing all features, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Solution already has drawing placeholder \exfigure{1321_q32_s1} (record's sketch_id is 1321_q32_s2; check which is intended). Sketch still to draw if not yet drawn: $x=4\cos\left(t-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ on $0\le t\le\pi$, start $(0,2)$, maximum $\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3},4\right)$, inflection and $t$-intercept $\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6},0\right)$, end point $(\pi,-2)$. Check: $4\cos\left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\right)=-2$. Marking: 3 | Correct answer.

solutions.latex:
From the graph, the particle moves towards the maximum at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ ($x = 4$), then reverses and moves back towards the origin. Split the motion at the turning point.

At $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$:

$$x = 4\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$$

At $t = \dfrac{6\pi}{7}$, $t - \dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{11\pi}{21}$:

$$x = 4\cos\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{21}\right)$$

From $t = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$ to $t = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ the particle travels $4 - 4\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$.

From $x = 4$ to the final position (which is negative, as $\dfrac{6\pi}{7} > \dfrac{5\pi}{6}$) it travels $4 + \left|4\cos\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{21}\right)\right|$.

$$\text{Total distance} = \left(4 - 4\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)\right) + 4 + \left|4\cos\left(\dfrac{11\pi}{21}\right)\right|$$

$$\therefore\ \text{total distance} \approx 4.835 \text{ m (3 d.p.)}$$
criteria: Finds either $f\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$ or $f\left(\dfrac{6\pi}{7}\right)$ with $+4$, or equivalent merit
Separates the distances, or equivalent merit

2814.stem:
A radioactive substance is decaying such that its mass, $m$ grams, at a time $t$ years after initial observation is given by

$$m = 60e^{kt}, \text{ where } k \text{ is a constant.}$$

After 100 years, the mass of radioactive substance is 42 grams.

parts.latex: Find the value of $k$, leaving your answer in exact form.
Find the value of $t$ when $m = 30$.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t = 100$ and $m = 42$ into $m = 60e^{kt}$.

$$\begin{aligned} 42 &= 60e^{100k} \\ 0.7 &= e^{100k} \\ 100k &= \ln 0.7 \\ k &= \dfrac{1}{100}\ln 0.7 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ k = \dfrac{1}{100}\ln 0.7$$

Using $k = \dfrac{1}{100}\ln 0.7$ and $m = 30$:

$$\begin{aligned} 30 &= 60e^{\frac{t}{100}\ln 0.7} \\ 0.5 &= e^{\frac{t}{100}\ln 0.7} \\ \ln 0.5 &= \dfrac{t}{100}\ln 0.7 \\ t &= 100\times\dfrac{\ln 0.5}{\ln 0.7} \\ &\approx 194.34 \text{ (2 d.p.)} \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ t \approx 194.34 \text{ years}$$

2844.stem: A tank contains 50 litres of water. A tap at the base of the tank allows water to flow out at a rate proportional to the quantity of water still in the tank at that time, given by the equation $W=W_0e^{-kt}$, where $W$ is the amount of water in the tank and $t$ is time in minutes. After 2 minutes, 10 litres of water has been released.

parts.latex: Show that $k=-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{4}{5}$.
How much water has been released from the tank after 10 minutes? Give your answer to the nearest litre.

solutions.latex:
Initially $W_0=50$, so $W=50e^{-kt}$.

After 2 minutes, 10 litres has been released, so $W=40$ when $t=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 40 &= 50e^{-2k} \\ \dfrac{4}{5} &= e^{-2k} \\ \ln\dfrac{4}{5} &= -2k \\ k &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{4}{5} \end{aligned}$$

When $t=10$, using $k=-\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{4}{5}$:
$$\begin{aligned} W &= 50e^{-10\times\left(-\frac{1}{2}\ln\frac{4}{5}\right)} \\ &= 16.384 \end{aligned}$$
So 16.384 litres of water are in the tank.
$$\begin{aligned} 50-16.384 &= 33.616 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 34 \text{ litres of water have been released}$$

2846.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line, starting from the origin. At time $t$ seconds, the particle has displacement $x$ metres from the origin and velocity $v$ m/s. The displacement is given by $x=2t-3\log_e(t+1)$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of displacement x against t

parts.latex: Find an expression for the velocity $v$.
Find the initial acceleration.
When does the particle come to rest?
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first three seconds. Answer correct to four decimal places.

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 2t-3\log_e(t+1) \\ v &= \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 2-\dfrac{3}{t+1} \end{aligned}$$

Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
$$v=2-3(t+1)^{-1}$$
$$\begin{aligned} a &= 3(t+1)^{-2} \\ &= \dfrac{3}{(t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} a &= \dfrac{3}{(0+1)^2} \\ &= 3 \text{ m/s}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct acceleration equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2-\dfrac{3}{t+1} &= 0 \\ \dfrac{3}{t+1} &= 2 \\ t+1 &= \dfrac{3}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is at rest when } t=\dfrac{1}{2} \text{ s}$$

The particle turns at $t=\dfrac{1}{2}$ (from part (c)), so find the displacement at the end and at the turning point.
$$\begin{aligned} t=3: \quad x &= 2\times 3-3\log_e 4 \\ &= 6-3\log_e 4 \\ &\approx 1.841116 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} t=\dfrac{1}{2}: \quad x &= 2\times\dfrac{1}{2}-3\log_e\left(\dfrac{1}{2}+1\right) \\ &= 1-3\log_e\dfrac{3}{2} \\ &\approx -0.216395 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{1322_q30_s1}

The particle goes from $0$ to $-0.216395$, then back past the origin to $1.841116$, so the total distance is
$$\begin{aligned} (6-3\log_e 4)+2\left|1-3\log_e\dfrac{3}{2}\right| &\approx 2.273907 \\ &\approx 2.2739 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Diagram 1322_q30_s1 kept as in source (number line of motion).

1322_q30_s1.notes: x=2t−3ln(t+1) plotted from its equation for 0≤t≤3.42 (0.9pt) at the crop's scale. Dots are at the computed points (0.5, −0.2164) and (3, 1.8411). Tick labels are tiny, as in the crop, and t and x are italic. CHECK: the '0.5' t-tick label sits on the minimum-point dot, as on the paper (rule 11). It needs a small shift down or left, which was not done because of the 2-round limit.

2881.stem: The rate at which the depth of water changes in a bay is given by $R=4\pi\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{6}$ m/h.

parts.latex:
When Maya goes swimming in the bay, the depth is initially $2$ m.

Find an equation for the depth of water, $d$ metres, over time $t$ hours.
Georgia goes swimming $3$ hours after Maya. Find the depth of water at this time.

solutions.latex:
Depth is the integral of the rate:
$$\begin{aligned} d &= \int 4\pi\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{6}\,dt \\ &= -\dfrac{24\pi}{\pi}\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+C \\ &= -24\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$ and $d=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2 &= -24+C \\ C &= 26 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ d=-24\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{6}+26$$

At $t=3$:
$$\begin{aligned} d &= -24\cos\dfrac{\pi}{2}+26 \\ &= 26 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Pete worked in a National Park in 1942 and he introduced $18$ koalas to the park. By 2002, the number of koalas had grown to $5000$. The number of koalas has grown exponentially according to the rule $N=N_0e^{kt}$, where $t$ is the number of years since 1942. $N_0$ represents the initial amount of koalas and $k$ is a constant. By first finding these values, predict the number of koalas expected to be in the National Park in 2022.

solutions.latex:
The initial number is $N_0=18$.

In 2002, $t=60$ and $N=5000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 5000 &= 18e^{60k} \\ \dfrac{5000}{18} &= e^{60k} \\ 60k &= \log_e\left(\dfrac{5000}{18}\right) \\ k &= 0.0937\ldots \end{aligned}$$
So $N=18e^{0.0937\ldots t}$.

In 2022, $t=80$:
$$\begin{aligned} N &= 18e^{0.0937\ldots\times80} \\ &\approx 32\,624 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about } 32\,624 \text{ koalas}$$

2886.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has a displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ m/s. Initially the particle is at $O$.

parts.latex: Use integration to show that $x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$.
Find when the particle is at rest.
Find the distance travelled in the first $24$ seconds of its motion.

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int\left(3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9\right)dt \\ &= \dfrac{3(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+C \\ &= 2(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially $t=0$ and $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 2-0+C \\ C &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$$

At rest, $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{t+1} &= 9 \\ \sqrt{t+1} &= 3 \\ t+1 &= 9 \\ t &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is at rest at } t=8 \text{ seconds}$$

The particle changes direction at $t=8$, so find the positions at $t=8$ and $t=24$.
$$\begin{aligned} x(8) &= 2(9)(3)-72-2 \\ &= -20 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x(24) &= 2(25)(5)-216-2 \\ &= 32 \end{aligned}$$
From $0$ to $-20$ is $20$ m, then from $-20$ to $32$ is $52$ m.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total distance} &= 20+20+32 \\ &= 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the position at rest $-20$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Initially, a water tank holds 800 litres of water. Water drains from the bottom of the tank at a rate of $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$ litres per minute where $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-100t$ after $t$ minutes. How long does it take the tank to empty?

solutions.latex:
Integrate the rate to find the volume:
$$V=-\dfrac{100t^2}{2}+C=-50t^2+C$$
When $t=0$, $V=800$, so $C=800$ and
$$V=-50t^2+800$$
The tank is empty when $V=0$:
$$t^2=16$$
so $t=4$ minutes (as $t>0$), which is option B.

2950.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. Initially, it is travelling to the left at 1 cm/min. Its acceleration as a function of time($t$) is given by $a=\pi\cos\pi t+\pi\sin\pi t$ for $0\leq t\leq 2$ where time and displacement are measured in minutes and cm respectively.

parts.latex: Find when the particle changes its direction for the first time.
Find the exact total distance travelled in the first half a minute.

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when $v=0$. Integrate the acceleration, using $v=-1$ when $t=0$ (travelling left at 1 cm/min).
$$\begin{aligned} v-(-1)&=\int_0^t(\pi\cos\pi t+\pi\sin\pi t)\,dt\\ v+1&=\Big[\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t\Big]_0^t\\ v+1&=\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t+1\\ v&=\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t\end{aligned}$$
Set $v=0$:
$$\tan\pi t=1$$
So $\pi t=\dfrac{\pi}{4},\dfrac{5\pi}{4},\dots$, giving $t=\dfrac14,\dfrac54$ minutes.
$$\therefore\ \text{the first change of direction is at } t=\dfrac14 \text{ min (15 seconds)}$$
criteria: Finds $v=\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Integrate the velocity $v=\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t$ from part (a), with $x=0$ when $t=0$.
$$x=\int(\sin\pi t-\cos\pi t)\,dt=-\dfrac{\cos\pi t}{\pi}-\dfrac{\sin\pi t}{\pi}+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$, so $C=\dfrac{1}{\pi}$. Hence
$$x=-\dfrac{1}{\pi}\left[\cos\pi t+\sin\pi t-1\right]$$
The particle turns at $t=\dfrac14$, so find $x$ there and at $t=\dfrac12$.
$$x\left(\dfrac14\right)=-\dfrac{1}{\pi}(\sqrt2-1),\qquad x\left(\dfrac12\right)=-\dfrac{1}{\pi}(0+1-1)=0$$
The particle moves to $-\dfrac{1}{\pi}(\sqrt2-1)$ and then returns to $0$, so the distance travelled for $0\le t\le\dfrac12$ is
$$\therefore\ 2\times\dfrac{1}{\pi}(\sqrt2-1) \text{ cm}$$
criteria: Finds the positions at $t=\dfrac14$ and $t=\dfrac12$, or equivalent merit
Finds the displacement function $x$, or equivalent merit

2959.stem:
In a laboratory, a food product is heated in an oven at $210^\circ$ C in an effort to kill harmful bacteria. The number of bacteria recorded when the food product is first placed in the oven is 1800. After ten minutes the number of bacteria recorded is 550.

It is found that $N$, the number of bacteria remaining $t$ minutes after being in the oven is given by $N=Ae^{-kt}$ where $A$ and $k$ are constants.

parts.latex: Find the value of $A$.
Calculate the value of $k$ correct to 4 decimal places.
If an acceptable number of bacteria present is 100 or less, For how long should the food product to be in the oven? Express your answer to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
When $t=10$, $N=550$:
$$\begin{aligned}550&=1800e^{-10k}\\ e^{-10k}&=\dfrac{55}{180}\\ k&=-\dfrac{1}{10}\ln\left(\dfrac{55}{180}\right)\\ &\approx0.1186\end{aligned}$$

We need $N\le100$.
$$\begin{aligned}1800e^{-0.1186t}&\le100\\ e^{-0.1186t}&\le\dfrac{1}{18}\\ -0.1186t&\le\ln\dfrac{1}{18}\\ t&\ge\dfrac{\ln18}{0.1186}\approx24.37\end{aligned}$$
The inequality reverses when dividing by $-0.1186$. Rounding $24.37$ to the nearest minute gives $24$, but $N(24)\approx105>100$, so round up to the next whole minute:
$$\therefore\ t=25 \text{ minutes}$$

meta.format_note: The source rounds 24.37 up to 25 minutes (nearest minute would be 24, but 25 is needed for $N\le100$); kept as in source.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the working said the answer came from rounding to the nearest minute; $24.37$ rounds to $24$, which is too early ($N(24)\approx105$), so it must be rounded up to $25$.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the working said the answer came from rounding to the nearest minute; $24.37$ rounds to $24$, which is too early ($N(24)\approx105$), so it must be rounded up to $25$.

parts.latex:
The population $N$, of a colony of ants grows exponentially according to the formula $N(t)=550e^{kt}$, where $k$ is the growth constant and $t$ is time in days.

If $N(\ln 4)=13750$, what is the exact value of $k$?

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=\ln 4$ into $N(t)=550e^{kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 13750 &= 550e^{k\ln 4} \\ 25 &= e^{k\ln 4} \\ \ln 25 &= k\ln 4 \\ k &= \dfrac{\ln 25}{\ln 4} \end{aligned}$$
This is option B.

figures.cap: displacement-time graph with turning points at t=2 and t=4

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when its velocity is zero, that is, when the gradient of the displacement graph is zero.

This occurs at $t=2$ and $t=4$.

This is option B.

2989.stem: The velocity $v$ of a particle initially at the origin is given by $v(t)=\sin\left(\dfrac{1}{4}t\right)$, in metres per second.

figures.cap: solution sketch: displacement-time graph, oscillating between 0 and 8

parts.latex: Find the displacement function $x(t)$
Find the acceleration function $a(t)$
Find the value of $x$ when $t=4\pi$
Sketch the displacement-time graph on the domain $0\le t\le 16\pi$ and briefly describe the motion.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the velocity.

$$\begin{aligned} x(t) &= \int v(t)\,dt \\ &= \int \sin\left(\dfrac{1}{4}t\right)dt \\ &= -4\cos\dfrac{1}{4}t+C \end{aligned}$$

When $t=0$, $x=0$:

$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -4\cos 0+C \\ C &= 4 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ x(t)=-4\cos\dfrac{1}{4}t+4$$
$$\begin{aligned} a(t) &= \dfrac{d}{dt}v(t) \\ &= \dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\sin\dfrac{1}{4}t\right) \\ &= \dfrac{1}{4}\cos\left(\dfrac{1}{4}t\right) \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; single row added.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} x(4\pi) &= -4\cos\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\times 4\pi\right)+4 \\ &= -4\cos\pi+4 \\ &= -4\times(-1)+4 \\ &= 8 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; single row added.

2990.stem:
The rate of fuel burn, $t$ minutes after the engine starts operation, $R$ kg per minute, is given by the relation

$$R=10+\dfrac{10}{1+2t}$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of R against t with asymptote R = 10

parts.latex: Draw a sketch of $R$ as a function of $t$, $t\ge 0$
What is the rate of burn, $R$, after 7 minutes?
What value does $R$ approaches as $t$ becomes very large?
Calculate the total amount of the fuel burnt in the first 7 minutes.

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1324_q29_s1}
criteria: Partially correct sketch, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: $R=10+\dfrac{10}{1+2t}$ for $t\ge 0$. Decreasing curve starting at $(0,20)$ and approaching the horizontal asymptote $R=10$ (label the asymptote).

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} R(7) &= 10+\dfrac{10}{1+2\times 7} \\ &= 10+\dfrac{10}{15} \\ &= 10\dfrac{2}{3} \text{ kg/minute} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; single row added.

solutions.latex:
As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{10}{1+2t}\to 0$.

$$\therefore\ R\to 10 \text{ kg/minute}$$

meta.format_note: Source had no criteria; single row added.

solutions.latex:
The total fuel burnt is the integral of the rate.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{Total} &= \int_0^7 R\,dt \\ &= \int_0^7\left(10+\dfrac{10}{1+2t}\right)dt \\ &= \left[10t+10\times\dfrac{\ln|1+2t|}{2}\right]_0^7 \\ &= 5\Big[2t+\ln|1+2t|\Big]_0^7 \\ &= 5\Big[\left(2\times 7+\ln|1+2\times 7|\right)-\left(2\times 0+\ln 1\right)\Big] \\ &= 5\left[14+\ln 15\right] \text{ kg} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit
Sets up the integral, or equivalent merit

3014.stem:
The velocity of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is given by:

$$\dot{x}=8-8e^{-2t}$$

where $t$ is the time in seconds and $x$ is the displacement in metres.

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of velocity 8-8e^{-2t} with asymptote at 8

parts.latex: Show that the particle is initially at rest.
Show that the acceleration of the particle is always positive.
Explain why the particle is moving in the positive direction for all $t>0$.
can_use: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.latex: As $t\to\infty$, the velocity of the particle approaches a constant. Find the value of the constant.
Sketch the graph of the particle's velocity as a function of time.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=0$ into $\dot x=8-8e^{-2t}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dot x&=8-8e^{0} \\ &=8-8 \\ &=0 \end{aligned}$$
So the particle is initially at rest.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Differentiate the velocity.
$$\ddot x=16e^{-2t}$$
Since $e^{-2t}>0$ for all $t$, $\ddot x>0$.

So the acceleration is always positive.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
From part (a) the particle is initially at rest, so $\dot x=0$ at $t=0$.

From part (b) the acceleration is always positive, so the velocity is increasing for all $t$.

Therefore the velocity is greater than $0$ for all $t>0$, and the particle moves in the positive direction.
criteria: Uses the initial velocity or the positive acceleration, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
As $t\to\infty$, $e^{-2t}\to 0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \dot x &= 8-8e^{-2t} \\ &\to 8-0 \\ &= 8 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the constant is } 8$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.
