parts.latex:
A town planning committee notes that the rate of growth of the town's population since 1985 has followed the formula: $\dfrac{dp}{dt}=(1500+200t)$ people per year

where $t$ is the number of years since 1st January 1985. On 1st January 1992 the population was $25\,000$. Find the formula for the city's population from 1985 onwards.

solutions.latex:
Population is the integral of the rate of growth.

$$\begin{aligned} P &= \int (1500+200t)\,dt \\ &= 1500t+\dfrac{200t^2}{2}+K \\ &= 1500t+100t^2+K \end{aligned}$$

On 1 January 1992, $t=7$ and $P=25\,000$.

$$\begin{aligned} 25\,000 &= 1500(7)+100(7)^2+K \\ &= 10\,500+4900+K \\ K &= 9600 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ P=100t^2+1500t+9600$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

3026.stem:
Under certain climatic conditions the number $N$ of blue-green algae satisfies the equation

$$N(t)=Ae^{0.15t}$$

where $t$ is measured in days and $A$ is a constant.

parts.latex: Show that the number of algae increases at a rate proportional to the number.
When $t=3$ the number of algae was estimated to be $1.7\times10^8$. Evaluate $A$.
The number of algae doubles every $x$ days. Find the value of $x$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $N(t)=Ae^{0.15t}$.

$$\begin{aligned} N'(t) &= 0.15Ae^{0.15t} \\ &= 0.15\,N(t) \end{aligned}$$

Since $0.15$ is a constant, $N'(t)\propto N(t)$, so the number increases at a rate proportional to the number.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=3$ and $N=1.7\times10^8$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1.7\times10^8 &= Ae^{0.15(3)} \\ &= Ae^{0.45} \\ A &= \dfrac{1.7\times10^8}{e^{0.45}} \\ &\approx 1.0839\times10^8 \\ &\approx 1.1\times10^8 \text{ (2 sig. fig.)} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$, $N(0)=Ae^{0}=A$, so after $x$ days $N(x)=2A$.

$$\begin{aligned} Ae^{0.15x} &= 2A \\ e^{0.15x} &= 2 \\ 0.15x &= \ln 2 \\ x &= \dfrac{\ln 2}{0.15} \\ &\approx 4.6209 \\ &\approx 4.6 \text{ days} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Forms the equation $e^{0.15x}=2$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

3045.stem:
Coal is extracted from a mine at a rate that is proportional to the amount of coal remaining in the mine. Hence the amount $R$ remaining after $t$ years is given by $R=R_0e^{-kt}$, where $k$ is a constant and $R_0$ is the initial amount of coal.

After 20 years, $50\%$ of the initial amount of coal remains.

parts.latex: Find the exact value of $k$.
How many more years will elapse before only $10\%$ of the original amount remains?

solutions.latex:
When $t=20$, $R=\dfrac{1}{2}R_0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}R_0&=R_0e^{-20k} \\ \dfrac{1}{2}&=e^{-20k} \\ \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=-20k \\ -\ln2&=-20k \\ k&=\dfrac{1}{20}\ln2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Substitutes the given values into the equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
From part (i), $k=\dfrac{1}{20}\ln 2$. Set $R=0.1R_0$ and solve for $t$.
$$\begin{aligned}0.1R_0&=R_0e^{-\frac{1}{20}\ln 2\times t}\\ 0.1&=e^{-\frac{1}{20}\ln 2\times t}\\ \ln(0.1)&=\ln e^{-\frac{1}{20}\ln 2\times t}\\ -\dfrac{1}{20}\ln 2\times t&=-\ln 10\\ t&=\dfrac{20\ln 10}{\ln 2}\\ &\approx 66.44\end{aligned}$$
The question asks for how many more years, so subtract the first 20 years.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{More years}&=66.44-20\\ &=46.44\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about } 46.44 \text{ more years}$$
criteria: Finds the correct value for $t$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: none needed; sketch_id on record is not used.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the subtraction read $66.43-20=40.43$; $t=\dfrac{20\ln10}{\ln2}\approx66.44$, so about $46.44$ more years (the school solution had the same slip).

3056.stem:
\exfigure{1326_q30_1}

A car and a jet plane race one another from rest down a runway. The car increases its speed $v_1$ at a constant rate, while the speed of the jet is given by $v_2=2t^2$. After 5 seconds the car and the jet have the same speed of 50 m/s, as shown on the graph.

figures.cap: velocity-time graphs of a car (line) and a jet (curve)

parts.latex: By considering the difference quotient, find the average acceleration of the jet during the $5^{\text{th}}$ second.
Find an equation for the speed $v_1$ of the car in terms of $t$.
For what times is the acceleration of the car greater than that of the jet?
Who is winning the race after 5 seconds and by how many metres?

solutions.latex:
The average acceleration is the change in speed over the change in time, from $t=4$ to $t=5$.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Average acceleration}&=\dfrac{v_2(5)-v_2(4)}{5-4}\\ &=\dfrac{50-2(4)^2}{1}\\ &=18 \text{ m/s}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some correct working, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The car's speed increases at a constant rate from rest, so $v_1=mt$. At $t=5$, $v_1=50$, so $m=10$.
$$\therefore\ v_1=10t$$

Acceleration is the derivative of speed: $a_{\text{car}}=10$ and $a_{\text{jet}}=4t$.

The car's acceleration is greater when
$$\begin{aligned}10&>4t\\ t&<\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{for } 0\le t<\dfrac{5}{2} \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Finds the derivative of velocity, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Distance is the area under the speed-time graph.

Distance of the car:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^5 10t\,dt&=\left[5t^2\right]_0^5\\ &=5\times5^2-0\\ &=125 \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
Distance of the jet:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^5 2t^2\,dt&=\left[\dfrac{2t^3}{3}\right]_0^5\\ &=\dfrac{2\times5^3}{3}-0\\ &\approx 83.3 \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Difference}&=125-83.3\\ &\approx 41\dfrac{2}{3} \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the car is winning by about } 41\dfrac{2}{3} \text{ m}$$
criteria: One correct element, or equivalent merit

1326_q30_1.notes: NOT TO SCALE. Axes, the car line, the intersection dot at (5,50), labels and leader arrows (-latex) placed from the crop. The jet curve is fitted through O, the intersection and the crop's top end. In round 2 it came out a little too flat near O and too steep before the intersection compared with the crop. Text is slightly larger than the crop's. Please check the curve shape first.

parts.latex:
A particle, initially at the origin, moves in a straight line with velocity $v = 8 - 4t$ m/s.

What is the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 4 seconds?

solutions.latex:
The velocity $v=8-4t$ is zero at $t=2$, so the particle changes direction there. The distance is the sum of the two areas between the velocity line and the $t$-axis, for $0\le t\le 2$ and $2\le t\le 4$.

At $t=0$, $v=8$, and at $t=4$, $v=-8$. Each area is a triangle:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\times 8=8$$
So the total distance is
$$8+8=16 \text{ m}$$
This is option B.

figures.cap: velocity-time graph

solutions.latex:
The particle changes direction when the velocity changes sign.

From the graph, $v$ changes from positive to negative only once, so the particle changes direction once.

This is option A.

It touches the t-axis at the first minimum without crossing, crosses once, and ends in an arrow just below the axis, as in the crop. The tilted t-axis is drawn level (rule 1), which accounts for most of the overlay mismatch. Labels v, t and 0 are in the same positions as the crop.

3077.stem: The acceleration of a particle moving on a straight line is given by $a = \sqrt{4t + 16}$ m/s$^2$.

parts.latex: What is the acceleration of the particle after 12 seconds?
If the particle starts from rest, find its velocity after 12 seconds.
Is the particle speeding up or slowing down after 12 seconds? Justify your answer.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=12$.
$$\begin{aligned} a&=\sqrt{4(12)+16}\\ &=8 \text{ m/s}^2\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the integral of acceleration.
$$\begin{aligned} v&=\displaystyle\int (4t+16)^{\frac{1}{2}}\,dt\\ &=\dfrac{(4t+16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{\frac{3}{2}\times 4}+c\\ &=\dfrac{(4t+16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}+c\end{aligned}$$
The particle starts from rest, so $v=0$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=\dfrac{16^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}+c\\ c&=-\dfrac{32}{3}\end{aligned}$$
So $v=\dfrac{(4t+16)^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}-\dfrac{32}{3}$. At $t=12$:
$$\begin{aligned} v&=\dfrac{64^{\frac{3}{2}}}{6}-\dfrac{32}{3}\\ &=\dfrac{224}{3} \text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the constant of integration, or equivalent merit
Integrates the acceleration correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The particle is speeding up when the velocity and acceleration have the same sign.

At $t=12$, $a=8>0$ and $v=\dfrac{224}{3}>0$.

Therefore the particle is speeding up, because both the acceleration and the velocity are positive.
criteria: Considers the signs of velocity and acceleration, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

parts.latex: A particle is moving with velocity $v = t^2 - 10t + 21$ for $t \ge 0$. For what value(s) of $t$ is the particle stationary?

solutions.latex:
The particle is stationary when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} t^2-10t+21 &= 0 \\ (t-3)(t-7) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $t=3$ or $t=7$, and both satisfy $t\ge 0$.

This is option C.

meta.generated_note: MCQ working written for keyed option C.

3116.stem:
Coal is extracted from a mine at a rate that is proportional to the amount of coal remaining in the mine. Hence, the amount $R$ remaining after $t$ years is given by

$$R = 250e^{-kt}$$

$k$ is a positive constant and $R$ is measured in tonnes.

parts.latex: If 80% of the coal remains after 2 years, show that the value of $k$ is approximately 0.1116.
Find the amount of coal remaining after 8 years, correct to the nearest tonne.
At what rate is the amount of coal decreasing after 1 year? Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.

The coal mine is abandoned when the amount of coal remaining is less than 80 tonnes. After how many years will the coal mine be abandoned?

Express your answer in years, correct to one decimal place.

solutions.latex:
After 2 years, 80% of 250 tonnes remains, so $R = 200$ when $t = 2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 200 &= 250e^{-2k} \\ 0.8 &= e^{-2k} \\ \ln 0.8 &= -2k \\ k &= \dfrac{\ln 0.8}{-2} \\ &\approx 0.11157 \\ &\approx 0.1116 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k \approx 0.1116$$
criteria: Correctly uses the given information to form an equation, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t = 8$ and $k = 0.1116$ into $R = 250e^{-kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} R &= 250e^{-0.1116\times 8} \\ &= 102 \text{ tonnes (nearest tonne)} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiate $R = 250e^{-kt}$.
$$\dfrac{dR}{dt} = -250ke^{-kt}$$
When $t = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dR}{dt} &= -250\times 0.1116\times e^{-0.1116\times 1} \\ &\approx -25 \text{ tonnes/year} \end{aligned}$$
So the coal is decreasing at about $25$ tonnes per year.
criteria: Correct derivative or solution obtained, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The mine is abandoned when $R < 80$.
$$\begin{aligned} 80 &> 250e^{-0.1116t} \\ \dfrac{80}{250} &> e^{-0.1116t} \\ \ln\dfrac{8}{25} &> -0.1116t \\ t &> 10.2 \end{aligned}$$
The last step divides by $-0.1116$, which reverses the inequality.
$$\therefore \text{After } 10.2 \text{ years the coal mine will have less than 80 tonnes of coal.}$$
criteria: Obtains the inequality or equation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A particle is accelerating according to the function $a = -\dfrac{3}{t^2}\ \text{ms}^{-2}$.

If, when $t = 0.5$ s, its velocity, $v = 6\ \text{ms}^{-1}$ and its displacement, $x = 1$ m, find the particle’s displacement function in simplest form.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration to find the velocity.
$$v = \dfrac{3}{t} + c$$
When $t = 0.5$, $v = 6$:
$$\begin{aligned} 6 &= \dfrac{3}{0.5} + c \\ 6 &= 6 + c \end{aligned}$$
So $c = 0$ and $v = \dfrac{3}{t}$.

Integrate the velocity to find the displacement.
$$x = 3\ln t + c_2$$
When $t = 0.5$, $x = 1$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 3\ln(0.5) + c_2 \\ &= 3\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) + c_2 \\ &= -3\ln 2 + c_2 \end{aligned}$$
So $c_2 = 1 + 3\ln 2$.
$$\therefore\ x = 3\ln t + 3\ln 2 + 1$$
criteria: Significant progress towards solution, or equivalent merit
Limited progress towards solution, or equivalent merit

3191.stem: An item is purchased for $\$20\,000$. It appreciates in value so that after $t$ years its value $\$V$ is given by the formula $V=20000p^t$ for some constant $p>1$. After 9 years its value is $\$32\,000$.

parts.latex: Find the value of $p$ correct to 4 decimal places.
Find correct to the nearest $\$10$ per year the rate at which the item is appreciating in value after 9 years.

solutions.latex:
When $t=9$, $V=32000$.
$$\begin{aligned} 20000p^9 &= 32000 \\ p^9 &= \dfrac{8}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ p=(1.6)^{\frac{1}{9}}\approx 1.0536$$
criteria: Writes and simplifies a numerical expression for $p^9$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The rate of appreciation is $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$. Differentiating $V=20000p^t$:
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=20\,000\ln p\,(p^t)$$
When $t=9$, $p^9=\dfrac{8}{5}$ and $\ln p=\dfrac{1}{9}\ln 1.6$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt} &= 20\,000\left(\dfrac{1}{9}\ln 1.6\right)\times\dfrac{8}{5} \\ &\approx 1670 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the rate of increase is } \$1670 \text{ per year (nearest } \$10\text{)}$$
criteria: Differentiates with respect to $t$, or equivalent merit

3194.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ metres per second. Initially the particle is at $O$.

parts.latex: Use integration to show that $x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$.
Find when and where the particle is at rest.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 24 seconds of its motion.

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement, so integrate $v$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= 3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9 \\ x &= 2(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+c \end{aligned}$$
Initially $x=0$ when $t=0$, so $0=2-0+c$ and $c=-2$.
$$\therefore\ x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$$
criteria: Integrates with respect to $t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{t+1}-9 &= 0 \\ \sqrt{t+1} &= 3 \\ t &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
Then $x=2(9)(3)-72-2=-20$.

Also, when $t=0$, $v=-3$, so the particle starts in the negative direction.

The particle is at rest at time 8 seconds, when it is 20 m from $O$ in the initial direction of travel.

At $t=24$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 2(25)(5)-9(24)-2 \\ &= 32 \end{aligned}$$
The particle changes direction at $t=8$, so in the first 24 seconds it travels from $x=0$ to $x=-20$, then to $x=32$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 20+(20+32) \\ &= 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the distance travelled is } 72 \text{ m}$$

3217.stem: The velocity of a particle travelling in a straight line is given by $v = 2t - 4$, where $t$ is time in seconds and $x$ its displacement from the origin in metres. The particle is initially at the origin.

parts.latex: Find the expression for the particle's displacement as a function of time.
Find the total distance travelled for the first 5 seconds.

solutions.latex:
$$x=\displaystyle\int(2t-4)\,dt=t^2-4t+c$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$, so $c=0$.
$$x=t^2-4t$$

meta.marker_note: $x=t^2-4t$ alone is not sufficient without evaluating $c$.

solutions.latex:
When $t=5$:
$$x=5^2-4(5)=5$$
The particle may change direction when it is stationary, $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2t-4 &= 0 \\ t &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
When $t=2$:
$$x=2^2-4(2)=-4$$
The particle moves from $x=0$ to $x=-4$, then to $x=5$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{distance} &= 4+9 \\ &= 13 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, the total distance is the area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis:
$$\dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times4+\dfrac{1}{2}\times3\times6=4+9=13 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds the change of direction at $t=2$ and $x=-4$, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: 0 marks for an answer of 5.

solutions.latex:
There are 6 subintervals of width $10$, so the trapezoidal rule gives:
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Water} &\approx \dfrac{10}{2}\Big[500+2(400+350+280+200+180)+150\Big] \\ &= 17350 \text{ L} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct trapezoidal rule substitution, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The height of water in a tank is initially 50cm. The height is decreasing at a rate of $0.5t$ cm/min. Calculate the time for the tank to empty, to the nearest second.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the rate, with $h=50$ when $t=0$.
$$\dfrac{dh}{dt}=-0.5t$$
$$\begin{aligned} h&=-\dfrac{t^{2}}{4}+c\\ 50&=0+c\\ h&=50-\dfrac{t^{2}}{4}\end{aligned}$$
The tank is empty when $h=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=50-\dfrac{t^{2}}{4}\\ t^{2}&=200\\ t&=\sqrt{200}\end{aligned}$$
We take the positive root since $t>0$.
$$\therefore\ t\approx 14 \text{ min } 9 \text{ s}$$
criteria: Finds the expression for $h$, or equivalent merit

3272.stem: A particle moves in a straight line from the origin, and after $t$ seconds its velocity in m/s is given by $v=4-2t$ m/s.

parts.latex: Find when the particle is stationary.
Find the distance travelled during the first 6 seconds.

solutions.latex:
The particle is stationary when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4-2t&=0\\ t&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=2 \text{ seconds}$$

Integrate the velocity, with $x=0$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\int(4-2t)\,dt\\ &=4t-t^{2}+c\end{aligned}$$
Since $c=0$, $x=t(4-t)$.

The particle turns at $t=2$ (from part (a)), so find the positions at $t=2$ and $t=6$.
$$\begin{aligned} t=2:&\ x=4 \text{ m}\\ t=6:&\ x=-12 \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
The particle moves from $0$ to $4$, then back from $4$ to $-12$.
$$\text{Distance}=4+4+12=20 \text{ m}$$
criteria: Finds the displacement function, or equivalent merit

3276.stem:
The acceleration of a particle is given by $a=\sin 2t$.

At time $t=0$, $v=0$ m/s and $x=1$ m.

parts.latex: Find the velocity when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ seconds.
Find displacement when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$ seconds.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration, with $v=0$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} v&=\int\sin 2t\,dt\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2t+c\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=-\dfrac{1}{2}+c\\ c&=\dfrac{1}{2}\end{aligned}$$
So $v=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2t+\dfrac{1}{2}$.

When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$:
$$\begin{aligned} v&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos\dfrac{\pi}{4}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}}+\dfrac{1}{2}\\ &=\dfrac{2-\sqrt{2}}{4} \text{ m/s}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the expression for $v$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Integrate the velocity from part (a), with $x=1$ when $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} x&=\int\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\cos 2t+\dfrac{1}{2}\right)dt\\ &=-\dfrac{1}{4}\sin 2t+\dfrac{1}{2}t+c\end{aligned}$$
Since $x=1$ when $t=0$, $c=1$.

When $t=\dfrac{\pi}{8}$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=-\dfrac{1}{4}\cdot\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}+\dfrac{\pi}{16}+1\\ &=-\dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{8}+\dfrac{\pi}{16}+1\\ &=\dfrac{\pi-2\sqrt{2}+16}{16} \text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the expression for $x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The rate of change of $Q$ with respect to time is given by $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$.

If $Q=2$ when $t=1$ and $Q=5$ when $t=2$, find $Q$ when $t=3$.

solutions.latex:
Since $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$, exponential growth gives $Q=Q_0e^{kt}$.

Substitute the two given conditions.
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=Q_0e^{k} &&(1)\\ 5&=Q_0e^{2k} &&(2)\end{aligned}$$
Dividing (2) by (1):
$$\begin{aligned} e^{k}&=\dfrac{5}{2}\\ k&=\ln\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Substitute into (1).
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=Q_0\cdot\dfrac{5}{2}\\ Q_0&=\dfrac{4}{5}\end{aligned}$$
So $Q=\dfrac{4}{5}e^{\left(\ln\frac{5}{2}\right)t}$.

When $t=3$:
$$Q=\dfrac{4}{5}e^{3\ln\frac{5}{2}}$$
$$\therefore\ Q=\dfrac{4}{5}\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)^{3}=\dfrac{25}{2}$$

meta.format_note: Source stopped at $Q=\dfrac45e^{3\ln\frac52}$; simplified to $\dfrac{25}{2}$ (equal value) and checked: $\dfrac45\cdot\dfrac{125}{8}=\dfrac{25}{2}$.

3306.stem:
A particle moves in a straight line such that its displacement is given by the function

$$x = 1 - \dfrac{3}{t + 1},$$

where $x$ is the particle's displacement from the origin, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in seconds.

figures.cap: blank x-t axes for sketching
solution sketch: displacement-time graph

parts.latex: What is the initial displacement of the particle?
Find the expressions for the velocity and acceleration of the particle in terms of $t$.
As $t$ increases indefinitely, describe the motion of the particle with reference to its displacement and velocity.

Sketch the graph of displacement as a function of time, labelling all important features.

\exfigure{1612_q28_1}

solutions.latex:
Initially $t = 0$:
$$x = 1 - \dfrac{3}{0+1} = -2$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is initially 2 metres to the left of the origin}$$

Write the displacement as a power, then differentiate.
$$x = 1 - 3(t+1)^{-1}$$
$$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 3(t+1)^{-2} = \dfrac{3}{(t+1)^2}$$
$$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -6(t+1)^{-3} = -\dfrac{6}{(t+1)^3}$$
criteria: Finds the expression for $v$ or $a$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
As $t \to \infty$, $\dfrac{3}{t+1} \to 0$, so $x \to 1$. The particle approaches $x = 1$ m.

As $t \to \infty$, $v = \dfrac{3}{(t+1)^2} \to 0$. The particle's velocity approaches $0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle approaches } x = 1 \text{ m with decreasing speed}$$
criteria: Describes the particle's displacement or velocity as $t \to \infty$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex: \exfigure{1612_q28_s1}

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: graph of $x=1-\dfrac{3}{t+1}$ for $t\ge0$. Starts at $(0,-2)$ on the vertical axis; crosses the $t$-axis at $(2,0)$ (since $1=\dfrac{3}{t+1}$); increasing and concave down, approaching the horizontal asymptote $x=1$ as $t\to\infty$ (dashed line labelled $x=1$).

1612_q28_1.notes: Blank x-t axes; the vertical axis runs below O to match the crop. Filled arrowheads; labels x, t, O. Rules 2, 3, 4.

1612_q28_s1.notes: Drew x=1-3/(t+1) for t from 0 to 10.8, 0.9pt with an arrow at the end. Dashed asymptote x=1 and ticks at 1, -1 and -2; the t-intercept 2 lies on the true curve. The y-intercept label is written -2: the scan lost the minus sign, and the solution gives x=-2 (rule 18). The vertical axis has arrows at both ends, as in the crop. Rules 4, 9, 10, 16, 18, 24.

3338.stem:
A particle moves in a straight line such that its displacement is given by the function

$$x = 2 - \dfrac{3}{t + 1},$$

where $x$ is the particle's displacement from the origin, in metres, and $t$ is the time, in seconds.

parts.latex: What is the initial displacement of the particle?
Find the expressions for the velocity and acceleration of the particle in terms of $t$.
As $t$ increases indefinitely, describe the motion of the particle with reference to its displacement and velocity.

solutions.latex:
Since $2 - \dfrac{3}{t + 1} = \dfrac{2t - 1}{t + 1}$, the displacement can be written $x = \dfrac{2t - 1}{t + 1}$.

The initial displacement is at $t = 0$.
$$x = \dfrac{2(0) - 1}{0 + 1} = -1$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is initially } 1 \text{ metre to the left of the origin}$$

Rewrite the displacement with a negative power, then differentiate.
$$x = 2 - 3(t + 1)^{-1}$$
$$v = \dfrac{dx}{dt} = 3(t + 1)^{-2} = \dfrac{3}{(t + 1)^2}$$
$$a = \dfrac{dv}{dt} = -6(t + 1)^{-3} = -\dfrac{6}{(t + 1)^3}$$
criteria: Finds the expression for $v$ OR $a$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
As $t \to \infty$, $\dfrac{3}{t + 1} \to 0$, so $x \to 2 - 0 = 2$.

The particle approaches $x = 2$ m.

As $t \to \infty$, $v = \dfrac{3}{(t+1)^2} \to 0$.

The particle's velocity decreases towards $0 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the particle approaches } x = 2 \text{ m with decreasing speed}$$
criteria: Describes the particle's displacement OR velocity as $t \to \infty$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: A particle, initially $3$ m to the right of the origin has a velocity given by $v=(7-3t)$ ms$^{-1}$. What is an expression for the the displacement of the particle?

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the integral of velocity:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int (7-3t)\,dt \\ &= 7t-\dfrac{3t^2}{2}+C \end{aligned}$$
Initially ($t=0$) the particle is $3$ m to the right of the origin, so $x=3$ when $t=0$:
$$3=0-0+C \quad\text{so}\quad C=3$$
Hence $x=7t-\dfrac{3t^2}{2}+3$, which is option A.

options.label: C
options.latex: The particle is initially at the origin

parts.latex:
The displacement $x$ metres of a particle moving in a straight line at time $t$ seconds is given by:

$$x=2t-4\log_e(2t+1)$$

Which of the following statements is false?

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $x=2t-4\ln(2t+1)$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 2-\dfrac{8}{2t+1} \\ a &= \dfrac{16}{(2t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
Test each statement.

A: $a=\dfrac{16}{(2t+1)^2}>0$ for all $t\ge0$, so it is true.

B: at $t=0$, $v=2-8=-6$ ms$^{-1}$, so it is true.

C: at $t=0$, $x=0-4\ln 1=0$, so the particle is at the origin and it is true.

D: as $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{8}{2t+1}\to0$, so $v\to2$, not $\infty$. This is false (although $x\to\infty$).

Hence the false statement is option D.

3374.stem:
Scientists have recently discovered a new drug to control a rare medical condition. It is known that the quantity $Q$ of the drug remaining in the body after $t$ hours satisfies an equation of the form

$$Q=Q_0e^{-kt}$$

where $Q_0$ and $k$ are positive constants.

The initial dose is 5 milligrams and after 17 hours the amount remaining in the body is half the initial dose.

parts.latex: Find the exact values of $Q_0$ and $k$.
When will one-seventh of the initial dose remain?

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$, $Q=5$:
$$5=Q_0e^{-k(0)}$$
so $Q_0=5$.

When $t=17$, $Q=\dfrac{5}{2}$:
$$\dfrac{5}{2}=5e^{-17k}$$
$$\dfrac{1}{2}=e^{-17k}$$
Taking natural logarithms:
$$\begin{aligned}\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)&=-17k\\k&=-\dfrac{1}{17}\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\&=\dfrac{1}{17}\ln 2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $Q_0=5$ and sets up $\dfrac{5}{2}=5e^{-17k}$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
One-seventh of the initial dose is $Q=\dfrac{5}{7}$.
$$\dfrac{5}{7}=5e^{-kt}$$
$$e^{-kt}=\dfrac{1}{7}$$
$$-kt=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{7}\right)$$
$$\begin{aligned}t&=-\dfrac{1}{k}\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{7}\right)\\&=\dfrac{17}{\ln 2}\ln 7\\&\approx 47.725\ldots\\&\approx 48 \text{ hours}\end{aligned}$$

3375.stem:
A particle with velocity, $v$ ms$^{-1}$ moves along a straight line from a fixed point $O$

$$v=-4\cos t$$

where the time $t$ is measured in seconds from $t=0$.

It is initially 1 metre to the right of the origin.

parts.latex: When, and where, does the particle first come to rest?
Show that the total distance travelled by the particle between $0\le t\le\dfrac{2\pi}{3}$ is $\left(8-2\sqrt{3}\right)$ metres.

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$-4\cos t=0,\quad \cos t=0$$
so $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2},\ \dfrac{3\pi}{2},\ldots$ and the first time is $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

The displacement is the integral of the velocity.
$$x=\int-4\cos t\,dt=-4\sin t+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=1$, so $C=1$ and
$$x=1-4\sin t$$
At $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$:
$$x=1-4=-3$$
The particle first comes to rest when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ seconds, at $3$ m to the left of the origin.

The particle changes direction at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ (where $v=0$), so split the distance there.
$$\text{Distance}=\left|\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}-4\cos t\,dt\right|+\left|\int_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}-4\cos t\,dt\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned}&=\left|-4\Big[\sin t\Big]_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}}\right|+\left|-4\Big[\sin t\Big]_{\frac{\pi}{2}}^{\frac{2\pi}{3}}\right|\\&=\left|-4(1-0)\right|+\left|-4\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}-1\right)\right|\\&=4+\left(4-2\sqrt{3}\right)\\&=8-2\sqrt{3}\text{ metres}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Integrates correctly over both intervals, or equivalent merit
Splits the distance at the change of direction, or equivalent merit

3440.stem:
The velocity-time graph of a particle moving in a straight line is shown below.

\exfigure{1336_q28_1}

figures.cap: velocity-time graph: straight line from (0,10) through (5,0)

parts.latex: Describe the motion of the particle in the first 8 seconds of the motion.
Find the acceleration of the particle.
Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 8 seconds.
If initially the particle is two units to the left of the origin, what is the location of the particle after 8 seconds?

solutions.latex:
The velocity is positive for the first 5 seconds and decreasing, so the particle moves in the positive direction with decreasing speed.

At 5 seconds the velocity is zero, so the particle comes to a stop, then reverses direction with increasing speed.

The velocity graph is a straight line with negative gradient, so the particle has constant acceleration in the negative direction throughout.
criteria: Describes part of the motion correctly, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is the gradient of the velocity-time graph.

$$\begin{aligned}a&=\dfrac{-10}{5}\\&=-2\text{ ms}^{-2}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Distance is the total area between the graph and the $t$-axis, counting areas below the axis as positive.

For $0\le t\le 5$ the area is a triangle with base 5 and height 10. For $5\le t\le 8$ it is a triangle with base 3 and height 6.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{distance}&=\dfrac{1}{2}\times 10\times 5+\dfrac{1}{2}\times 3\times 6\\&=25+9\\&=34\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one of the two areas, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the signed area: the first triangle is above the axis (positive) and the second is below (negative).

The particle starts 2 units to the left of the origin.

$$\begin{aligned}\text{position}&=-2+25-9\\&=14\text{ m}\end{aligned}$$

The particle is 14 m to the right of the origin.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

1336_q28_1.notes: Velocity-time graph v=10-2t from t=0 to 9.5 at 0.9pt. Unit ticks on both axes, labels 2,4,5,6,8,10 and 10,5,-5 as on the paper, axis titles v (m/s) and t (s), filled arrowheads (rule 4). Score is about 0.84; the leftover colour is font-size differences in the labels.

3447.stem:
An engineer models the rates of change of the amount of oil produced (in hundred barrels per day) by oil companies $A$ and $B$ respectively by

$$f'(t)=6\ln(t)\quad\text{and}\quad g'(t)=\dfrac{60t}{1+5t},$$

where $t$ is the number of days after some initial time $(2\leq t\leq 14)$.

parts.latex: Using the trapezoidal rule with 3 sub-intervals, estimate the total amount of oil produced by oil company $A$ from $t=2$ to $t=14$.

It can be shown that $\dfrac{5t}{1+5t}=1-\dfrac{1}{1+5t}$. DO NOT prove this.

Use this result to find $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{60t}{1+5t}\,dt$.

The engineer claims that the total amount of oil produced by oil company $A$ from $t=2$ to $t=14$, is less than that of oil company $B$. Do you agree?

Justify your answer.

solutions.latex:
Using the trapezoidal rule with 3 sub-intervals, the strip width is

$$h=\dfrac{14-2}{3}=4$$

so the $t$ values are $2,6,10,14$.

$$\begin{aligned}\int_2^{14}f'(t)\,dt&\approx\dfrac{h}{2}\Big[f'(2)+f'(14)+2\big(f'(6)+f'(10)\big)\Big]\\&=2\Big[6\ln 2+6\ln 14+2\big(6\ln 6+6\ln 10\big)\Big]\\&\approx 138.25\end{aligned}$$

So company $A$ produced approximately 138.25 hundred barrels.
criteria: Applies the trapezoidal rule with correct $t$ values, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Since $60t=12\times 5t$, use the given result:

$$\begin{aligned}\int\dfrac{60t}{1+5t}\,dt&=12\int\dfrac{5t}{1+5t}\,dt\\&=12\int\left(1-\dfrac{1}{1+5t}\right)dt\\&=12\left[t-\dfrac{1}{5}\ln(1+5t)\right]+C\\&=12t-\dfrac{12}{5}\ln(1+5t)+C\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Source wrote the constant as $C$ inside the bracket then $C_1$; merged into a single $C$ (same result).

solutions.latex:
Total oil produced by company $B$, using part (b):

$$\begin{aligned}\int_2^{14}\dfrac{60t}{1+5t}\,dt&=12\left[t-\dfrac{1}{5}\ln(1+5t)\right]_2^{14}\\&=12\left[14-\dfrac{1}{5}\ln(71)-2+\dfrac{1}{5}\ln(11)\right]\\&=12\left[12-\dfrac{1}{5}\ln\left(\dfrac{71}{11}\right)\right]\\&\approx 139.52\end{aligned}$$

So company $B$ produces approximately 139.52 hundred barrels, while from part (a) company $A$ produced approximately 138.25 hundred barrels.

On these estimates, company $B$ produces more.

However, the estimate for company $A$ used the trapezoidal rule. The graph of $\ln t$ is concave down, so the trapezoidal rule gives an underestimate, and the two values are very close.

So it is not possible to say from these values which company produces more oil over that period.

$$\therefore\ \text{We cannot agree or disagree with the engineer's claim from these values.}$$
criteria: Finds the total for company $B$ and compares it with the estimate for company $A$, or equivalent merit
Substitutes the limits into the integral from part (b), or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Source's conclusion kept: inconclusive because of the trapezoidal underestimate.

parts.latex:
The share price (\$$P$) of a renewable energy company is increasing such that $\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{3}{t+1}$, where $t$ is the time in months.

If the initial price of the share price is \$2.00, find the price after 6 months. Write your answer to the nearest cent.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the rate of change to find $P$.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{3}{t+1}\,dt\\ &=3\ln|t+1|+c \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $P=2$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2&=3\ln 1+c\\ c&=2 \end{aligned}$$
So $P=3\ln|t+1|+2$.

When $t=6$:
$$\begin{aligned} P&=3\ln 7+2\\ &\approx \$7.84 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct solution with only one error, or equivalent merit
Correct expression for $P$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
The share price (\$P) of a renewable energy company is increasing such that

$$\dfrac{dP}{dt}=\dfrac{3}{t+1},$$

where $t$ is the time in months.

If the initial price of the share price is \$2.00, find the price after 6 months. Write your answer to the nearest cent.

solutions.latex:
Integrate to find $P$.
$$P=3\ln(t+1)+C$$
When $t=0$, $P=2$:
$$\begin{aligned}2&=3\ln1+C\\ C&=2\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}P&=3\ln(t+1)+2\\ P(6)&=3\ln7+2\\ &\approx 7.84\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{after 6 months the price is } \$7.84$$
criteria: Finds the constant of integration, or equivalent merit
Correct primitive function, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Currently, there is a mouse plague in Western NSW. The population of mice can be found using the formula $N=10\left(e^{kt}\right)$, where $N$ is the number of mice and $t$ is the time in months.

The plague started with $10$ mice and increased to $100$ mice after $3$ months.

By first finding the value of $k$, show that the exact rate of increase after $12$ months is $\dfrac{10\ln10}{3}\left(e^{\ln10000}\right)$ mice/month.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $N=100$ and $t=3$ into $N=10e^{kt}$.
$$\begin{aligned} 100&=10e^{3k}\\ 10&=e^{3k}\\ \ln 10&=3k\\ k&=\dfrac{\ln 10}{3} \end{aligned}$$
So $N=10e^{\frac{\ln 10}{3}t}$.

Differentiating, the rate of increase is
$$N'=10\times\dfrac{\ln 10}{3}e^{\frac{\ln 10}{3}t}$$
At $t=12$:
$$\begin{aligned} N'&=\dfrac{10\ln 10}{3}e^{\frac{\ln 10}{3}(12)}\\ &=\dfrac{10\ln 10}{3}e^{4\ln 10}\\ &=\dfrac{10\ln 10}{3}e^{\ln 10^4}\\ &=\dfrac{10\ln 10}{3}e^{\ln 10000} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ N'=\dfrac{10\ln 10}{3}\left(e^{\ln 10000}\right) \text{ mice/month}$$
criteria: Finds the derivative and substitutes $t=12$, or equivalent merit
Finds $k=\dfrac{\ln 10}{3}$ and the derivative, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: Leave $k$ as an exact value; both of the last lines are needed for the final mark (this is a show question).

parts.latex:
Dr Katyal pours $500$ mL of liquid fertiliser into a previously empty bucket. She then fills the bucket with water at a rate of $\dfrac{dV}{dt}$ litres per minute, where $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=\dfrac{5}{t+1}$ and $t$ is time in minutes.

Find the time, to the nearest second, at which there is $10$ L of liquid in the bucket.

solutions.latex:
The volume is the integral of the rate.
$$\begin{aligned} V&=\displaystyle\int\dfrac{5}{t+1}\,dt\\ &=5\ln|t+1|+C \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $V=0.5$ L.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.5&=5\ln|1|+C\\ C&=0.5 \end{aligned}$$
So $V=5\ln|t+1|+0.5$.

When $V=10$:
$$\begin{aligned} 10&=5\ln|t+1|+0.5\\ \dfrac{9.5}{5}&=\ln|t+1|\\ t+1&=e^{\frac{9.5}{5}}\\ t&=e^{\frac{9.5}{5}}-1\\ &\approx 5.686\text{ min} \end{aligned}$$
This is $5$ min $41$ sec to the nearest second.

$$\therefore\ t=5\text{ min }41\text{ sec}$$
criteria: Finds $C=0.5$ (with $V$ in litres), or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: The integral $\displaystyle\int\dfrac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\,dx=\ln|f(x)|+C$ is on the reference sheet; $t$ is in minutes.

3588.stem:
A particle starts to move from the origin along the $x$-axis.

Its velocity, measured in metres, at some time $t$ seconds, is given by $v=4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1}$ m/s.

parts.latex: Explain why the particle is never at rest.
Find the acceleration of the particle at $t=3$ seconds.
Find the exact distance travelled by the particle between $t=0$ and $t=5$ seconds.
Find the particle’s limiting velocity.

solutions.latex:
If the particle is at rest, $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1} &= 0 \\ 4(3t+1) &= 2 \\ 12t &= -2 \\ t &= -\dfrac16 \end{aligned}$$
But $t\ge0$, so the particle is never at rest.

Write $v=4-2(3t+1)^{-1}$ and differentiate.
$$\begin{aligned} a=\dfrac{dv}{dt} &= -2\times(-1)(3t+1)^{-2}\times3 \\ &= \dfrac{6}{(3t+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$
When $t=3$:
$$a=\dfrac{6}{(3\times3+1)^2}=\dfrac{6}{100}=0.06\ \text{m/s}^2$$
criteria: Correct expression for $a$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
By part (a) the particle is never at rest and $v>0$, so it never changes direction. The distance equals the displacement.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{distance} &= \int_0^5\left(4-\dfrac{2}{3t+1}\right)dt \\ &= \Big[4t-\dfrac23\ln|3t+1|\Big]_0^5 \\ &= 20-\dfrac23\ln16 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, $x=4t-\dfrac23\ln|3t+1|+C$, and $x=0$ when $t=0$ gives $C=0$. At $t=5$, $x=20-\dfrac23\ln16$.

$$\therefore\ \text{distance}=\left(20-\dfrac23\ln16\right)\text{ m}$$
criteria: Correct integral set up, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
As $t\to\infty$, $\dfrac{2}{3t+1}\to0$, so $v\to4$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the limiting velocity is } 4 \text{ m/s}$$

3589.stem:
At the beginning of the year 1935, 100 cane toads were introduced into Australia. Exactly 5 years later, the population had grown to 1000.

Assume that the number of cane toads is increasing exponentially and satisfies an equation of the form

$$N=N_0e^{kt}$$

where $N_0$ and $k$ are constants and $t$ is measured in years from the start of 1935.

parts.latex: Show that $N_0=100$ and $k=\dfrac{\ln 10}{5}$.
How long does it take for the population to reach 2 million? Give your answer to the nearest year.

criteria: Finds $N_0=100$ or sets up $10=e^{5k}$, or equivalent merit
Correct equation and rearrangement, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Doctor Hopper is investigating the population of kangaroos in New South Wales.

The doctor found, based on historical data that the population of kangaroos, $P$, could be modelled by

$$P = 7500 + 500(1.09)^t,$$

where $t$ is the number of years since the start of the year 2000, $t \ge 0$.

Find the rate at which the population of kangaroos is growing at the end of 2021.

Leave your answer correct to two significant figures.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(a^t\right) = a^t\ln a$.
$$\dfrac{dP}{dt} = 500 \times (1.09)^t \ln 1.09$$
The end of 2021 is $t = 22$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dP}{dt} &= 500 \times (1.09)^{22}\ln 1.09 \\ &\approx 290 \text{ per year} \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

3631.stem:
A particle moves along a straight line so that it is $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ at time $t$ seconds. The acceleration of the particle is given by

$$\ddot{x} = -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t \ \text{ m/s}^2$$

Initially the particle is travelling with a velocity of 3 m/s.

parts.latex: Find the first two times when the particle is stationary.
How far does the particle travel in the first four seconds.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration.
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x} &= -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t \\ \dot{x} &= -\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\times\left(-\dfrac{3}{\pi}\right)\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t + C \\ &= 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t + C \end{aligned}$$
When $t = 0$, $v = 3$:
$$3 = 2\cos 0 + C, \quad\text{so}\quad C = 1$$
$$\dot{x} = 1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t$$
The particle is stationary when $v = 0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t + 1 &= 0 \\ \cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \\ \dfrac{\pi}{3}t &= \dfrac{2\pi}{3}, \dfrac{4\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t = 2 \text{ and } t = 4$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us.

solutions.latex:
From (a), $v = 1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t$ is positive for $0 \le t < 2$ and negative for $2 < t \le 4$ (it is zero at $t=2$ and $t=4$). So the particle turns at $t = 2$ and the distance is found in two parts.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= \int_0^2 \left(1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right)dt + \left|\int_2^4 \left(1 + 2\cos\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right)dt\right| \\ &= \left[t + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right]_0^2 + \left|\left[t + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\sin\dfrac{\pi}{3}t\right]_2^4\right| \\ &= 2 + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} + \left|4 - \dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - \left(2 + \dfrac{6}{\pi}\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right| \\ &= 2 + \dfrac{3\sqrt{3}}{\pi} + \left|2 - \dfrac{6\sqrt{3}}{\pi}\right| \\ &= \dfrac{9\sqrt{3}}{\pi} \\ &\approx 4.96 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct integrals with absolute value, or equivalent merit
Identifies the change of direction at $t=2$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us. Check: $2+\dfrac{3\sqrt3}{\pi}\approx3.654$, $\left|2-\dfrac{6\sqrt3}{\pi}\right|\approx1.308$, sum $\approx4.96$, matching $\dfrac{9\sqrt3}{\pi}$.

3651.stem:
The graph below is composed of three line segments and shows the velocity $V$ of a particle which is moving in a straight line. The velocity is given in metres per second at time $t$ seconds, where $0 \le t \le 8$.

\exfigure{1342_q18_1}

figures.cap: velocity-time graph of three line segments through (0,-5),(2,0),(3,4),(8,0)

parts.latex: Determine the total distance covered by the particle during the 8 seconds.
What is the particle's position relative to its starting position when $t = 8$ seconds?

solutions.latex:
Distance is the total area between the graph and the $t$-axis.
$$\begin{aligned} d &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times2\times5+\dfrac{1}{2}\times4\times6 \\ &= 5+12 \\ &= 17 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds one correct area, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Displacement is the signed area, with the part below the axis negative.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Displacement} &= -5+12 \\ &= 7 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$
The particle is $7$ m to the right of its starting position.

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

Tick labels 4 to -5 sit left of the axis and 1 to 8 sit below it, as in the crop (rule 24). The t-axis is drawn level; the scan tilts down about 15 px to the right (rule 1 'draw level'). Low scores come from this tilt correction and the scan's bold, heavy glyphs/strokes; placement matches.

parts.latex:
The rate of 'flu infection' in a population of a city is proportional to the number of infected individuals. That is the number of infected people $F$ after $t$ weeks is modelled by the equation $F = F_0 e^{kt}$

where $F_0$ and $k$ are constants. It is known that after 3 weeks, there is twice the number of infections to begin with. If there were 1000 cases of flu infection originally, how many are there after 7 weeks? Express your answer correct to three significant figures.

solutions.latex:
When $t=3$, $F=2F_0$ and $F_0=1000$:
$$\begin{aligned} 2000&=1000e^{3k} \\ 2&=e^{3k} \\ k&=\dfrac{\ln2}{3} \end{aligned}$$
When $t=7$:
$$\begin{aligned} F&=1000e^{\frac{7\ln2}{3}} \\ &=5039.68\ldots \\ &\approx5040 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about 5040 cases after 7 weeks}$$
criteria: Finds $k$ and substitutes $t=7$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source printed answer was about 5000, but 5039.68 to 3 significant figures is 5040; corrected to 5040 (source note said the same).

3666.stem:
A prototype rocket which is initially at rest, takes off from a launchpad on the ground.

It has a time of flight of $T$ seconds, and $t$ is the time in seconds, where $0 \le t \le T$.

The velocity of the rocket, $v\ \text{ms}^{-1}$, is given by:

$$v(t) = 0.5e^{t}\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)$$

parts.latex: Shortly after the rocket takes off, the engine stops and it begins to descend towards the ground. Find the time at which the rocket begins to descend.
Before the rocket starts to descend it reaches its maximum velocity. Find the time it takes for the rocket to achieve its maximum velocity. Give your answer correct to two decimal places.

solutions.latex:
The rocket begins to descend when $v=0$.
$$0=0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)$$
Since $0.5e^t\neq0$, we need $\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=0$.

So $\dfrac{\pi t}{10}=0,\pi,2\pi,\ldots$ and $\dfrac{t}{10}=0,1,2,\ldots$

The first positive solution is $t=10$.
$$\therefore\ t=10 \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Sets $v=0$ and notes $0.5e^t$ is never $0$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uw)=u'w+uw'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=0.5e^t & w&=\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\\ u'&=0.5e^t & w'&=\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dv}{dt}&=0.5e^t\cdot\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)+0.5e^t\sin\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right) \\ &=0.5e^t\left(\dfrac{\pi}{10}\cos\dfrac{\pi t}{10}+\sin\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Setting $\dfrac{dv}{dt}=0$ (as $0.5e^t\neq0$):
$$\tan\left(\dfrac{\pi t}{10}\right)=-\dfrac{\pi}{10}$$
For $0<t<10$, $\dfrac{\pi t}{10}$ lies between $0$ and $\pi$, so $\dfrac{\pi t}{10}=2.837\ldots$
$$\begin{aligned} t&=2.837\ldots\times\dfrac{10}{\pi} \\ &\approx9.03 \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Obtains the tan equation, or equivalent merit
Differentiates and sets the derivative to zero, or equivalent merit

meta.marker_note: No carry-on errors accepted for the final mark.
meta.format_note: Maximum not tested in source; kept as is.

figures.cap: velocity-time graph for t from 0 to 6

solutions.latex:
Speed decreases when $v$ and the acceleration have opposite signs.
$$\begin{aligned} 1<t<2:&\ v>0,\ v \text{ decreasing} \\ 4<t<6:&\ v<0,\ v \text{ increasing} \end{aligned}$$
So the speed is decreasing for $1<t<2$ and $4<t<6$, which matches option B.

1343_q10_1.notes: Velocity-time sketch drawn with sine-shaped quarter/half pieces fitted to the crop's points: max at t=1, zeros at 2 and 6, min at 4. The tick spacing is the crop's own, which is not to scale (rule 1). Curve 0.9pt because it touches the axis (rule 9); filled arrowheads (rule 4). Rule 11: the curve passes through the ticks at 2 and 6, so the '2' label moved below-left and the '6' label below-right. Both stay below the axis (rule 24). Most of the remaining overlay colour comes from these moved labels and the thicker curve.

options.label: A
options.latex: At $t=2$, the particle is to the left of the origin, and travelling towards the origin.

options.label: B
options.latex: At $t=5$, the particle is at the origin, and at rest.

options.label: C
options.latex: At $t=10$, the particle is to the right of the origin, and at rest.

options.label: D
options.latex: At $t=15$, the particle is at the origin, and travelling from left to right.

figures.cap: velocity-time graph of a particle for 0 to 16 seconds

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the gradient of the displacement graph, and displacement is the signed area between the velocity graph and the $t$-axis. The particle is at rest when $v=0$.

From the graph:
$$\begin{aligned} v&<0 &&\text{for } 0\le t<2 &&\text{moving left}\\ v&>0 &&\text{for } 2<t<10 &&\text{moving right}\\ v&<0 &&\text{for } 10<t<16 &&\text{moving left} \end{aligned}$$
Option A: at $t=2$, $v=0$, so the particle is at rest, not travelling towards the origin. False.

Option B: at $t=5$, $v$ is at its maximum and positive, so the particle is moving, not at rest. False.

Option D: at $t=15$, $v<0$, so the particle is travelling from right to left. False.

Option C: at $t=10$, $v=0$, so the particle is at rest. The positive area for $2<t<10$ is much larger than the negative area for $0<t<2$, so the displacement at $t=10$ is positive and the particle is to the right of the origin. True.

The answer is option C.

Minor ticks every unit, longer ticks at 5, 10 and 15. The label 15 sat on the curve in the crop, so it is moved to the mirror position above the axis (21 Nov rule, rule 11); 5 and 10 stay below. Filled arrowheads (rule 4), curve at 0.9pt (rule 9), v and t in italic (rule 19).

3751.stem:
A particle moves along a straight line so that its displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point $O$ is given by

$$x=12\ln(t+2)-2t+5$$

where $t$ is measured in seconds.

parts.latex: What is the inititial position of the particle? Give your answer in exact form.
Find an expression for the velocity of the particle at time $t$.
Find when the particle comes to rest.
What happened to the acceleration eventually?

solutions.latex:
Initially $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} x&=12\ln 2-0+5\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=12\ln 2+5 \text{ m}$$

meta.source_flag: Source answer printed $x=\ln 2+5$, but substituting $t=0$ into $x=12\ln(t+2)-2t+5$ gives $12\ln 2+5$; the line here is corrected to follow the given equation.

solutions.latex: $$\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac{12}{t+2}-2$$

At rest, $v=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{12}{t+2}&=2\\ 6&=t+2\\ t&=4\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is at rest after 4 seconds}$$

$$\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}=-\dfrac{12}{(t+2)^2}$$
As $t\to\infty$, $(t+2)^2\to\infty$, so
$$\dfrac{d^2x}{dt^2}\to 0$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the acceleration tends to } 0$$

3767.stem: A particle is moving in a horizontal straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres to the right of a fixed point O on the line given by $x=t(t-3)^2$ where velocity $v$ is in $\text{ms}^{-1}$ and acceleration $\ddot{x}$ is in $\text{ms}^{-2}$.

parts.latex: Show that $v=3(t-1)(t-3)$ and $\ddot{x}=6(t-2)$
Find when the particle is moving towards O.
can_use: Particles at rest and changing direction

parts.latex: Find when the particle is moving towards O and slowing down.
How far has the particle travelled in the first 4 seconds?

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $x=t(t-3)^2$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=t & v&=(t-3)^2\\ u'&=1 & v'&=2(t-3)\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}&=(t-3)^2+2t(t-3) \\ &=(t-3)(t-3+2t) \\ &=(t-3)(3t-3) \\ &=3(t-1)(t-3) \end{aligned}$$
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity, again by the product rule with $u=t-1$, $v=t-3$.
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x}&=3\big((t-1)\cdot 1+(t-3)\cdot 1\big) \\ &=3(2t-4) \\ &=6(t-2) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct use of the product rule, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $x=t(t-3)^2\ge 0$ for $t\ge 0$, the particle is never left of O, so it moves towards O when $v<0$.
$$3(t-1)(t-3)<0$$
This parabola opens upward, so it is negative between the roots.
$$\therefore\ 1<t<3$$

The particle slows down when $v$ and $\ddot{x}$ have opposite signs. Moving towards O means $v<0$, so we need $\ddot{x}>0$.
$$6(t-2)>0$$
Hence $t>2$.

From part (b), $v<0$ for $1<t<3$.

Therefore both conditions hold when
$$2<t<3$$

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: none needed for this part (sketch_id 1036_q14_s1 not used). Reasoning for $v<0$ taken from part (b) as $1<t<3$ since $v=3(t-1)(t-3)$.

solutions.latex:
The particle may change direction where $v=0$, so find the positions at the endpoints and turning points.
$$\begin{aligned} t=0:&\quad x=0\\ t=4:&\quad x=4 \end{aligned}$$
From $v=3(t-1)(t-3)=0$, the particle is at rest at $t=1$ and $t=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} t=1:&\quad x=4\\ t=3:&\quad x=0 \end{aligned}$$
The particle goes from $0$ to $4$, back to $0$, then to $4$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 4+4+4\\ &= 12 \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the positions at the turning points and endpoints, or equivalent merit

3804.stem: An item is purchased for \$20 000. It appreciates in value so that after $t$ years its value $\$V$ is given by the formula $V=20000p^t$ for some constant $p>1$. After 9 years its value is \$32 000.

parts.latex: Find the value of $p$ correct to 4 decimal places.
Find correct to the nearest \$10 per year the rate at which the item is appreciating in value after 9 years.

solutions.latex:
Substitute $t=9$, $V=32000$ into $V=20000p^t$.
$$\begin{aligned} 32000 &= 20000p^9 \\ p^9 &= \dfrac{8}{5} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ p=(1.6)^{\frac{1}{9}}\approx 1.0536$$
criteria: Writes and simplifies a numerical expression for $p^9$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiate $V=20000p^t$ with respect to $t$.
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=20000\ln p\cdot p^t$$
At $t=9$, $\ln p=\dfrac{1}{9}\ln 1.6$ and $p^9=\dfrac{8}{5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dV}{dt} &= 20000\left(\dfrac{1}{9}\ln 1.6\right)\times\dfrac{8}{5} \\ &\approx 1670 \end{aligned}$$
The item is appreciating at \$1670 per year (nearest \$10 per year).
criteria: Differentiates with respect to $t$, or equivalent merit

3807.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line and velocity $v=3\sqrt{t+1}-9$ metres per second. Initially the particle is at $O$.

parts.latex: Use integration to show that $x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$.
Find when and where the particle is at rest.
Find the distance travelled by the particle in the first 24 seconds of its motion.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the velocity.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dx}{dt} &= 3(t+1)^{\frac{1}{2}}-9 \\ x &= 2(t+1)^{\frac{3}{2}}-9t+c \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$, so $0=2+c$ and $c=-2$.
$$\therefore\ x=2(t+1)\sqrt{t+1}-9t-2$$
criteria: Integrates with respect to $t$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
At rest, $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sqrt{t+1}-9 &= 0 \\ \sqrt{t+1} &= 3 \\ t &= 8 \end{aligned}$$
When $t=8$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 2(9)(3)-72-2 \\ &= -20 \end{aligned}$$
At $t=0$, $v=-3$, so the particle initially moves in the negative direction.

The particle is at rest at $t=8$ seconds, when it is 20 m from $O$ in its initial direction of travel.

When $t=24$, $x=32$.

The particle moves from $x=0$ to $x=-20$ (at rest at $t=8$), then to $x=32$ by $t=24$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= 20+(20+32) \\ &= 72 \text{ m} \end{aligned}$$

figures.cap: graph of x = ln(t^2+6) starting at ln(6)

parts.latex:
A particle moves on the $x$-axis so that it’s displacement in metres from the origin at a time $t$ seconds is given by the equation $x=\ln(t^2+6)$.

The particle starts from rest at the point $x=\ln(6)$ and accelerates in a positive direction as shown in the distance-time graph below.

\exfigure{1547_q15_1}

Determine when the acceleration of the particle becomes zero and find the velocity at this time.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate the displacement to find the velocity.
$$\dot{x}=\dfrac{2t}{t^2+6}$$
Differentiate using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=2t & v&=t^2+6\\ u'&=2 & v'&=2t \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \ddot{x}&=\dfrac{2(t^2+6)-2t\cdot 2t}{(t^2+6)^2}\\ &=\dfrac{12-2t^2}{(t^2+6)^2} \end{aligned}$$
The acceleration is zero when $12-2t^2=0$, so $t^2=6$.

Since $t\ge 0$, $t=\sqrt{6}$.

The velocity at this time is
$$\begin{aligned} v&=\dfrac{2\sqrt{6}}{(\sqrt{6})^2+6}\\ &=\dfrac{2\sqrt{6}}{12}\\ &=\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{6} \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\sqrt{6}\text{ s and } v=\dfrac{\sqrt{6}}{6}\text{ m/s}$$
criteria: Correct equations for $\dot{x}$ and $\ddot{x}$, or equivalent merit
Correct equation for $\dot{x}$, or equivalent merit

1547_q15_1.notes: Curve x=ln(t^2+6) plotted from the equation (smooth, 90 samples, 0.9pt because it starts on the x-axis), fitted to the crop: ln6 at the crop height and an arrowhead at t of about 7.3. The vertical axis has arrows at both ends; the t-axis has an arrow on the right only, as in the crop. The ln(6) label sits left of the axis. The equation label sits above the curve with a gap and uses \left( \right) brackets. Rules 1,3a,4,9,10,11.

3861.stem:
A particle moves such that its velocity at a given time is given by:

$\dot{x} = 8 - 16\sin t$

parts.latex: What is the initial acceleration of the particle?
When is the particle first at rest?
Given that the particle is initially at the origin, find an equation for the displacement ($x$), at a time $t$.
Find the distance travelled between the first two times when the particle is at rest.

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
$$\dot{x} = 8 - 16\sin t$$
$$\ddot{x} = -16\cos t$$
Initially $t = 0$:
$$\ddot{x} = -16\cos 0 = -16$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Initially the acceleration is } 16 \text{ m/s}^2 \text{ towards the left}$$

The particle is at rest when the velocity is zero.
$$\begin{aligned} 8 - 16\sin t &= 0 \\ 16\sin t &= 8 \\ \sin t &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ t &= \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \dfrac{5\pi}{6}, \ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{The particle is first at rest after } \dfrac{\pi}{6} \text{ seconds}$$

Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$x = \displaystyle\int (8 - 16\sin t)\,dt = 8t + 16\cos t + C$$
When $t = 0$, $x = 0$ (initially at the origin):
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= 8 \times 0 + 16\cos 0 + C \\ C &= -16 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x = 8t + 16\cos t - 16$$

The particle is at rest at $t=\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ and $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{6}$, so find the displacement at each time using the result of part (c).
$$\begin{aligned} x\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) &= 8\times\dfrac{\pi}{6}+16\cos\dfrac{\pi}{6}-16 \\ &= \dfrac{4\pi}{3}+8\sqrt{3}-16 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} x\left(\dfrac{5\pi}{6}\right) &= 8\times\dfrac{5\pi}{6}+16\cos\dfrac{5\pi}{6}-16 \\ &= \dfrac{20\pi}{3}-8\sqrt{3}-16 \end{aligned}$$
The velocity is not zero between these times, so the distance is the size of the change in displacement.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Distance} &= \left|\left(\dfrac{20\pi}{3}-8\sqrt{3}-16\right)-\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{3}+8\sqrt{3}-16\right)\right| \\ &= \left|\dfrac{16\pi}{3}-16\sqrt{3}\right| \\ &= 16\sqrt{3}-\dfrac{16\pi}{3} \ (\approx 10.96) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes some progress, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Sketch still to draw: none required; \exfigure not added since reasoning does not need a sketch. The source has a sketch_id 1302_q16_s1 but the solution does not rely on it.
meta.corrected: Corrected from source: the distance was given as $\dfrac{16\pi}{3}-16\sqrt3\approx-10.96$, a negative number; it is $16\sqrt3-\dfrac{16\pi}{3}$.
meta.overwritten_from_source: Corrected from source: the distance was given as $\dfrac{16\pi}{3}-16\sqrt3\approx-10.96$, a negative number; it is $16\sqrt3-\dfrac{16\pi}{3}$.

3875.stem:
The concentration of a pesticide in the soil is modelled by the equation given by:

$P = P_0e^{-kt}$

where $P_0$ and $k$ are constants, and $t$ is the number of days after the application of the pesticide.

parts.latex: Once in the soil, the half-life of the pesticide is the time taken for its concentration to be reduced to one half of its initial value. If the half-life of the pesticide is 25 days, find the value of $k$. Answer correct to 2 significant figures.
What is the percentage decrease in concentration of the pesticide after 80 days? Answer to the nearest whole number.

criteria: Uses the exponential decay formula with one correct value, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
With $k=0.028$ and $t=80$:
$$\begin{aligned} P &= P_0e^{-0.028\times 80} \\ &= 0.1064\ldots P_0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage decrease} &= 1-0.1064\ldots \\ &= 0.8936\ldots \\ &\approx 89\% \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Shows some understanding, or equivalent merit

figures.cap: velocity-time graph with zeros at t=0, 6, 10, 18

solutions.latex:
Displacement is a maximum when $v$ changes from positive to negative, that is when the particle turns round.

From the graph this happens at $t=10$.

Hence the answer is option B.

3966.stem: The displacement of an object measured in metres after $t$ seconds is given by $x = e^{t^2} - 2t^2$.

parts.latex: Given that the velocity is the rate of change of the displacement, find an expression for the velocity.
Find the two times when the object is stationary.
Find an expression for the acceleration of the object.

solutions.latex:
Velocity is the derivative of displacement.

$$v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=\dfrac{d}{dt}\left(e^{t^2}-2t^2\right)$$

$$v=2te^{t^2}-4t$$
criteria: Differentiates one term correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The object is stationary when $v=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} 2te^{t^2}-4t&=0 \\ 2t\left(e^{t^2}-2\right)&=0 \end{aligned}$$

So $t=0$ or $e^{t^2}=2$.

$$\begin{aligned} e^{t^2}&=2 \\ t^2&=\ln2 \\ t&=\pm\sqrt{\ln2} \end{aligned}$$

Time cannot be negative, so $t\ge0$ and $t=-\sqrt{\ln2}$ is rejected.

$$\therefore\ t=0 \text{ s or } t=\sqrt{\ln2} \text{ s}$$
criteria: Solves one factor and finds both candidate times, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Acceleration is $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$. Differentiate $2te^{t^2}$ using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dt}(uw)=u'w+uw'$, with

$$\begin{aligned} u&=2t & w&=e^{t^2} \\ u'&=2 & w'&=2te^{t^2} \end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned} a&=2e^{t^2}+2t\times2te^{t^2}-4 \\ &=2e^{t^2}+4t^2e^{t^2}-4 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Applies the product rule, or equivalent merit

3968.stem: The population of an ant colony is modelled by the equation $P = 1000e^{kt}$, where $t$ is measured in weeks.

parts.latex: Find the initial population.

After 10 weeks the population is 25 000.

Show that $k = 0.3219$, correct to 4 decimal places.
During which week will the population exceed 80 000 for the first time?

solutions.latex:
The initial population is at $t=0$.

$$\begin{aligned} P&=1000e^{0} \\ &=1000 \end{aligned}$$

Solve $P=80000$ using $k=0.3219$.

$$\begin{aligned} 80000&=1000e^{0.3219t} \\ 80&=e^{0.3219t} \\ 0.3219t&=\ln80 \\ t&=\dfrac{\ln80}{0.3219} \\ &\approx13.613 \end{aligned}$$

The population passes 80 000 after 13.613 weeks, which is during the 14th week.

$$\therefore\ \text{14th week}$$

3971.stem: A block of ice in the form of a cube melts in such a way that the block remains cubic. After a time $t$ hours the volume of the block is $V\ \text{m}^3$. Initially the cube has edge length of 4 metres and after 9 hours the cube has edge length of 1 metre.

parts.latex: If the rate of change of volume, $R\ \text{m}^3$ per hour, is given by $R = -k$ for some constant $k > 0$, show that $V = 64 - 7t$.
Find when the cube has edge length 2 metres.

solutions.latex:
The rate of change of volume is constant.

$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-k$$

Integrating gives

$$V=-kt+c$$

Initially the edge is $4$ m, so when $t=0$, $V=4^3=64$.

$$V=64-kt$$

After 9 hours the edge is $1$ m, so $V=1$ when $t=9$.

$$\begin{aligned} 1&=64-9k \\ 9k&=63 \\ k&=7 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ V=64-7t$$
criteria: Finds $V=64-kt$ and uses $t=9$, $V=1$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source's alternative (constant rate $k=\dfrac{64-1}{9}=7$) omitted as equivalent.

solutions.latex:
An edge length of 2 m gives volume $2^3=8 \text{ m}^3$.

$$\begin{aligned} 8&=64-7t \\ 7t&=56 \\ t&=8 \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore\ \text{the edge length is 2 m after 8 hours}$$

parts.latex: A particle is moving is moving with velocity $v=t^2-10t+21,\ t\ge 0$. The particle is stationary when:

solutions.latex:
The particle is stationary when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} t^2-10t+21 &= 0 \\ (t-3)(t-7) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $t=3$ or $t=7$, and both satisfy $t\ge 0$. Hence the answer is option C.

4046.stem: A drug is used to control a medical condition. It is known that the quantity $Q$ milligrams of drug remaining in the body after $t$ hours satisfies an equation of the form $Q=Q_0e^{kt}$ where $Q_0$ and $k$ are constants. The initial dose is 6 milligrams and after 15 hours the amount remaining in the body is half the initial dose.

parts.latex: Find the values of $Q_0$ and $k$.
After how long will one-eighth of the initial dose remain?

solutions.latex:
When $t=0$, $Q=Q_0$, so $Q_0=6$.

After 15 hours the amount is half the initial dose, so $Q=3$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3 &= 6e^{15k} \\ \dfrac{1}{2} &= e^{15k} \\ 15k &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$k = \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}{15}$$

One-eighth of the initial dose is $\dfrac{6}{8}=\dfrac{3}{4}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{3}{4} &= 6e^{kt} \\ \dfrac{1}{8} &= e^{kt} \\ kt &= \ln\left(\dfrac{1}{8}\right) \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $k$ from part (a).
$$t = \dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{1}{8}\right)}{\ln\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)\div 15} = 45 \text{ hours}$$
criteria: Sets up equation for one-eighth of the dose, or equivalent merit

4056.stem: The acceleration of a particle is given by $\ddot{x}=4\cos 2t$, where $x$ is displacement in metres and $t$ is time in seconds. Initially the particle is at the origin with a velocity of 1 ms$^{-1}$.

parts.latex: Show that the velocity of the particle is given by $\dot{x}=2\sin 2t+1$
Find the time when the particle first comes to rest.
Find the displacement, $x$, of the particle in terms of $t$.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration.
$$\dot{x}=\displaystyle\int 4\cos 2t\,dt=2\sin 2t+C$$
When $t=0$, $\dot{x}=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} 1 &= 2\sin 0+C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \dot{x}=2\sin 2t+1$$

The particle is at rest when $\dot{x}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\sin 2t+1 &= 0 \\ \sin 2t &= -\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
The first time $2t>0$ with $\sin 2t=-\dfrac{1}{2}$ is in the third quadrant.
$$\begin{aligned} 2t &= \dfrac{7\pi}{6} \\ t &= \dfrac{7\pi}{12} \text{ seconds} \end{aligned}$$

Integrate the velocity.
$$x=\displaystyle\int(2\sin 2t+1)\,dt=-\cos 2t+t+C$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= -\cos 0+C \\ C &= 1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=-\cos 2t+t+1$$
